stepByStep.text: The supplement is 90° more than the complement, because 180° is 90° more than 90°.
The supplement is 3 times the complement, so the extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
The complement is 45°, so find the angle.
Check: the supplement is 135°, which is 3 times 45°. The angle is 45°.

misconceptions.A: For 60° the supplement is 120° and the complement is 30°. That is 4 times, not 3 times.
misconceptions.B: For 30° the supplement is 150° and the complement is 60°. That is less than 3 times.
misconceptions.C: 135° is the supplement of the angle we want. An angle bigger than 90° has no complement at all.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The supplement of 45° is 135° and its complement is 45°, and 135 = 3 × 45.

G4A_ANGLES_009.questionText: Two straight lines cross each other. One of the angles formed is 4 times the angle beside it. What is the largest angle formed?
hints: When two straight lines cross, two angles that are beside each other lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.
Think of the smaller angle as 1 part and the angle beside it as 4 parts. Together the 5 parts make 180°.
A similar one: if one angle is twice the angle beside it, then 3 parts make 180°. One part is 60°, so the angles are 60° and 120°, and the largest is 120°.

stepByStep.text: Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.
The angles are 1 part and 4 parts, which is 5 parts in all.
The larger angle is 4 parts.
The largest angle formed is 144°.

misconceptions.A: 36° is the smaller angle. The angle beside it is 4 times as big.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 36° and 144° lie on a straight line and add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: 72° shares the whole turn of 360° into 5 parts. The two angles beside each other share 180°.
misconceptions.D: 288° uses 360° for the two angles. Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.

G4A_ANGLES_010.questionText: Five angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn around it. One of them is 80° and the other four are equal. How big is each of the four equal angles?
hints: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360°. Take away the angle you know, then share the rest.
Take 80° away from 360°. What is left is shared equally among the four equal angles.
A similar one: four angles fill the turn around a point. One is 60° and the other three are equal. They share 360° − 60° = 300°, so each is 100°.

stepByStep.text: Angles around a point add up to 360°. Take away the known angle.
Share the rest equally among the four angles.
Each of the four equal angles is 70°.

misconceptions.A: 25° uses 180° as the total. Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°.
misconceptions.B: 56° shares 280° among five angles. Only four angles are equal, and the 80° angle has been taken out already.
misconceptions.D: 280° is the four equal angles together. Share it among the four.

G4A_ANGLES_011.questionText: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 2:40?
hints: At 2:40 the hour hand is not pointing exactly at the 2. It has been moving all the time since 2 o'clock.
The minute hand is on the 8. The hour hand moves 30° in a whole hour, so work out how far it moves in 40 minutes, which is two thirds of an hour.

Similar problem: at 4:20 the minute hand is on the 4, which is 120° from the 12. The hour hand has moved one third of 30°, which is 10°, past the 4, so it is 130° from the 12. The angle between the hands is 130 - 120 = 10°.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand is on the 8. Each number on the clock is 30° from the next.
The hour hand moves 30° in 60 minutes, so in 40 minutes it moves 20°.
So the hour hand is 20° past the 2.
Subtract to find the angle between the hands.
So the smaller angle between the hands is 160°.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The minute hand is at 240° and the hour hand at 80°, so the angle is 160°.
misconceptions.B: This keeps the hour hand exactly on the 2. By 2:40 it has moved two thirds of the way towards the 3.
misconceptions.C: This is the angle measured the long way round. The question asks for the smaller angle.
misconceptions.D: The hour hand moves 30° in an hour, so in 40 minutes it moves 20°, not 10°. Try once more.

G4A_ANGLES_012.questionText: From 2:10 to 2:50 on the same afternoon, both hands of a clock keep turning. How many more degrees does the minute hand turn than the hour hand in this time?
hints: Both hands move during this time, one fast and one slowly. Find how far each one turns, then compare.
From 2:10 to 2:50 is 40 minutes. The minute hand turns 6° every minute. The hour hand turns 30° in a whole hour.
Similar problem: from 5:00 to 5:30. The minute hand turns half a full turn, 180°. The hour hand turns half of 30°, which is 15°. The minute hand turns 180 - 15 = 165° more.

stepByStep.text: Find the time that passes.
The minute hand turns 6° each minute.
The hour hand turns 30° in 60 minutes, so 1° every 2 minutes.
Find how much more the minute hand turns.
So the minute hand turns 220° more than the hour hand.

misconceptions.A: This is how far the minute hand turns. The hour hand has also turned a little in 40 minutes. Take its turn away.
misconceptions.B: This adds the two turns. 'How many more' asks for the difference between them.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The minute hand turns 240°, the hour hand 20°, and 240 - 20 = 220.
misconceptions.D: This is how far the hour hand turns. Compare it with the turn of the minute hand.

G4A_ANGLES_013.questionText: At 12 noon the hour hand of a clock points straight up at the 12. Later the same afternoon, the hour hand has turned through exactly 75° from that position. What time is it?
hints: Work backwards from the angle. Think about how many degrees the hour hand turns in one hour, and be careful when you change a part of an hour into minutes.
The hour hand turns 30° every hour. Find how many 30s there are in 75, and what is left over.
Similar problem: the hour hand has turned 105° since noon. Three hours take 90°, and 15° are left. Since 15° is half of 30°, that is half an hour, or 30 minutes. The time is 3:30 pm.

stepByStep.text: The hour hand turns 30° in one hour.
Two hours take 60° of the turn. Find what is left.
15° is half of 30°, so it takes half an hour.
So 2 hours and 30 minutes have passed since noon.
So the time is 2:30 pm.

misconceptions.A: 75 ÷ 30 is 2 and a half hours. Half an hour is 30 minutes, not 50 minutes.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Two hours use 60°, the last 15° is half an hour, so it is 2:30 pm.
misconceptions.C: This treats 75° as 75 minutes. The hour hand is slow: it turns only 30° in a whole hour.
misconceptions.D: Two full hours use 60°. The remaining 15° is half of an hour's turn, which is much more than 5 minutes.

G4A_ANGLES_014.questionText: At 12:20, Sana says: "The minute hand is on the 4 and the hour hand is on the 12, so the angle between the hands is 120°." By how many degrees is Sana's answer different from the true angle between the hands?
hints: Check each part of what Sana says. Is each hand exactly where she says it is at 12:20?
The minute hand is exactly on the 4. Now think about the hour hand: 20 minutes is one third of an hour, and the hour hand moves 30° in an hour.
Similar problem: at 12:30 someone says the angle is 180°. But the hour hand has moved half of 30°, which is 15°, past the 12. The true angle is 180 - 15 = 165°, so that answer is 15° too big.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand is on the 4, so it is 120° from the 12.
In 20 minutes the hour hand has moved one third of 30° past the 12.
The true angle between the hands is smaller than Sana's.
Compare Sana's answer with the true angle.
So Sana's answer is different from the true angle by 10°.

misconceptions.A: Wonderful! The hour hand has crept 10° past the 12, so the true angle is 110° and Sana is 10° out.
misconceptions.B: Sana's idea sounds right, but the hour hand does not stay on the 12. In 20 minutes it moves a little towards the 1.
misconceptions.C: The hour hand moves 30° in a whole hour. In 20 minutes it moves one third of that.
misconceptions.D: 110° is the true angle between the hands. The question asks how far Sana's answer is from it.

G4A_ANGLES_015.questionText: Farhan is facing North-East. He turns 90° clockwise, then 225° anticlockwise, and then 135° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: Follow the turns one at a time and keep track of the direction after each turn. Watch which way each turn goes.
The eight compass directions are 45° apart. A turn of 90° clockwise from North-East moves two directions on: find where that is first.

Similar problem: Asha faces North, turns 90° clockwise and then 135° anticlockwise. After the first turn she faces East. Going back 135° is three steps of 45°: North-East, North, North-West. She faces North-West.

stepByStep.text: From North-East, a 90° clockwise turn moves two steps of 45°: he faces South-East.
225° is five steps of 45°.
Five steps anticlockwise from South-East go East, North-East, North, North-West, West: he faces West.
135° is three steps of 45°.
Three steps clockwise from West go North-West, North, North-East.
So Farhan is facing North-East, the direction he started in.

misconceptions.A: This takes all three turns clockwise. The middle turn of 225° goes anticlockwise, the other way.
misconceptions.B: West is where he faces after the second turn. There is still a 135° clockwise turn to make.
misconceptions.C: Check the first two turns: the 90° turn is clockwise and the 225° turn is anticlockwise, not the other way round.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The turns take him to South-East, then West, then back to North-East.

G4A_ANGLES_016.questionText: Ravi turns 135° clockwise and then 90° anticlockwise. Now he is facing South. Which direction was he facing before he turned?
hints: You know where Ravi ends, not where he starts. To go back in time, undo each turn by turning the opposite way.
Start from South. The last thing Ravi did was turn 90° anticlockwise, so undo it first by turning 90° clockwise.
Similar problem: after turning 90° clockwise, Asha faces West. To undo this, turn 90° anticlockwise from West, which gives South. So Asha was facing South at the start.

stepByStep.text: Start from where Ravi ends: South.
Undo the last turn. It was 90° anticlockwise, so turn 90° clockwise from South: West.
Undo the first turn. It was 135° clockwise, so turn 135° anticlockwise from West: South-West, South, South-East.
Check forwards: from South-East, 135° clockwise is West, and then 90° anticlockwise is South.
So Ravi was facing South-East before he turned.

misconceptions.A: This makes the two turns again, starting from South. South is where Ravi ends, so the turns must be undone instead.
misconceptions.B: Yes! From South-East, 135° clockwise reaches West, and 90° anticlockwise from West reaches South.
misconceptions.C: West is where Ravi was facing between the two turns. Undo the first turn as well.
misconceptions.D: Each turn must be undone in the opposite direction. Check: starting from North-West, where would the two turns take him?

G4A_ANGLES_017.questionText: A toy robot is facing North. Each time Kavya presses a button, the robot turns 45° clockwise. Which direction is the robot facing after Kavya has pressed the button 13 times?
hints: The robot keeps going round and round. Look for the number of presses that brings it back to where it started.
A full turn is 360°. Find how many presses of 45° make a full turn, and then how many presses are left over after that.

Similar problem: a robot facing North turns 90° clockwise at each press. Four presses make a full turn. After 10 presses, 8 presses make two full turns and 2 are left, so it faces East and then South. It ends facing South.

stepByStep.text: Find how many presses make one full turn.
After 8 presses the robot is facing North again.
Find how many presses are left.
Five more presses from North go North-East, East, South-East, South, South-West.
So the robot is facing South-West.

misconceptions.A: So close! After the first press the robot already faces North-East. North is where it starts, before any press.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! Eight presses bring it back to North, and five more take it to South-West.
misconceptions.C: This is one press too many. Count again: 8 presses for the full turn, then 5 more.
misconceptions.D: This is where the robot faces after 1 press. A full turn takes 8 presses, not 12, so 5 presses are left over.

G4A_ANGLES_018.questionText: Three angles meet at a point and together fill the whole turn around the point, with no gaps and no overlaps. The second angle is twice the first, and the third angle is three times the first. What kind of angle is the largest of the three?
hints: First decide what the three angles add up to. Read carefully: do they lie on a straight line, inside a triangle, or all the way round a point?
Call the first angle one part. Then the three angles are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts. Find how many parts there are in the whole turn.

Similar problem: two angles fill the whole turn around a point, and one is 3 times the other. There are 4 parts in 360°, so one part is 90°. The angles are 90° and 270°, and the larger one is a reflex angle.

stepByStep.text: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360°.
The angles are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts, which is 6 parts.
The largest angle is 3 parts.
An angle of 180° makes a straight line.
So the largest angle is a straight angle.

misconceptions.A: This comes from a total of 180°. These angles go all the way round the point, so they add up to 360°.
misconceptions.B: The second angle, 120°, is obtuse. The question asks about the largest of the three.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! The angles are 60°, 120° and 180°, and 180° is a straight angle.
misconceptions.D: A reflex angle is more than 180°. Work out the largest angle exactly: is it more than 180°?

G4A_ANGLES_019.questionText: Two straight lines cross each other and make four angles around the crossing point. Three of these angles add up to 250°. What is the size of the smallest of the four angles?
hints: The four angles go all the way round the point. Find the angle that was left out, then use what you know about the angles made when two straight lines cross.
Take 250° away from the whole turn to find the fourth angle. The angle beside it lies with it on a straight line.
Similar problem: three of the four angles add up to 300°. The fourth is 360 - 300 = 60°. The angle beside it is 180 - 60 = 120°. The four angles are 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°, so the largest is 120°.

stepByStep.text: The four angles add up to a whole turn, so find the fourth angle.
The angle beside it makes a straight line with it.
Angles opposite each other are equal, so the four angles are 110°, 70°, 110° and 70°.
Check the three that were added.
So the smallest of the four angles is 70°.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The four angles are 110°, 70°, 110° and 70°, so the smallest is 70°.
misconceptions.B: 110° is the fourth angle, the one left out of the total. Now find the angle beside it on the straight line.
misconceptions.C: This halves the fourth angle. The angle beside 110° on a straight line is what is left from 180°.
misconceptions.D: This halves 70°. The angles around the crossing point come in two equal pairs, 110° and 70°.

G4A_ANGLES_020.questionText: An angle is 30° more than its complement. What is the supplement of this angle?
hints: There are two different ideas here, complement and supplement. Find the angle first using its complement, and then answer what is asked.
The angle and its complement add up to 90°, and the angle is 30° bigger. Take the extra 30° away from 90° and share what is left equally.
Similar problem: an angle is 10° more than its complement. Taking 10 from 90 leaves 80, so the complement is 40° and the angle is 50°. The supplement of the angle is 180 - 50 = 130°.

stepByStep.text: The angle and its complement add up to 90°. Take away the extra 30° and halve.
The complement is 30°, so the angle is 30° more.
The supplement is what the angle needs to make 180°.
So the supplement of the angle is 120°.

misconceptions.A: 60° is the angle itself. The question asks for its supplement, the angle that goes with it to make 180°.
misconceptions.B: 30° is the complement of the angle. Find the angle, and then find its supplement.
misconceptions.C: This is the supplement of 30°, which is the complement. Use the angle itself, which is 60°.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! The angle is 60°, and 180 - 60 = 120.

G4A_ANGLES_021.questionText: Angle P and angle Q are complementary, so they add up to 90°. Angle Q and angle R are supplementary, so they add up to 180°. Which of these is true whatever the size of angle P?

options.text: Angle R is equal to angle P
Angle P and angle R are supplementary
Angle R is 90° more than angle P
Angle R is twice angle Q

hints: No sizes are given, so the statement must hold for every possible angle P. Try one size for angle P, and then try a different size to make sure.
Let angle P be 20°. Find angle Q from the first clue and angle R from the second clue. Then do the same again with angle P as 40°.

Similar problem: angle X and angle Y add up to 180°, and angle Y and angle Z also add up to 180°. If X is 50°, Y is 130° and Z is 50°. If X is 70°, Y is 110° and Z is 70°. Whatever X is, Z is equal to X.

stepByStep.text: Try angle P = 20°. Then angle Q is 70° and angle R is 110°.
Try angle P = 40°. Then angle Q is 50° and angle R is 130°.
Both times angle R is 90° more than angle P.
This always happens: going from 90° to 180° adds 90° to the total, and angle Q is the same in both.
So angle R is 90° more than angle P.

misconceptions.A: Try angle P = 20°: angle Q is 70° and angle R is 110°. Angle R is much bigger than angle P.
misconceptions.B: This is true only when angle P is 45°. Try angle P = 20°: angle R is 110°, and 20 + 110 is not 180.
misconceptions.C: Well reasoned! Whatever angle P is, angle R is always 90° more.
misconceptions.D: This is true when angle P is 30°, but try another size. With angle P = 20°, angle Q is 70° and angle R is 110°, which is not twice 70°.

G4A_ANGLES_022.questionText: Angle AOB is 70°. A ray OC is drawn from the same point O so that angle BOC is 30°. Riya says angle AOC must be 100°. Which of these is true about angle AOC?

options.text: It could be any angle from 40° to 100°

hints: There is no picture, so imagine it. The ray OC can be drawn on either side of the ray OB.
First picture OC on the far side of OB, away from OA. Then picture OC on the near side of OB, between OA and OB. Find angle AOC each time.

Similar problem: angle XOY is 50° and angle YOZ is 20°. If OZ is outside angle XOY, angle XOZ is 50 + 20 = 70°. If OZ is inside angle XOY, angle XOZ is 50 - 20 = 30°. So angle XOZ could be 70° or 30°.

stepByStep.text: The ray OC makes 30° with OB, and it can lie on either side of OB.
If OC is on the side away from OA, the two angles add.
If OC is between OA and OB, the smaller angle is taken away.
These are the only two places where OC can be.
So angle AOC could be 100° or 40°.

misconceptions.A: Riya has added the angles, which is right if OC is outside angle AOB. But OC could also be drawn between OA and OB.
misconceptions.B: 40° is right if OC lies between OA and OB. But OC could also be on the other side of OB.
misconceptions.C: Angle BOC is fixed at 30°, so OC has only two possible places, one on each side of OB. It cannot be anywhere in between.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! OC can be on either side of OB, giving 70 + 30 = 100 or 70 - 30 = 40.

G4A_CIRCLE_001.questionText: The diameter of a circular plate is 18 cm. What is its radius?
hints: Think about how the radius and the diameter of a circle are related.
The radius is half of the diameter. Find half of 18.
Example: A circle has diameter 10 cm. Its radius is 10 divided by 2 = 5 cm.

stepByStep.text: The radius goes from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across through the centre, so it is two radii.
Halve the diameter.
The radius is 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: This doubles 18. Doubling turns a radius into a diameter; here you need to go from diameter to radius, so halve.
misconceptions.B: The radius is shorter than the diameter. It is exactly half of it.
misconceptions.C: This divides 18 by 3. A diameter is made of 2 radii, so divide by 2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Half of 18 cm is 9 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_002.questionText: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 cm with a compass. How far apart should the needle point and the pencil tip be?
hints: The needle of a compass sits at the centre and the pencil draws the circle. Think about which length that is.
The opening of the compass is the radius. Find the radius of a circle whose diameter is 12 cm.
Example: For a circle of diameter 20 cm, the compass is opened to the radius, 20 divided by 2 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: The needle is at the centre and the pencil is on the circle, so the opening of the compass is the radius.
The radius is half the diameter.
The needle point and pencil tip should be 6 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The compass is opened to the radius, and half of 12 cm is 6 cm.
misconceptions.B: An opening of 12 cm would give a circle 24 cm across. The compass is opened to the radius, not the diameter.
misconceptions.C: This doubles 12. The compass opening is the radius, which is half of the diameter.
misconceptions.D: This halves 12 twice. Halve only once to go from diameter to radius.

G4A_CIRCLE_003.questionText: A circle has a radius of 8 cm. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on a circle. Think about which chord is the longest of all.
The longest chord passes through the centre, so it is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 8 cm.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 cm, the longest chord is the diameter, 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: The longest chord of a circle is the one through the centre, which is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius.
The longest chord is 16 cm.

misconceptions.A: 8 cm is the radius. The longest chord goes right across the circle through the centre.
misconceptions.B: That is right! The longest chord is the diameter, 16 cm.
misconceptions.C: This halves the radius. The longest chord is the diameter, which is twice the radius.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 8 by 8. The longest chord is the diameter, 2 times the radius.

G4A_CIRCLE_004.questionText: A circle has a radius of 6 cm. Point P is 4 cm away from the centre of the circle. Where is point P?

options.text: At the centre of the circle

hints: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius away from the centre. Compare the point's distance with the radius.
Is 4 cm less than, equal to, or more than the radius of 6 cm?
Example: A circle has radius 5 cm and a point is 9 cm from the centre. Since 9 is more than 5, that point is outside the circle.

stepByStep.text: Points on the circle are exactly 6 cm from the centre.
Point P is 4 cm from the centre, and 4 is less than 6.
A point closer to the centre than the radius lies inside the circle, so P is inside the circle.

misconceptions.A: A point on the circle would be exactly 6 cm from the centre. P is only 4 cm away.
misconceptions.B: A point outside the circle would be more than 6 cm from the centre. P is only 4 cm away.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 4 cm is less than the radius of 6 cm, so P is inside the circle.
misconceptions.D: The centre is 0 cm away from itself. P is 4 cm away from the centre, so it is not at the centre.

G4A_CIRCLE_005.questionText: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two different points on the circle. If OA = 7 cm, how long is OB?
hints: Think about what kind of line joins the centre of a circle to a point on the circle.
OA and OB both go from the centre to the circle, so both are radii. What do you know about all the radii of one circle?
Example: In a circle with centre C, if CP = 4 cm and Q is also on the circle, then CQ is also a radius, so CQ = 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: OA joins the centre to a point on the circle, so OA is a radius.
OB also joins the centre to a point on the circle, so OB is a radius too.
All radii of a circle are equal, so OB = 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter. OB stops at the centre, so it is a radius.
misconceptions.B: This halves the radius. OB is a full radius, just like OA.
misconceptions.C: This is three radii. OB is one radius, just like OA.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Every radius of the same circle has the same length, 7 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_006.questionText: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 cm, are drawn in a straight row so that each circle touches the next one. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: When two equal circles touch, think about how far apart their centres are.
The centres of two touching circles are one radius plus one radius apart. Find that distance for radius 3 cm.
Example: Three circles of radius 2 cm touch in a row. Neighbouring centres are 4 cm apart, and there are 2 gaps from first to last, so the distance is 2 x 4 = 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Centres of neighbouring circles are two radii apart.
From the first centre to the fourth centre there are 3 gaps.
Multiply.
The distance between the first and last centres is 18 cm.

misconceptions.A: Great thinking! 3 gaps of 6 cm make 18 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is the full length of the row, 4 diameters. From centre to centre, half a circle is left out at each end.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 4 circles by the radius. Count the gaps between centres: there are 3, each 6 cm.
misconceptions.D: This uses 3 gaps of 3 cm. Each gap between centres is two radii, 6 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_007.questionText: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 cm, are placed in a straight row on a table so that each bangle touches the next. How long is the row from end to end?
hints: Each bangle takes up its full width in the row. Think about which length of a circle is its width.
The width of one bangle is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 4 cm.
Example: Five coins of radius 1 cm in a row. Each coin is 2 cm wide, so the row is 5 x 2 = 10 cm long.

stepByStep.text: Each bangle is one diameter wide.
There are 6 bangles in the row.
The row is 48 cm long.

misconceptions.A: This uses the radius as the width. Each bangle is a full diameter, 8 cm, wide.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 6 bangles, each 8 cm wide, make 48 cm.
misconceptions.C: This counts 5 gaps between centres. From end to end, all 6 full bangles are counted.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the diameter again. Each bangle is 8 cm wide, and there are 6 of them.

G4A_CIRCLE_008.questionText: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 cm so that it just touches all four sides of the square. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: Picture the circle fitting snugly in the square. Think about which length of the circle stretches from one side of the square to the opposite side.
The circle reaches from one side to the opposite side, so its diameter equals the side of the square, 10 cm.
Example: A circle just fits in a square of side 8 cm. Its diameter is 8 cm, so its radius is 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circle touches opposite sides of the square, so its diameter equals the side of the square.
The diameter is 10 cm.
The radius is half the diameter.
The radius of the circle is 5 cm.

misconceptions.A: 10 cm is the diameter of the circle. The radius is half of that.
misconceptions.B: This doubles the side. The side of the square equals the diameter, and the radius is half of it.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is 5 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is the perimeter of the square. The radius is half of one side.

G4A_CIRCLE_009.questionText: A circle of radius 6 cm fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: First find the side of the square from the circle, then find the distance around the square.
The side of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 cm.
Example: A circle of radius 2 cm fits exactly in a square. The side is 4 cm, so the perimeter is 4 x 4 = 16 cm.

stepByStep.text: The side of the square equals the diameter.
A square has 4 equal sides.
The perimeter of the square is 48 cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses the radius as the side. The side of the square is the diameter, 12 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is one side of the square. The perimeter is all 4 sides together.
misconceptions.C: This is the area of the square, 12 x 12. The perimeter is 4 times the side.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each side is 12 cm, and 4 sides make 48 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_010.questionText: Two coins lie flat on a table and touch each other. The radius of one coin is 5 cm and the radius of the other is 3 cm. How far apart are their centres?
hints: Imagine a straight line from one centre to the other. It passes through the point where the coins touch.
The line goes from the first centre to the touching point (one radius), then on to the second centre (the other radius).
Example: Circles of radius 4 cm and 2 cm touch side by side. Their centres are 4 + 2 = 6 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: The line joining the centres passes through the point where the coins touch.
It is made of the radius of one coin and the radius of the other.
Add the two radii.
The centres are 8 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: That is right! One radius of 5 cm and one of 3 cm make 8 cm.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts the radii. The coins lie side by side, so the two radii are added.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two diameters. From centre to centre you need only one radius of each coin.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies the radii. The distance is one radius plus the other radius.

G4A_CIRCLE_011.questionText: Two circles are drawn with the same centre. The radius of the big circle is 9 cm and the radius of the small circle is 5 cm. How wide is the ring between the two circles?
hints: Walk in a straight line from the centre outwards. You cross the small circle first and then the big circle.
The width of the ring is how much farther the big circle is from the centre than the small circle.
Example: Circles with the same centre have radii 10 cm and 7 cm. The ring between them is 10 - 7 = 3 cm wide.

stepByStep.text: Going out from the centre, the small circle is 5 cm away and the big circle is 9 cm away.
The ring is the gap between them.
The ring is 4 cm wide.

misconceptions.A: This adds the radii. The ring is the gap between the circles, so subtract.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The big circle is 4 cm farther from the centre than the small one.
misconceptions.C: This subtracts the diameters, 18 and 10. The ring's width on one side is the difference of the radii.
misconceptions.D: This halves the gap. The ring's width is the full difference of the radii, 9 - 5.

G4A_CIRCLE_012.questionText: The diameter of a circle is 12 cm longer than its radius. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: A diameter is made of two radii. Think about what is left when you take one radius away from the diameter.
Diameter = radius + radius. If the diameter is also radius + 12 cm, what must the second radius be?
Example: A diameter is 5 cm longer than its radius. Since the diameter is radius + radius, the extra part is one radius, so the radius is 5 cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter is two radii: radius + radius.
We are told the diameter is radius + 12 cm.
Comparing the two, the second radius must be the extra 12 cm.
Check: the diameter is 24 cm, and it is 12 cm longer than the radius.
The radius is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: This halves 12. Check it: a radius of 6 cm gives a diameter of 12 cm, which is only 6 cm longer.
misconceptions.B: 24 cm is the diameter of this circle. The question asks for the radius.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! The diameter, 24 cm, is exactly 12 cm longer than the radius, 12 cm.
misconceptions.D: This divides 12 by 3. Check it: a radius of 4 cm gives a diameter of 8 cm, which is only 4 cm longer.

G4A_CIRCLE_013.questionText: A circle has a radius of 6 cm. Which of these lengths can NOT be the length of a chord of this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on the circle. Think about how long the longest possible chord is.
The longest chord is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 cm.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 cm the longest chord is 10 cm, so a chord of 11 cm is not possible, but chords of 3 cm or 10 cm are.

stepByStep.text: The longest chord is the diameter.
So a chord can be any length up to 12 cm, but never longer.
4 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm are all possible. The length that cannot be a chord is 13 cm.

misconceptions.A: A short chord of 4 cm fits easily near the edge of the circle. Look for a length longer than the diameter.
misconceptions.B: A chord of 9 cm is shorter than the diameter of 12 cm, so it fits. Look for a length longer than the diameter.
misconceptions.C: 12 cm is exactly the diameter, which is the longest chord, so it is possible.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 13 cm is longer than the diameter of 12 cm, so no chord can be that long.

G4A_CIRCLE_014.questionText: A rectangular tray is 20 cm long and 8 cm wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 cm are laid flat on it in straight rows, touching each other but not overlapping. What is the greatest number of biscuits that fit on the tray?
hints: Each round biscuit needs a square space as wide as the biscuit. Find how many fit along the length and along the width.
The width of one biscuit is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 2 cm.
Example: A tray 12 cm by 6 cm holds circles of radius 3 cm. Each is 6 cm wide, so 2 fit along the length and 1 along the width: 2 x 1 = 2 circles.

stepByStep.text: Each biscuit is one diameter wide.
Biscuits along the length.
Rows along the width.
Multiply.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 2 rows of 5 biscuits make 10.
misconceptions.B: This is one row only. The tray is 8 cm wide, so a second row of 4 cm biscuits fits too.
misconceptions.C: This uses 2 cm as the width of a biscuit across the tray. Each biscuit is a full 4 cm wide in both directions.
misconceptions.D: This uses the radius, 2 cm, as the width of a biscuit. Each biscuit is one diameter, 4 cm, wide.

G4A_CIRCLE_015.questionText: A piece of wire is bent to make a circle of radius 7 cm. The same wire is straightened and bent again to make a square. What is the side of the square? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The length of the wire does not change. It is the distance around the circle, and then the distance around the square.
Find the circumference of the circle: 2 times 22/7 times 7.
Example: A wire makes a circle of radius 14 cm. Its length is 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 88 cm. Bent into a square, each side is 88 divided by 4 = 22 cm.

stepByStep.text: The length of the wire is the circumference of the circle.
The same 44 cm of wire goes around the square.
A square has 4 equal sides.
The side of the square is 11 cm.

misconceptions.A: 44 cm is the whole length of the wire. Share it among the 4 sides of the square.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 44 cm of wire makes a square of side 11 cm.
misconceptions.C: 14 cm is the diameter of the circle. The side of the square comes from the wire's length, 44 cm, shared among 4 sides.
misconceptions.D: This divides the wire by 2. A square has 4 equal sides, so divide 44 by 4.

G4A_CIRCLE_016.questionText: The radius of a big circle is equal to the diameter of a small circle. The radius of the small circle is 3 cm. What is the diameter of the big circle?
hints: Go one step at a time: small radius, small diameter, big radius, big diameter.
Find the diameter of the small circle first: twice 3 cm.
Example: A small circle has radius 2 cm, so its diameter is 4 cm. A big circle with radius 4 cm has diameter 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Diameter of the small circle.
This is the radius of the big circle, so the big radius is 6 cm.
Diameter of the big circle.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm is the radius of the big circle. Double it to get the big circle's diameter.
misconceptions.B: 3 cm is the radius of the small circle. Double it to get the big radius, then double again.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Doubling twice takes 3 cm to 6 cm and then to 12 cm.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 3 by 3. Each step from radius to diameter is a doubling.

G4A_CIRCLE_017.questionText: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 cm. Each circle touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle ABC?
hints: Each side of the triangle joins the centres of two touching circles. Find the length of one side first.
When two circles touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius: 4 + 4.
Example: Three circles of radius 5 cm touch each other. Each side of the triangle of centres is 10 cm, so its perimeter is 3 x 10 = 30 cm.

stepByStep.text: Each side joins two centres of touching circles.
The triangle has 3 such sides.
The perimeter of triangle ABC is 24 cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses 4 cm for each side. Each side is two radii, 8 cm.
misconceptions.B: 8 cm is one side of the triangle. The perimeter is all 3 sides together.
misconceptions.C: This doubles once too often. Each side is 8 cm, and 3 sides make the perimeter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3 sides of 8 cm make 24 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_018.questionText: Ten equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the outer circles touch the sides of the rectangle. The perimeter of the rectangle is 84 cm. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Write the length and the width of the rectangle as a number of diameters, then use the perimeter.
The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters. How many diameters make up half of the perimeter?
Example: Six circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of perimeter 40 cm. Length + width = 3 + 2 = 5 diameters = 20 cm, so a diameter is 4 cm and the radius is 2 cm.

stepByStep.text: The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.
Length + width is half the perimeter.
Length + width is 7 diameters.
The radius is half the diameter.
The radius of each circle is 3 cm.

misconceptions.A: Great work! The diameter is 6 cm, so the radius is 3 cm.
misconceptions.B: 6 cm is the diameter of each circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.C: This divides the whole perimeter by 7. Only half the perimeter, 42 cm, equals 7 diameters.
misconceptions.D: This divides 84 by 4 as if the rectangle were a square. The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.

G4A_CIRCLE_019.questionText: A small circle of radius 3 cm lies inside a big circle of radius 10 cm and touches it at exactly one point. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Draw a line from the big centre to the touching point. The small circle's centre lies on this line.
From the big centre to the touching point is 10 cm. From the small centre to the same point is 3 cm.
Example: A circle of radius 2 cm touches a circle of radius 8 cm from inside. The centres are 8 - 2 = 6 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: The big centre, the small centre and the touching point lie on one straight line.
The big centre is 10 cm from the touching point, and the small centre is 3 cm from it.
The distance between the centres is the difference.
The centres are 7 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Adding the radii is for circles that touch side by side from outside. Here the small circle is inside the big one.
misconceptions.B: That is right! The small centre is 3 cm back from the touching point, so it is 7 cm from the big centre.
misconceptions.C: This takes away the small circle's diameter. Only its radius lies between its centre and the touching point.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies the radii. The centres are apart by the difference of the radii.

G4A_CIRCLE_020.questionText: Three circles of radii 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm are drawn in a row with their centres on one straight line. The middle circle, of radius 3 cm, touches the other two. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: Travel along the line from the first centre to the last centre and note which parts of each circle you cross.
You cross one radius of the first circle, then the whole middle circle, then one radius of the last circle.
Example: Circles of radii 1 cm, 2 cm and 5 cm in a row. From first centre to last centre: 1 + (2 + 2) + 5 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: From the first centre to its edge is one radius, 2 cm.
Crossing the whole middle circle is its diameter.
From the edge of the last circle to its centre is one radius, 4 cm.
Add the three parts.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: This adds the three radii once each. The middle circle is crossed completely, so its radius is counted twice.
misconceptions.B: This is the full length of the row from end to end. From centre to centre, only one radius of each end circle is counted.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 2 + 6 + 4 = 12.
misconceptions.D: This counts the whole last circle. Stop at its centre, so count only one radius, 4 cm, for it.

G4A_CIRCLE_021.questionText: The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. The circle fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Work backwards from the circumference to the radius, then think about how the circle sits in the square.
Circumference = 2 times 22/7 times radius. So 44/7 times the radius is 88.
Example: A circle has circumference 44 cm. Then 44/7 times the radius is 44, so the radius is 7 cm. The square around it has side equal to the diameter, 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circumference is 2 times 22/7 times the radius.
So the radius is 14 cm.
The side of the square equals the diameter.
The side of the square is 28 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the radius of the circle. The side of the square is the diameter.
misconceptions.B: This shares 88 cm among 4 sides. The 88 cm goes around the circle, not around the square.
misconceptions.C: This doubles the diameter. The side of the square is equal to one diameter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The radius is 14 cm, so the diameter and the side of the square are 28 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_022.questionText: A circle of radius 7 cm is cut out of a square sheet of paper of side 14 cm. What is the area of the paper that is left? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. Find two areas.
Find the area of the square first: 14 times 14.
Example: A circle of area 154 sq cm is cut from a square sheet of side 20 cm. The square is 400 sq cm, so 400 - 154 = 246 sq cm is left.

stepByStep.text: Area of the square.
Area of the circle.
Take the circle away from the square.
The area of paper left is 42 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 196 - 154 = 42.
misconceptions.B: This takes away the circumference, 44, from the area of the square. Take away the area of the circle, 154.
misconceptions.C: This is the area of the circle that was cut out. The question asks for the paper left behind.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two areas. The circle is cut out, so subtract it from the square.

G4A_CIRCLE_023.questionText: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Each chord joins two of the points. Count the pairs in an orderly way so that none is counted twice.
Call the points P, Q, R, S, T. Start by counting the chords from P to each of the other four points.
Example: With 4 points on a circle, the first point joins 3 others, the next joins 2 new ones, and the next joins 1 new one: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 chords.

stepByStep.text: From the first point, 4 chords go to the other points.
From the second point, 3 new chords can be drawn, then 2 from the third and 1 from the fourth.
Add them.
10 chords are drawn.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the chords joining neighbouring points. Points that are not neighbours are joined too.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 chords.
misconceptions.C: This counts 4 chords from each of the 5 points, but then every chord is counted twice, once from each end.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 5 by 5. A point is not joined to itself, and each chord should be counted only once.

G4A_CIRCLE_024.questionText: Two square trays each have a side of 24 cm. The first tray is exactly filled by 9 equal round plates in 3 rows of 3. The second tray is exactly filled by 16 equal round plates in 4 rows of 4. In each tray the plates touch each other and the sides. How much longer is the radius of a plate in the first tray than in the second tray?
hints: In each tray, the plates in one row share the 24 cm side equally. Find each plate's diameter, then its radius.
In the first tray, 3 plates fit across 24 cm. Find the diameter of one plate: 24 divided by 3.
Example: A 20 cm square tray holds 2 plates across, so each is 10 cm wide with radius 5 cm. If it holds 5 plates across, each is 4 cm wide with radius 2 cm. The radii differ by 5 - 2 = 3 cm.

stepByStep.text: First tray: 3 plates across.
So the radius of a plate in the first tray is 4 cm.
Second tray: 4 plates across.
So the radius of a plate in the second tray is 3 cm.
Compare the radii.
The radius in the first tray is longer by 1 cm.

misconceptions.A: This compares the diameters, 8 cm and 6 cm. The question asks about the radii, 4 cm and 3 cm.
misconceptions.B: 3 cm is the radius of a plate in the second tray. Compare it with the radius in the first tray, 4 cm.
misconceptions.C: Great work! The radii are 4 cm and 3 cm, so the difference is 1 cm.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two radii. To find how much longer, subtract.

G4A_CIRCLE_025.questionText: A wire 132 cm long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent to make a circle. What is the radius of each circle? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Each piece of wire becomes the distance around one circle. Find the length of one piece first.
Divide 132 cm by 3 to find the length of one piece.
Example: A wire 176 cm long is cut into 2 equal pieces of 88 cm. For a circle, 44/7 times the radius is 88, so the radius is 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: Length of one piece.
This is the circumference of one circle: 2 times 22/7 times the radius is 44.
A radius of 7 cm fits.
The radius of each circle is 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter of each circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.B: This is the radius if the whole 132 cm wire made one circle. The wire is first cut into 3 equal pieces.
misconceptions.C: 44 cm is the length of one piece, which is the circumference. Use it to find the radius.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each piece is 44 cm, and a circle of radius 7 cm has circumference 44 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_026.questionText: Twelve equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 3 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the circles on the outside touch the sides of the rectangle. The area of the rectangle is 432 sq cm. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Each circle sits snugly inside its own little square, and the twelve little squares fill the rectangle exactly. Work backwards from the area.
Share the area of the rectangle equally among the 12 little squares. Then find the side of one little square, and think about how that side is related to the circle inside it.

Similar problem: 6 equal circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of area 96 sq cm. Each little square has area 96 ÷ 6 = 16 sq cm, so its side is 4 cm. That side is the diameter of a circle, so the radius is 2 cm.

stepByStep.text: The rectangle is made of 12 equal little squares, one around each circle.
A square of area 36 sq cm has a side of 6 cm.
The side of the little square is the diameter of the circle inside it.
The radius is half the diameter.
So the radius of each circle is 3 cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm is the side of each little square, which is the diameter of a circle. The question asks for the radius.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Each circle fits a 6 cm square, so its diameter is 6 cm and its radius is 3 cm.
misconceptions.C: Check with a radius of 9 cm: the rectangle would be 72 cm by 54 cm, far bigger than 432 sq cm.
misconceptions.D: Check with a radius of 12 cm: four circles side by side would already be 96 cm long. Try sharing the area among 12 little squares.

G4A_CIRCLE_027.questionText: A round pond has a radius of 7 m. A path 7 m wide runs all the way around the pond. What is the area of the path? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The path is a ring. A ring is what is left when a small circle is taken out of a bigger circle with the same centre.
Find the radius of the big circle made by the pond and the path together. It reaches from the centre of the pond to the outer edge of the path.

Similar problem: a pond of radius 14 m with a path 7 m wide. The big circle has radius 21 m and area 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 1386 sq m. The pond has area 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 sq m. The path is 1386 - 616 = 770 sq m.

stepByStep.text: The pond and path together make a big circle. Find its radius.
Find the area of the big circle.
Find the area of the pond.
Take the pond out of the big circle.
So the area of the path is 462 sq m.

misconceptions.A: This is the area of a circle of radius 7 m, which is the pond. The path is the ring around it, out to 14 m from the centre.
misconceptions.B: This is the area of the pond and the path together. Take the area of the pond away.
misconceptions.C: Great work! The big circle is 616 sq m, the pond is 154 sq m, and 616 - 154 = 462.
misconceptions.D: The path is not twice the pond. Find the big circle of radius 14 m and take the pond away from it.

G4A_CIRCLE_028.questionText: When the radius of a circle is made twice as long, its circumference becomes 88 cm longer than before. What was the radius of the circle at the start? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Think about what happens to the circumference when the radius is doubled. You can also test each choice: find the circumference before and after, and see how much it grows.
Try a radius of 7 cm. The circumference is 44 cm. With a radius of 14 cm it is 88 cm. Find how much it has grown, and compare with what the question says.

Similar problem: doubling the radius makes the circumference 132 cm longer. Doubling the radius doubles the circumference, so the extra part equals the old circumference, 132 cm. Since 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 132, the radius at the start was 21 cm.

stepByStep.text: When the radius is doubled, the circumference is doubled too.
So the extra length is exactly as long as the old circumference: the old circumference is 88 cm.
Find the radius of a circle with circumference 88 cm.
Check: the new radius is 28 cm, and the circumference has grown by 88 cm.
So the radius at the start was 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: Test it: with 7 cm the circumference is 44 cm, and with 14 cm it is 88 cm. It grows by only 44 cm. Here 88 cm is the extra length, not the new circumference.
misconceptions.B: 28 cm is the radius after doubling. The question asks for the radius at the start.
misconceptions.C: This halves 88. Try finding the circumference for each radius and see how much it grows when the radius is doubled.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The circumference goes from 88 cm to 176 cm, which is 88 cm longer.

G4A_CIRCLE_029.questionText: Seven points are marked on a circle. Each point is joined by a straight chord to every other point, except the two points right next to it. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Work out how many chords leave one point. Then think carefully before you multiply: every chord has two ends.
From one point there are 6 other points. Two of them are its neighbours, so find how many chords start at this point.

Similar problem: five points on a circle, each joined to every point except its two neighbours. Each point sends out 2 chords, and 5 x 2 = 10. But every chord has been counted from both of its ends, so there are 10 ÷ 2 = 5 chords.

stepByStep.text: From each point, take away the point itself and its two neighbours.
Seven points each send out 4 chords.
Each chord joins two points, so it has been counted twice.
Halve the total.
So 14 chords are drawn.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Each point sends out 4 chords, and halving 7 x 4 gives 14.
misconceptions.B: This is 7 x 4. Each chord joins two points, so it has been counted once from each end.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of chords when every pair of points is joined. Here the points right next to each other are not joined.
misconceptions.D: These are the 7 short joins between neighbours, which are the ones left out. Count the other chords.

G4A_CIRCLE_030.questionText: Eight points are marked on a circle, equally spaced all the way round. Every pair of points is joined by a chord. How many of these chords are NOT diameters of the circle?
hints: Count all the chords first, in an orderly way. Then decide which chords pass through the centre, and be careful not to count any of those twice.
The first point is joined to 7 others, the second to 6 new ones, and so on. A chord is a diameter only when it joins a point to the point exactly opposite.

Similar problem: six equally spaced points. The chords number 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. The six points make 3 opposite pairs, so 3 chords are diameters. That leaves 15 - 3 = 12 chords that are not diameters.

stepByStep.text: Count all the chords.
A chord is a diameter when it joins two opposite points.
Eight points make 4 opposite pairs, so there are 4 diameters.
Take the diameters away from all the chords.
So 24 of the chords are not diameters.

misconceptions.A: This takes away 8 diameters, one for each point. Each diameter joins two opposite points, so 8 points share only 4 diameters.
misconceptions.B: Exactly! There are 28 chords, 4 of them are diameters, and 28 - 4 = 24.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of all the chords. Some of them pass through the centre, and those must be left out.
misconceptions.D: 4 is the number of diameters. The question asks for the chords that are not diameters.

G4A_CIRCLE_031.questionText: A small circle is drawn inside a big circle. The small circle touches the big circle at exactly one point, and it also passes through the centre of the big circle. The diameter of the big circle is 24 cm. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Imagine a straight line from the point where the circles touch to the centre of the big circle. Think about what this line is for each of the two circles.
That line is a radius of the big circle. It also goes right across the small circle, from one side to the other through its centre.

Similar problem: the big circle has diameter 40 cm. Its radius is 20 cm, and this is the diameter of the small circle. The small circle's centre is halfway along, 10 cm from the big centre. So the centres are 10 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: Find the radius of the big circle.
The line from the touching point to the big centre is 12 cm long, and it is a diameter of the small circle.
The centre of the small circle is halfway along this line.
So the small centre is 6 cm from the big centre.
So the centres of the two circles are 6 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Lovely! The small circle's diameter is 12 cm, so its centre is 6 cm from the centre of the big circle.
misconceptions.B: 12 cm is the radius of the big circle, and the whole width of the small circle. The small circle's centre is only halfway along it.
misconceptions.C: 18 cm is how far the small centre is from the far side of the big circle. Measure from centre to centre.
misconceptions.D: This halves once too often. The small circle's diameter is 12 cm and its radius is 6 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_032.questionText: Three coins of different sizes lie flat on a table, and each coin touches the other two. The distances between their centres are 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm. What is the radius of the largest coin?
hints: When two coins touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius. Think about what you get if you add all three distances.
Add 7, 8 and 9. In that total every radius has been counted twice. Halve it to find the three radii added together.
Similar problem: the distances are 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. They add up to 18 cm, so the three radii add up to 9 cm. The two smaller coins are 5 cm apart, so the largest coin has radius 9 - 5 = 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the three distances. Each radius is counted twice.
Halve to get the three radii added together.
The two smaller coins have the closest centres, 7 cm apart. Take their radii away.
Check: the radii are 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
So the radius of the largest coin is 5 cm.

misconceptions.A: This halves 9 cm. That would be right for two equal coins, but these coins are all different sizes.
misconceptions.B: 4 cm is the radius of the middle coin. Check which coin is the largest: the radii are 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The radii are 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and they give distances of 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm.
misconceptions.D: 9 cm is the distance between two centres. It is made of two radii added together.

G4A_CIRCLE_033.questionText: Two round tins, each of radius 7 cm, stand on a table touching each other. A ribbon is pulled tight around the two tins together. It goes straight across from one tin to the other on both sides, and it curves around the outer half of each tin. How long is the ribbon? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Break the ribbon into its parts: the straight parts and the curved parts. Find each part and add them up.
Each straight part runs from the widest point of one tin to the widest point of the other, so it is as long as the distance between the two centres. The two curved parts are half circles.

Similar problem: two tins of radius 14 cm. The centres are 28 cm apart, so the two straight parts are 28 cm each. The two half circles make one whole circle of 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 88 cm. The ribbon is 28 + 28 + 88 = 144 cm long.

stepByStep.text: The tins touch, so their centres are two radii apart. Each straight part is this long.
There are two straight parts.
The two curved parts are half circles, which together make one whole circle.
Add the straight parts and the curved parts.
So the ribbon is 72 cm long.

misconceptions.A: This is the distance around both tins separately. The ribbon only curves around the outer half of each tin, and it has two straight parts.
misconceptions.B: This has only one straight part. The ribbon crosses from tin to tin on both sides.
misconceptions.C: Wonderful! Two straight parts of 14 cm and one whole circle of 44 cm make 72 cm.
misconceptions.D: Each straight part is 14 cm long, the distance between the centres, so the two together are 28 cm, not 56 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_034.questionText: The hour hand of a wall clock is 7 cm long. How far does the tip of the hour hand travel in one full day of 24 hours? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The tip of the hand moves along a circle. Before you calculate, think about how many times the hour hand goes all the way round in a whole day.
The hour hand takes 12 hours to go once round the clock face. Work out how many times it goes round in 24 hours.
Similar problem: a minute hand 21 cm long, over 2 hours. The minute hand goes round once every hour, so twice in 2 hours. One round is 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 132 cm, so the tip travels 2 x 132 = 264 cm.

stepByStep.text: The tip moves on a circle of radius 7 cm. Find the distance once round.
The hour hand goes once round in 12 hours. Find how many times it goes round in a day.
Multiply the distance once round by the number of rounds.
So the tip of the hour hand travels 88 cm.

misconceptions.A: 44 cm is once round the clock. The hour hand goes round once every 12 hours, and a day has 24 hours.
misconceptions.B: This takes the hand round 24 times, once every hour. That is what the minute hand does. The hour hand is much slower.
misconceptions.C: This is only half a round. In 24 hours the hour hand goes all the way round, and more than once.
misconceptions.D: Great job! The hour hand goes round twice in a day, and 2 x 44 = 88.

G4A_COUNTING_001.questionText: How many whole numbers are there from 15 to 42, counting both 15 and 42?
hints: When you count from one number up to another and both ends are included, think about whether subtracting alone counts every number.
Find 42 − 15 first. Then ask yourself whether the starting number 15 has been counted yet.
A similar problem: from 6 to 10 the numbers are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. Subtracting gives 10 − 6 = 4, and adding 1 for the starting number gives 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Subtract the smaller number from the larger one.
This counts the jumps. Add 1 so that the starting number 15 is counted too.
There are 28 whole numbers from 15 to 42.

misconceptions.A: This is 42 − 15, which counts the jumps between the numbers. Add 1 more so that 15 itself is counted.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 42 − 15 = 27, and one more for the starting number gives 28.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 after subtracting. Only one extra is needed, for the starting number.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out both 15 and 42. The question asks you to count both of them.

G4A_COUNTING_002.questionText: Meera stands in a queue at the school canteen. She is 7th from the front and 5th from the back. How many children are in the queue?
hints: A position from the front and a position from the back both count the same child. Think about what happens if you simply add them.
There are 6 children in front of Meera. Work out how many are behind her, then count Meera once.
A similar problem: Raju is 3rd from the front and 4th from the back. In front of him are 2 children, behind him are 3, and Raju makes 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 children.

stepByStep.text: Count the children in front of Meera and behind her.
Add them, and add Meera herself once.
There are 11 children in the queue.

misconceptions.A: This is 7 + 5, which counts Meera twice. Take 1 away so she is counted only once.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to 7 + 5. Meera has already been counted twice, so 1 must be taken away instead.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 6 in front, 4 behind, and Meera herself make 11.
misconceptions.D: This counts the 6 in front and the 4 behind but leaves out Meera. Remember to count her once.

G4A_COUNTING_003.questionText: A straight fence is 40 metres long. A post stands every 5 metres, with a post at each end. How many posts are there?
hints: Posts stand at the ends of the gaps. In a straight line with a post at both ends, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
First find how many 5-metre gaps fit into 40 metres.
A similar problem: a 12-metre fence with a post every 4 metres has 12 ÷ 4 = 3 gaps. The posts stand at 0, 4, 8 and 12 metres, so there are 4 posts.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of gaps between posts.
A straight line of gaps has one more post than gaps.
There are 9 posts.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 8 gaps need 9 posts, because there is a post at both ends.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of gaps, 40 ÷ 5. The post at the very start still needs to be counted.
misconceptions.C: This takes 1 away from the 8 gaps. With a post at each end, there is one more post than gaps.
misconceptions.D: This adds 2 to the number of gaps. Only one extra post is needed.

G4A_COUNTING_004.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers end in the digit 5?
hints: Think about which digits are allowed in the tens place of a 2-digit number.
Start listing them: 15, 25, 35, and keep going until the last 2-digit number that ends in 5.
A similar problem: the 2-digit numbers smaller than 60 that end in 2 are 12, 22, 32, 42 and 52. The tens digit runs from 1 to 5, so there are 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The ones digit is fixed as 5. The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9.
There are 9 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 itself (or 05) as well. The number 5 has only one digit, so it is not a 2-digit number.
misconceptions.B: This looks like the ending digit, not the count. Try listing the numbers: 15, 25, 35 and so on.
misconceptions.C: One number has been missed. Check that 55 and 95 are both in your list.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! The tens digit can be any of 1 to 9, so there are 9 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_005.questionText: Riya has 3 different tops and 2 different skirts. An outfit is one top worn with one skirt. How many different outfits can she make?
hints: Every top can be paired with every skirt. Think about how many pairs each top makes.
Take the first top. How many outfits can it make with the 2 skirts? Then do the same for the other tops.
A similar problem: with 4 caps and 2 scarves, each cap can go with 2 scarves, so there are 4 × 2 = 8 pairs.

stepByStep.text: Each top can be worn with either of the 2 skirts, so each top gives 2 outfits.
There are 3 tops.
Riya can make 6 different outfits.

misconceptions.A: This adds 3 + 2. Each top goes with every skirt, so the numbers are multiplied.
misconceptions.B: Great job! Each of the 3 tops makes 2 outfits, so 3 × 2 = 6.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 3. There are only 2 skirts for each top, so it is 3 × 2.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the tops. Each top makes 2 different outfits, one for each skirt.

G4A_COUNTING_006.questionText: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 30?
hints: Even and odd numbers take turns as you count. Think about what share of the numbers are even.
The even numbers start 2, 4, 6. Find the last even number in the range and see which place it holds in the list.
A similar problem: from 1 to 10 the even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Every second number is even, so there are 10 ÷ 2 = 5 of them.

stepByStep.text: From 1 to 30, every second number is even: 2, 4, 6, and so on up to 30.
Half of the 30 numbers are even.
There are 15 even numbers from 1 to 30.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Every second number is even, and 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
misconceptions.B: This leaves out one even number. Check that 30 itself is counted, because 30 is even.
misconceptions.C: This counts one too many. Zero is not in the range 1 to 30, so the list starts at 2.
misconceptions.D: This is how many numbers there are altogether. Only every second one is even.

G4A_COUNTING_007.questionText: A carpenter cuts a long wooden plank into 6 pieces. He cuts one piece at a time. How many cuts does he make?
hints: Think about what one cut does to the number of pieces.
Before any cut there is 1 piece. After the first cut there are 2 pieces. Keep going until there are 6.
A similar problem: to cut a ribbon into 3 pieces, the first cut makes 2 pieces and the second cut makes 3 pieces. So 2 cuts are needed.

stepByStep.text: The plank starts as 1 piece. Every cut adds 1 more piece.
To reach 6 pieces, 5 more pieces are needed.
The carpenter makes 5 cuts.

misconceptions.A: This matches the number of pieces. The plank is already 1 piece before any cut, so one cut fewer is needed.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to the number of pieces. Cuts are one fewer than pieces, not one more.
misconceptions.C: You got it! Each cut adds one piece, so 5 cuts turn 1 piece into 6.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the pieces. Try it with a paper strip: each cut makes just one extra piece.

G4A_COUNTING_008.questionText: How many different 2-digit numbers can you make using only the digits 3 and 8? A digit may be used twice in a number.
hints: Think about the choices for the tens place and the choices for the ones place.
Write the numbers that start with 3 first. Then write the ones that start with 8.
A similar problem: with the digits 1, 2 and 5 and repeats allowed, there are 3 choices for the tens place and 3 for the ones place, so 3 × 3 = 9 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit can be 3 or 8, and the ones digit can be 3 or 8.
That gives 2 choices for each place.
The numbers are 33, 38, 83 and 88, so 4 numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This counts only 38 and 83. A digit may be used twice, so 33 and 88 count too.
misconceptions.B: One number has been missed. Check your list for 33, 38, 83 and 88.
misconceptions.C: This is more than can be made. With 2 choices for each of the 2 places there are 2 × 2 numbers.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 33, 38, 83 and 88 make 4 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_009.questionText: The pages of a small story book are numbered from 1 to 25. How many digits are printed in all to number the pages?
hints: Some page numbers have one digit and some have two. Count the two groups separately.
Pages 1 to 9 use one digit each. Work out how many pages are left from 10 to 25.
A similar problem: for pages 1 to 12, pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Pages 10, 11 and 12 are 3 pages using 2 digits each, which is 6 digits. In all, 9 + 6 = 15 digits.

stepByStep.text: Pages 1 to 9 have one digit each.
Pages 10 to 25 are 16 pages with two digits each.
Add the two groups.
In all, 41 digits are printed.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 9 digits for pages 1 to 9 and 32 digits for pages 10 to 25 make 41.
misconceptions.B: This gives two digits to every page. Pages 1 to 9 have only one digit each.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of pages, not the number of digits. Pages from 10 onwards use two digits each.
misconceptions.D: This is 9 + 25. Count only the pages from 10 to 25 as two-digit pages: there are 16 of them, and each uses 2 digits.

G4A_COUNTING_010.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers have digits that add up to 7?
hints: Work in an organised way: choose the tens digit first, and the ones digit is then decided.
Start with tens digit 1. The ones digit must be 6, giving 16. Now try tens digit 2, and carry on.
A similar problem: 2-digit numbers with digits adding to 4 are 13, 22, 31 and 40. The tens digit runs from 1 to 4, so there are 4 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7. It cannot be 0.
For each tens digit there is exactly one ones digit that makes the total 7.
The numbers are 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70.
There are 7 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been left out. Remember 70, because 7 + 0 = 7.
misconceptions.B: This also counts 07. That is just 7, which has only one digit.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70 are the 7 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the count. Each tens digit from 1 to 7 gives just one number.

G4A_COUNTING_011.questionText: Kiran writes all the numbers from 1 to 40 in her notebook. How many times does she write the digit 3?
hints: A digit can appear in the ones place or in the tens place. Count each place separately.
First list the numbers that have 3 in the ones place: 3, 13, and so on. Then look at the numbers that have 3 in the tens place.

A similar problem: from 1 to 30, the digit 2 is in the ones place in 2, 12 and 22, which is 3 times. It is in the tens place in 20 to 29, which is 10 times. In all it is written 13 times, and 22 is counted twice because it has two 2s.

stepByStep.text: In the ones place, 3 appears in 3, 13, 23 and 33.
In the tens place, 3 appears in 30, 31, 32, and so on up to 39.
Add the two counts. The number 33 has two 3s, so it is rightly counted in both.
She writes the digit 3 a total of 14 times.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the ones place. The numbers 30 to 39 each have a 3 in the tens place too.
misconceptions.B: This counts 33 only once. It has two 3s, and the question asks how many times the digit is written.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the tens place. The numbers 3, 13, 23 and 33 also have a 3 in the ones place.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 4 times in the ones place and 10 times in the tens place make 14.

G4A_COUNTING_012.questionText: 30 children stand in a line for the morning assembly. Arjun is 12th from the front. What is his position from the back?
hints: Find how many children stand behind him. His place from the back is one more than that.
Arjun is 12th from the front, so take 12 away from 30 to find how many children are behind him.
A similar problem: in a line of 10 children, Sita is 4th from the front. Behind her are 10 − 4 = 6 children, so she is 7th from the back.

stepByStep.text: Find how many children are behind Arjun.
Counting from the back, those 18 children come first and Arjun is next.
Arjun is 19th from the back.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of children behind Arjun. He comes just after them, so his position is one more.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 18 children are behind him, so Arjun is 19th from the back.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 to the 18 children behind him. Only Arjun himself needs to be added, which is 1.
misconceptions.D: This adds 30 and 12. A position in the line cannot be bigger than the number of children.

G4A_COUNTING_013.questionText: A square garden has sides of 12 metres. Posts are fixed all around its edge, one at every corner and one every 3 metres along each side. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go all the way around and come back to the start. In a closed loop, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
Find the distance all the way around the garden first. Then see how many 3-metre gaps fit into it.
A similar problem: a square of side 6 metres with a post every 2 metres has a distance around of 24 metres. That is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 gaps, and going around a loop needs exactly 12 posts.

stepByStep.text: Find the distance around the garden.
Find the number of 3-metre gaps.
Around a closed loop the last gap ends at the first post, so the number of posts equals the number of gaps.
16 posts are needed.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 posts on each of the 4 sides. Each corner post then gets counted twice, once for each side it joins.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to the 16 gaps, as for a straight fence. Around a loop the last post is the first post again.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! 48 metres around gives 16 gaps, and a loop needs 16 posts.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the 3 posts in the middle of each side. The 4 corner posts must be added.

G4A_COUNTING_014.questionText: Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row for a photo. In how many different orders can they stand?
hints: Think place by place: who can stand first, then who can stand next, then who is left.
Suppose Anu stands first. Write the orders the other two can stand in. Then let Binu stand first, and then Charu.
A similar problem: two friends, Raj and Sam, can stand as Raj then Sam, or Sam then Raj. There are 2 choices for the first place and 1 for the second, so 2 × 1 = 2 orders.

stepByStep.text: Any of the 3 children can stand first.
Once the first is chosen, 2 children are left for the second place, and then 1 for the last place.
Multiply the choices.
They can stand in 6 different orders.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 × 3. After one child takes the first place, only 2 are left for the next place.
misconceptions.B: This counts only who stands first. For each first child, the other two can stand in 2 ways.
misconceptions.C: Some orders have been missed. List them by first child: each child can be first in 2 orders.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 3 choices, then 2, then 1 give 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders.

G4A_COUNTING_015.questionText: A window has 4 small square panes, arranged as 2 rows of 2. Counting squares of every size, how many squares can you see in the window?
hints: Squares can be of different sizes. Count the small ones, then look for bigger squares made by joining small ones.
Count the small panes first. Then ask whether all four panes together make a square.
A similar problem: a single square pane has just 1 square. A row of 2 panes has 2 small squares and no bigger square, because the two together make a long rectangle. So it has 2 squares.

stepByStep.text: There are 4 small square panes.
The whole window, made of all 4 panes, is 1 big square.
Add them.
There are 5 squares in the window.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 4 small squares and 1 big square make 5.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the small panes. The whole window is a square too.
misconceptions.C: This counts one square too many. Two panes side by side make a rectangle, not a square.
misconceptions.D: This counts the pairs of panes as squares. Two panes joined together are longer than they are tall, so they are rectangles.

G4A_COUNTING_016.questionText: 16 players enter a knockout badminton tournament. In every match the loser goes out and the winner plays on. How many matches are played to find the champion?
hints: Each match sends exactly one player out. Think about how many players must go out before one champion is left.
Count round by round: 16 players play 8 matches in the first round, leaving 8 players. Carry on until one player is left.
A similar problem: with 4 players, the first round has 2 matches and the final is 1 match. That is 2 + 1 = 3 matches, and 3 players have gone out.

stepByStep.text: Count the matches in each round.
Another way to see it: each match sends one player out, and 15 players must go out to leave 1 champion.
15 matches are played.

misconceptions.A: This is only the first round. The 8 winners must keep playing until one champion is left.
misconceptions.B: This matches the number of players. The champion never loses, so there is one match fewer.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 matches, one for each player who goes out.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of rounds. Each round has several matches, so add up the matches in all the rounds.

G4A_COUNTING_017.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers are multiples of 7?
hints: Find the smallest and the largest 2-digit multiples, then count how many multiples lie from one to the other.
The first multiple of 7 with two digits is 14, which is 7 × 2. Find the largest multiple of 7 that is below 100.
A similar problem: the 2-digit multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60 and 80. They are 20 × 1 up to 20 × 4, so there are 4 of them.

stepByStep.text: The smallest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 14.
The largest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 98.
Count the multipliers from 2 to 14.
There are 13 two-digit multiples of 7.

misconceptions.A: This counts all multiples of 7 up to 98, including 7 itself. The number 7 has only one digit.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The multiples run from 7 × 2 to 7 × 14, which is 13 numbers.
misconceptions.C: This takes away one too many. From 7 × 2 to 7 × 14 there are 14 − 2 + 1 multipliers.
misconceptions.D: This counts too many. 7 × 15 = 105 has three digits, and 7 × 1 = 7 has one digit.

G4A_COUNTING_018.questionText: Sunita walks up from the 1st floor to the 4th floor and climbs 48 steps. Every floor has the same number of steps. How many steps would she climb from the 1st floor to the 7th floor?
hints: Going from one floor to another, count the flights of stairs climbed, not the floor numbers.
From the 1st floor to the 4th floor Sunita climbs 3 flights of stairs. Use this to find the steps in one flight.
A similar problem: going from the 1st floor to the 3rd floor is 2 flights. If that is 20 steps, each flight has 10 steps. From the 1st floor to the 5th floor is 4 flights, which is 40 steps.

stepByStep.text: From the 1st to the 4th floor there are 3 flights of stairs.
Find the steps in one flight.
From the 1st to the 7th floor there are 6 flights.
She would climb 96 steps.

misconceptions.A: This divides 48 by 4 and multiplies by 7. Starting on the 1st floor, reaching the 4th floor takes only 3 flights.
misconceptions.B: This uses 16 steps per flight, which is right, but counts 7 flights. From the 1st floor to the 7th there are 6 flights.
misconceptions.C: This uses 6 flights, which is right, but divides 48 by 4. The 48 steps are shared among 3 flights.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Each flight has 16 steps, and 6 flights make 96 steps.
