G4A_COUNTING_019.questionText: An ice-cream shop has 4 flavours: mango, chocolate, vanilla and strawberry. Rohan picks 2 different flavours for his cup. How many different pairs of flavours can he choose?
hints: A pair is the same whichever flavour is named first. List the pairs in an organised way so that none is repeated.
Start with mango and pair it with each of the other three. Then move to chocolate, pairing it only with flavours not used with it before.
A similar problem: from 3 fruits, apple, banana and cherry, the pairs are apple-banana, apple-cherry and banana-cherry. That is 2 + 1 = 3 pairs.

stepByStep.text: Mango can pair with chocolate, vanilla or strawberry: 3 pairs.
Chocolate can pair with vanilla or strawberry: 2 new pairs. Vanilla can pair with strawberry: 1 new pair.
Add the pairs.
Rohan can choose 6 different pairs.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 pairs.
misconceptions.B: This is 4 × 3, which counts mango with chocolate and chocolate with mango as two pairs. In a cup they are the same pair, so halve it.
misconceptions.C: This is 4 × 2. Try listing the pairs: mango goes with 3 others, chocolate with 2 new ones, vanilla with 1 new one.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of flavours. Each pair uses two flavours, so list the pairs to count them.

G4A_COUNTING_020.questionText: Using each of the digits 2, 0 and 5 exactly once, how many 3-digit numbers can be made?
hints: Look carefully at the hundreds place. One of these digits cannot go there.
A 3-digit number cannot begin with 0. So the hundreds digit is 2 or 5. List the numbers that begin with 2 first.
A similar problem: with the digits 0 and 7 used once each, 07 is just 7, so the only 2-digit number is 70. That is 1 number, not 2.

stepByStep.text: The hundreds digit can be 2 or 5, but not 0.
Starting with 2: 205 and 250. Starting with 5: 502 and 520.
Count them.
4 three-digit numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 × 2 × 1, which also counts 025 and 052. Those begin with 0, so they are really 2-digit numbers.
misconceptions.B: One number has been missed. For each of the two possible hundreds digits there are 2 numbers.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 205, 250, 502 and 520 are the 4 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This counts the choices for the hundreds place only. Each choice gives 2 different numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_021.questionText: A big triangle has two straight lines drawn from its top corner down to its base. These lines split it into 3 small triangles side by side. Counting triangles of every size, how many triangles are there in the figure?
hints: Count the small triangles first, then triangles made by joining neighbouring small ones.
There are 3 small triangles. Next, count the triangles made of 2 small triangles that are next to each other.
A similar problem: one line from the top corner to the base splits a triangle into 2 small triangles. Together with the big one, that makes 2 + 1 = 3 triangles.

stepByStep.text: There are 3 small triangles.
Two neighbouring small triangles together make a bigger triangle. This can be done in 2 ways: left with middle, and middle with right.
All three together make the 1 big triangle.
Add them all.
There are 6 triangles in the figure.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the small triangles. Neighbouring ones join to make bigger triangles too.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 3 small, 2 made of two parts, and 1 big one make 6.
misconceptions.C: One triangle has been missed. Check the two-part triangles: left with middle, and middle with right.
misconceptions.D: This counts the small triangles and the big one. Two neighbouring small triangles also make a triangle.

G4A_COUNTING_022.questionText: In a ticket queue at the railway station, Ravi is 8th from the front and Sana is 15th from the front. How many people stand between them?
hints: The people between them hold the positions after Ravi and before Sana. Neither Ravi nor Sana is counted.
List the positions between them, starting 9th, 10th, and stopping just before the 15th.
A similar problem: between the 3rd and the 6th person stand the 4th and the 5th. Subtracting gives 6 − 3 = 3, and taking 1 away gives 2 people.

stepByStep.text: The people between them are at positions 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
A quick way: subtract the positions and take away 1.
6 people stand between them.

misconceptions.A: This is 15 − 8, which counts Sana as well. Take 1 away so that only the people in between are counted.
misconceptions.B: This adds the two positions. To find who is between them, look at the positions from 9th to 14th.
misconceptions.C: This counts both Ravi and Sana along with the people between them. Count only positions 9 to 14.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Positions 9 to 14 hold 6 people.

G4A_COUNTING_023.questionText: How many numbers from 100 to 200, counting both 100 and 200, end in the digit 0?
hints: Numbers ending in 0 come once in every ten numbers. Be careful with both ends of the range.
List them: 100, 110, 120, and keep going. Check whether 200 belongs in your list.
A similar problem: from 10 to 50, the numbers ending in 0 are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. There are 4 jumps of ten, and 4 + 1 = 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: From 100 to 200 there are 10 jumps of ten, and one more for the starting number.
There are 11 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Ten jumps of ten from 100 to 200 give 11 numbers.
misconceptions.B: This counts the jumps of ten. Both 100 and 200 are in the range, so there is one more number than jumps.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out both 100 and 200. The question says to count both.
misconceptions.D: This counts too many. Only one number in every ten ends in 0.

G4A_COUNTING_024.questionText: The pages of a book are numbered starting from 1. In all, 129 digits were printed for the page numbers. How many pages does the book have?
hints: Work backwards. Take away the digits used by the one-digit pages, then see how many two-digit pages the remaining digits can number.
Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Subtract these from 129 to find the digits left for pages with two digits.
A similar problem: a booklet uses 29 digits. Pages 1 to 9 use 9, leaving 20 digits. That numbers 20 ÷ 2 = 10 two-digit pages, so the booklet has 9 + 10 = 19 pages.

stepByStep.text: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Find the digits left.
Each page from 10 onwards uses 2 digits.
Add the one-digit pages and the two-digit pages.
The book has 69 pages.

misconceptions.A: This halves 129 as if every page used two digits. Pages 1 to 9 use only one digit each.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 9 one-digit pages and 60 two-digit pages make 69 pages.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of two-digit pages only. The 9 one-digit pages must be added.
misconceptions.D: This adds 10 one-digit pages. The one-digit pages are 1 to 9, which is 9 pages.

G4A_COUNTING_025.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers have a tens digit that is bigger than the ones digit? For example, 72 is such a number but 27 is not.
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the tens digit and count the ones digits that are smaller than it. Look for a pattern.
With tens digit 1, the only smaller ones digit is 0, giving 10. With tens digit 2, the ones digit can be 0 or 1. Carry on up to tens digit 9.
A similar problem: among numbers from 10 to 39, tens digit 1 gives 1 number (10), tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers (20, 21) and tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers (30, 31, 32). That is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Tens digit 1 gives 1 number (10). Tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers (20, 21). Tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers, and so on.
Tens digit 9 gives 9 numbers (90 to 98).
Add the counts.
There are 45 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the numbers with ones digit 0, such as 10, 20 and 30. Zero is smaller than every tens digit.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 + 2 + 3 up to 10. The largest tens digit is 9, so the adding stops at 9.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 9 = 45.
misconceptions.D: This only removes the 9 numbers with equal digits, like 11 and 22. Numbers such as 27, where the tens digit is smaller, must also be left out.

G4A_COUNTING_026.questionText: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 4?
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the hundreds digit, then count the ways the other two digits can make up the rest.
Start with hundreds digit 1. The other two digits must add up to 3. List these numbers, then move on to hundreds digit 2.
A similar problem: 3-digit numbers with digits adding to 2 are 101, 110 and 200. Hundreds digit 1 gives 2 numbers and hundreds digit 2 gives 1 number, so there are 3.

stepByStep.text: Hundreds digit 1: the other digits add to 3, giving 103, 112, 121 and 130. That is 4 numbers.
Hundreds digit 2: 202, 211 and 220. That is 3 numbers.
Hundreds digit 3: 301 and 310. Hundreds digit 4: 400. That is 2 numbers and 1 number.
Add the counts.
There are 10 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been missed. Check for 400, where the digits are 4, 0 and 0.
misconceptions.B: This also counts numbers like 013 and 004 that begin with 0. Those are not 3-digit numbers.
misconceptions.C: This only arranges the digits 1, 0 and 3. Other sets of digits also add up to 4, such as 1, 1, 2 and 2, 2, 0.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_027.questionText: A square board is divided into 9 small squares, in 3 rows of 3. Counting squares of every size, how many squares are there on the board?
hints: Squares come in different sizes. Count each size separately: the smallest, the middle size, and the largest.
There are 9 small squares. Now count the squares that are 2 small squares wide and 2 tall. One sits in each corner of the board.
A similar problem: a board with 2 rows of 2 has 4 small squares and 1 big square, so 4 + 1 = 5 squares.

stepByStep.text: There are 9 small squares.
Squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall: one fits in each corner of the board, so there are 4.
The whole board is 1 large square.
Add all the sizes.
There are 14 squares on the board.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 9 small, 4 middle-sized and 1 large make 14.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the small squares. Bigger squares are made by joining small ones.
misconceptions.C: This counts the small squares and the whole board. There are also 4 squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the whole board, which is the largest square of all.

G4A_COUNTING_028.questionText: Four small squares are joined in a single row to make a long strip. Counting rectangles of every size, with the small squares counted too, how many rectangles are there in the strip?
hints: A rectangle in the strip is made of 1, 2, 3 or 4 neighbouring squares. Count each length separately.
There are 4 rectangles made of 1 square. Next, count the rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: first with second, second with third, and so on.
A similar problem: a strip of 3 squares has 3 rectangles of one square, 2 of two squares and 1 of three squares. That is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 rectangles.

stepByStep.text: Rectangles made of 1 square: 4.
Rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: 3. Made of 3 neighbouring squares: 2.
The whole strip of 4 squares: 1.
Add them.
There are 10 rectangles in the strip.

misconceptions.A: This counts the single squares and the pairs. Rectangles made of 3 squares and the whole strip count too.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 rectangles.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the small squares. Neighbouring squares join to make longer rectangles.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the whole strip, which is the longest rectangle.

G4A_COUNTING_029.questionText: At a birthday party, every child gave one card to every other child. In all, 30 cards were given. How many children were at the party?
hints: Each child gives a card to everyone except themselves. So the total is the number of children times one less than that number.
Try a small party: with 3 children, each gives 2 cards. Work out the total for 4 children, then 5, and keep going until you reach 30.
A similar problem: if 12 cards were given, try 4 children. Each gives 3 cards, and 4 × 3 = 12. So there were 4 children.

stepByStep.text: If there are some children, each one gives a card to all the others, which is one fewer than the number of children.
Look for two numbers next to each other that multiply to 30.
So 6 children each gave 5 cards.
There were 6 children at the party.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of cards each child gave. The number of children is one more than that.
misconceptions.B: This halves 30, as for handshakes. A card goes one way only, so every card is counted just once.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 6 children giving 5 cards each makes 30 cards.
misconceptions.D: With 10 children, each would give 9 cards, making 90 cards. Look for two neighbouring numbers that multiply to 30.

G4A_COUNTING_030.questionText: Using the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3, with no digit repeated in a number, how many 3-digit even numbers can be made?
hints: Two places need care: the ones place must make the number even, and the hundreds place cannot be 0. Split into cases by the last digit.
An even number here ends in 0 or 2. First count the numbers that end in 0. The other two places are filled from 1, 2 and 3.
A similar problem: 2-digit even numbers from the digits 0, 3 and 4 with no repeats. Ending in 0: 30 and 40. Ending in 4: only 34, because 04 is not a 2-digit number. That is 2 + 1 = 3 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Ending in 0: the hundreds digit has 3 choices (1, 2 or 3) and the tens digit then has 2 choices.
Ending in 2: the hundreds digit can only be 1 or 3, and the tens digit then has 2 choices.
Add the two cases.
10 such numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This allows 0 in the hundreds place for numbers ending in 2, such as 012 and 032. Those are not 3-digit numbers.
misconceptions.B: Some numbers ending in 2 have been missed. They are 102, 132, 302 and 312.
misconceptions.C: This is the count of all 3-digit numbers that can be made. Only those ending in 0 or 2 are even.
misconceptions.D: Great job! 6 numbers end in 0 and 4 end in 2, making 10.

G4A_COUNTING_031.questionText: A temple bell takes 6 seconds to ring 4 times, measured from the first ring to the last ring. The rings are evenly spaced. How many seconds does it take to ring 10 times?
hints: The time is spent in the gaps between the rings, not on the rings themselves. Count the gaps.
Between 4 rings there are 3 gaps. Use this to find how long one gap lasts.
A similar problem: a bell takes 8 seconds to ring 3 times. That is 2 gaps, so each gap is 4 seconds. Ringing 6 times has 5 gaps, which takes 5 × 4 = 20 seconds.

stepByStep.text: 4 rings have 3 gaps between them. Find the length of one gap.
10 rings have 9 gaps between them.
Multiply the gaps by the length of each gap.
It takes 18 seconds to ring 10 times.

misconceptions.A: This divides 6 seconds by 4 rings. The time is taken by the 3 gaps between the rings, so each gap is 2 seconds.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! 9 gaps of 2 seconds each take 18 seconds.
misconceptions.C: This uses 2 seconds per gap, which is right, but counts 10 gaps. Between 10 rings there are only 9 gaps.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the 6 seconds. Count the gaps instead: 4 rings have 3 gaps and 10 rings have 9 gaps.

G4A_COUNTING_032.questionText: Children stand in a row. Tara is 9th from the left and Uma is 6th from the right. They swap places, and now Tara is 15th from the left. How many children are in the row?
hints: After the swap, Tara stands exactly where Uma stood. So you know one spot's position from both ends.
Uma's old spot is 6th from the right. After the swap Tara is in that spot, and it is 15th from the left. Use both positions for this one spot.
A similar problem: a spot is 4th from the left and 3rd from the right. There are 3 children to its left and 2 to its right, so the row has 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 children.

stepByStep.text: After swapping, Tara stands in Uma's old spot. That spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right.
Add the two positions and take away 1, because the spot is counted twice.
There are 20 children in the row.

misconceptions.A: This adds 15 and 6 but counts the child in that spot twice. Take 1 away.
misconceptions.B: This is Tara's new position from the left. There are still 5 more children to her right.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The same spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right, so 15 + 6 − 1 = 20.
misconceptions.D: This adds Tara's old and new positions, 9 and 15. Use the two positions of the same spot instead: 15th from the left and 6th from the right.

G4A_COUNTING_033.questionText: Aman writes all the numbers from 1 to 100. How many times does he write the digit 1?
hints: Count place by place: how often the digit is in the ones place, in the tens place, and in the hundreds place.
In the ones place the digit 1 appears in 1, 11, 21, and so on up to 91. Count these first, then look at the tens place.
A similar problem: from 1 to 50, the digit 4 is in the ones place 5 times (4, 14, 24, 34, 44) and in the tens place 10 times (40 to 49). That makes 15 times.

stepByStep.text: Tens place: 10, 11, 12, and so on up to 19.
Hundreds place: only in 100.
Add them.
Aman writes the digit 1 a total of 21 times.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 10 in the ones place, 10 in the tens place and 1 in the number 100 make 21.
misconceptions.B: This leaves out the 1 in 100. The number 100 is in the list too.
misconceptions.C: This counts 11 only once and leaves out 100. The number 11 has two 1s, and both are written.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the ones place and the 1 in 100. The numbers 10 to 19 each have a 1 in the tens place as well.

G4A_COUNTING_034.questionText: How many numbers from 1 to 60 can be divided exactly by 2 or by 3, or by both?
hints: Some numbers can be divided by both 2 and 3. If you count the two groups and add, those numbers get counted twice.
Count the multiples of 2 up to 60, and the multiples of 3 up to 60. Then find how many numbers are in both lists.
A similar problem: from 1 to 12 there are 6 multiples of 2 and 4 multiples of 3. The numbers 6 and 12 are in both lists. So the count is 6 + 4 − 2 = 8.

stepByStep.text: Count the multiples of 2 and the multiples of 3.
Numbers in both lists are the multiples of 6.
Add the two lists and take away the numbers counted twice.
There are 40 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This adds 30 and 20, which counts the multiples of 6 twice. Take away those 10 numbers.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the multiples of 2. Odd multiples of 3, such as 3, 9 and 15, belong too.
misconceptions.C: This is how many numbers are divisible by both 2 and 3. The question also wants numbers divisible by just one of them.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 30 + 20 − 10 = 40.

G4A_COUNTING_035.questionText: A flag has 3 stripes in a row. Each stripe is painted red, green or blue. Stripes that touch each other must be different colours. How many different flags can be made?
hints: Choose the colours stripe by stripe. Read the rule with care: only stripes that touch must differ.
The first stripe can be any of the 3 colours. The second stripe must differ from the first. Think about how many colours the third stripe can take.
A similar problem: a flag with 2 stripes and 3 colours, where the stripes must differ. The first stripe has 3 choices and the second has 2, so there are 3 × 2 = 6 flags.

stepByStep.text: The first stripe can be any of 3 colours.
The second stripe touches the first, so it has 2 choices.
The third stripe touches only the second, so it also has 2 choices. It may match the first stripe.
Multiply the choices.
12 different flags can be made.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 flags.
misconceptions.B: This makes all three stripes different. The first and third stripes do not touch, so they may be the same colour.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 3 × 3, which lets touching stripes share a colour. The second and third stripes each have only 2 choices.
misconceptions.D: This is 3 × 3. Count the choices for each stripe in turn: 3, then 2, then 2.

G4A_COUNTING_036.questionText: How many numbers are in this list?  4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24
hints: Count the numbers one at a time. You are counting how many there are, not looking at how big they are.
Point to each number in turn and count: 4 is the first, 8 is the second, and so on.
A similar problem: the list 5, 10, 15 has three numbers, because we count 5 as one, 10 as two and 15 as three.

stepByStep.text: Count the numbers one by one: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.
There are 6 numbers in the list.

misconceptions.A: One number has been missed. Point to each number as you count.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Counting one by one gives 6 numbers.
misconceptions.C: This is the last number in the list. The question asks how many numbers there are.
misconceptions.D: One number has been counted twice. Point to each number as you count.

G4A_COUNTING_037.questionText: Ria writes down all the whole numbers from 6 to 10: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. How many numbers does she write?
hints: Count the numbers Ria writes, one at a time.
Point to each number in the list 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and count as you go.
A similar problem: the whole numbers from 2 to 4 are 2, 3, 4. Counting them one by one gives 3 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Count the numbers one by one: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
Ria writes 5 numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been missed. Count 6 as the first number.
misconceptions.B: This is the last number Ria writes. The question asks how many numbers she writes.
misconceptions.C: Great job! 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 make 5 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This is the first number Ria writes. The question asks how many numbers she writes.

G4A_COUNTING_038.questionText: How many whole numbers lie between 10 and 15? Do not count 10 or 15.
hints: Write out the numbers that come after the first number and before the last one, then count them.
The first number after 10 is 11. Keep writing numbers until you reach the one just before 15.
A similar problem: the whole numbers between 3 and 6 are 4 and 5, so there are 2 of them.

stepByStep.text: Write the numbers that come after 10 and before 15: 11, 12, 13, 14.
Count them. There are 4 whole numbers between 10 and 15.

misconceptions.A: You got it! The numbers are 11, 12, 13 and 14, which makes 4.
misconceptions.B: This counts one of the end numbers too. Count only 11, 12, 13 and 14.
misconceptions.C: This counts 10 and 15 as well. They are the ends, so leave them out.
misconceptions.D: One number has been missed. The numbers are 11, 12, 13 and 14.

G4A_COUNTING_039.questionText: Anu and Bala stand in a line, one behind the other. In how many different orders can they stand?
hints: Write down every order you can think of, then count them.
Start with Anu in front and Bala behind. Is there another way?
A similar problem: a red cup and a blue cup on a shelf can be placed as red then blue, or blue then red. That is 2 orders.

stepByStep.text: List the orders: Anu in front with Bala behind, or Bala in front with Anu behind.
There are no other ways, so they can stand in 2 different orders.

misconceptions.A: There is one more way. The two children can swap places.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Anu then Bala, or Bala then Anu, makes 2 orders.
misconceptions.C: There are only two children, so only two orders are possible. List them to check.
misconceptions.D: There are only two children, so only two orders are possible. List them to check.

G4A_COUNTING_040.questionText: Using the digits 4 and 7 once each, how many different 2-digit numbers can you make?
hints: Write down every number you can make, then count them.
Put 4 in the tens place and 7 in the ones place. Then try the digits the other way round.
A similar problem: with the digits 2 and 5 once each, the numbers are 25 and 52. That is 2 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Put 4 first and then 7 to make 47. Put 7 first and then 4 to make 74.
There are no other ways, so you can make 2 different numbers.

misconceptions.A: Great job! The numbers are 47 and 74, which makes 2.
misconceptions.B: This would count 44 and 77 too. Each digit may be used only once in a number.
misconceptions.C: There is one more number. Swap the two digits around.
misconceptions.D: Each digit is used once, so the only numbers are 47 and 74. Count them again.

G4A_COUNTING_041.questionText: Five children stand in a queue in this order, starting from the front: Asha, Bina, Chetan, Dev, Esha. Who is 3rd in the queue?
hints: Count along the queue from the front, one child at a time.
Asha is 1st because she is at the front. Keep counting: 2nd, 3rd.
A similar problem: in the queue Ravi, Sita, Tara, counting from the front, Ravi is 1st and Sita is 2nd.

stepByStep.text: Count from the front: Asha is 1st and Bina is 2nd.
The next child is 3rd. So Chetan is 3rd in the queue.

misconceptions.A: Bina is 2nd in the queue. Count one more child along.
misconceptions.B: Dev is 4th in the queue. Count from the front again: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Asha is 1st, Bina is 2nd and Chetan is 3rd.
misconceptions.D: Esha is 5th, at the back of the queue. Count from the front: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.

G4A_COUNTING_042.questionText: Ravi is 4th in a queue. How many children are standing in front of him?
hints: Think about the places in the queue that come before Ravi's place.
The places in front of the 4th place are the 1st, the 2nd and so on. List them.
A similar problem: Sita is 6th in a queue. The children in front of her are 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th, so 5 children are in front of her.

stepByStep.text: The places in front of the 4th place are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd places.
So 3 children are standing in front of Ravi.

misconceptions.A: This counts Ravi too. Ravi is the 4th child, so the ones in front are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd.
misconceptions.B: This is one more than Ravi's place. Count only the places before the 4th.
misconceptions.C: One place has been missed. The places in front are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd.
misconceptions.D: You got it! The 1st, 2nd and 3rd children are in front of Ravi.

G4A_COUNTING_043.questionText: There are 6 children in a queue. Meena is at the very front. How many children are behind her?
hints: Everyone in the queue except Meena is behind her.
Take Meena away from the 6 children and see how many are left.
A similar problem: 9 children are in a queue and Arun is at the very front. The other 9 − 1 = 8 children are behind him.

stepByStep.text: Meena is at the front, so all the other children are behind her.
Take Meena away from the 6 children. So 5 children are behind her.

misconceptions.A: This counts Meena too. She is at the front, so take her away from the 6.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 6 − 1 = 5 children are behind Meena.
misconceptions.C: This takes away one child too many. Only Meena is not behind herself.
misconceptions.D: This is more than the whole queue. Take Meena away from the 6 children.

G4A_COUNTING_044.questionText: How many even numbers are in this list?  3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 13
hints: An even number can be shared into two equal groups. Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Go through the list one number at a time and look at the last digit of each.
A similar problem: in the list 1, 2, 5, 6 the even numbers are 2 and 6, so there are 2 even numbers.

stepByStep.text: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. In the list, these are 4, 8 and 10.
So there are 3 even numbers in the list.

misconceptions.A: One even number has been missed. Remember that 10 ends in 0, so it is even.
misconceptions.B: This counts every number in the list. Count only the even ones: 4, 8 and 10.
misconceptions.C: One odd number has been counted. The numbers 3, 7 and 13 are odd.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The even numbers are 4, 8 and 10, which makes 3.

G4A_COUNTING_045.questionText: Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row. Writing A for Anu, B for Binu and C for Charu, all the possible orders are: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA. In how many of these orders is Anu first?
hints: Look at the first letter of each order in the list.
Anu is shown by the letter A. Find the orders that begin with A and count them.
A similar problem: in the same list, the orders that begin with C are CAB and CBA, so Charu is first in 2 orders.

stepByStep.text: Look for the orders that begin with A: they are ABC and ACB.
So Anu is first in 2 of the orders.

misconceptions.A: You got it! Only ABC and ACB begin with A.
misconceptions.B: Count again, looking only at the first letter. Only ABC and ACB begin with A.
misconceptions.C: There is one more. Both ABC and ACB begin with A.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of orders in the whole list. Count only the ones that begin with A.

G4A_COUNTING_046.questionText: Count the days from Monday to Thursday, counting both Monday and Thursday. How many days is that?
hints: Say the days in order and count each one as you say it.
Start with Monday as the first day. Keep going until you have said Thursday.
A similar problem: from Friday to Sunday, counting both, the days are Friday, Saturday, Sunday. That is 3 days.

stepByStep.text: List the days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday.
Count them. That is 4 days.

misconceptions.A: One day has been left out. Count Monday and Thursday too.
misconceptions.B: One day too many has been counted. Stop at Thursday.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the days in between. The question says to count Monday and Thursday too.
misconceptions.D: Great job! Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday make 4 days.

G4A_COUNTING_047.questionText: Seven chairs stand in a row. They are numbered 1 to 7 in order. Which chair is exactly in the middle?
hints: The middle chair has the same number of chairs on each side of it.
Write the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in a row. Cross off one from each end, again and again, until one is left.
A similar problem: for five chairs numbered 1 to 5, cross off 1 and 5, then 2 and 4. Chair 3 is left, with two chairs on each side.

stepByStep.text: Write the chairs in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
Chairs 1, 2 and 3 are on one side and chairs 5, 6 and 7 are on the other side.
With three chairs on each side, the middle one is Chair 4.

misconceptions.A: Chair 3 has two chairs on one side and four on the other. The middle chair has the same number on each side.
misconceptions.B: Chair 5 has four chairs on one side and two on the other. The middle chair has the same number on each side.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Chair 4 has three chairs on each side.
misconceptions.D: Chair 7 is at the end of the row. The middle chair has the same number of chairs on each side.

G4A_DATA_001.questionText: Rohit's runs in five cricket matches were: Match 1 34, Match 2 52, Match 3 47, Match 4 25, Match 5 43. In which match did he score the most runs?
hints: This asks you to find the biggest number in a list and say which match it belongs to.
Compare the tens digits of the five scores first. Which scores have the biggest tens digit?
Example: Scores of Game 1 18, Game 2 31, Game 3 27. The biggest number is 31, so the most runs came in Game 2.

stepByStep.text: Look at the tens digits: 34, 52, 47, 25 and 43 have tens digits 3, 5, 4, 2 and 4.
The biggest tens digit is 5, so 52 is the biggest score.
52 runs were scored in Match 2, so the answer is Match 2.

misconceptions.A: Match 3 has 47 runs, which is the second biggest score. Check whether any score is in the fifties.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 52 is bigger than 34, 47, 25 and 43, and it belongs to Match 2.
misconceptions.C: Match 5 has 43 runs. Compare it with 52 and 47 to see which is biggest.
misconceptions.D: Match 4 has 25 runs, which is the smallest score. The question asks for the most runs, so look for the biggest number.

G4A_DATA_002.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture of a book stands for 5 books sold. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures, Wednesday has 3 pictures and Thursday has 5 pictures. On which day were the fewest books sold?
hints: Every picture stands for the same number of books, so think about what the number of pictures tells you.
The day with the fewest pictures has the fewest books. Compare 4, 6, 3 and 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 kites. Ravi has 7 pictures, Sita has 2 pictures and Anu has 5 pictures. Sita has the fewest pictures, so Sita has the fewest kites.

stepByStep.text: Each picture stands for the same number of books, so fewer pictures means fewer books.
The numbers of pictures are 4, 6, 3 and 5. The smallest is 3.
Wednesday has 3 pictures, which is 15 books.
The fewest books were sold on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: Monday has 4 pictures, which is 20 books. Is there a day with fewer pictures than 4?
misconceptions.B: Tuesday has 6 pictures, the most of all. The question asks for the fewest, so look for the smallest number of pictures.
misconceptions.C: Thursday has 5 pictures, which is 25 books. Look for a day with fewer pictures.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Wednesday has only 3 pictures, fewer than any other day, so it has the fewest books.

G4A_DATA_003.questionText: In a tally chart, each bundle stands for 5 and each single stroke stands for 1. The row for parrots has 3 bundles and 2 single strokes. How many parrots were counted?
hints: A tally chart counts in fives. Work out the bundles first, then add the single strokes.
Find how many the 3 bundles stand for by multiplying 3 by 5.
Example: 2 bundles and 4 single strokes. The bundles give 2 x 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

stepByStep.text: Each bundle stands for 5, so 3 bundles stand for 15.
Add the 2 single strokes.
17 parrots were counted.

misconceptions.A: Great counting! 3 bundles make 15, and 2 more strokes make 17.
misconceptions.B: This adds 3 and 2 as if every mark stood for 1. Remember that each bundle stands for 5.
misconceptions.C: This counts the 3 bundles but leaves out the 2 single strokes. Add them on.
misconceptions.D: This writes the 3 and the 2 side by side. Each bundle is worth 5, so multiply 3 by 5 and then add 2.

G4A_DATA_004.questionText: The number of children present in Class 4 was: Mon 38, Tue 35, Wed 40, Thu 32. How many more children were present on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
hints: The words 'how many more' ask you to compare two numbers from the list.
Pick out the numbers for Wednesday and Tuesday only. They are 40 and 35.
Example: Mon 26, Tue 19. To find how many more on Monday, subtract: 26 - 19 = 7.

stepByStep.text: Wednesday has 40 children and Tuesday has 35 children.
Subtract to find how many more.
5 more children were present on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: This adds 40 and 35. To find how many more, subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
misconceptions.B: This compares Wednesday with Thursday. The question asks about Wednesday and Tuesday.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 40 - 35 = 5, so 5 more children came on Wednesday.
misconceptions.D: This compares Monday with Tuesday. Use Wednesday's number, 40, and Tuesday's number, 35.

G4A_DATA_005.questionText: A bar graph shows the samosas sold at a stall: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 11. Which two days have bars of the same height?
hints: Bars of the same height show the same number. Look for a number that appears twice.
Read the five numbers one by one: 12, 15, 9, 15, 11. Which number do you see two times?
Example: Red 7, Blue 4, Green 7, Yellow 6. The number 7 appears twice, so the bars for Red and Green are equally tall.

stepByStep.text: Bars are equally tall when their numbers are equal.
In the list 12, 15, 9, 15, 11 only the number 15 appears twice.
15 belongs to Tuesday and Thursday, so the equal bars are Tuesday and Thursday.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Both Tuesday and Thursday show 15 samosas, so their bars are the same height.
misconceptions.B: Monday shows 12 and Friday shows 11. They are close, but not equal. Look for two numbers that match exactly.
misconceptions.C: Monday shows 12 and Thursday shows 15. Find the other day that also shows 15.
misconceptions.D: Wednesday shows 9 and Friday shows 11. Look for two days with exactly the same number.

G4A_DATA_006.questionText: The children of Class 4 each chose one favourite fruit: Mango 14, Banana 6, Apple 9, Guava 5. How many children chose banana or guava?
hints: You need to put two groups from the table together.
Pick out only the numbers for banana and guava. They are 6 and 5.
Example: Rose 8, Lily 7, Lotus 4. The children who chose rose or lotus are 8 + 4 = 12.

stepByStep.text: Banana was chosen by 6 children and guava by 5 children.
Add the two groups.
11 children chose banana or guava.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 5 from 6. The question asks for both groups together, so add them.
misconceptions.B: This adds mango and banana. The question asks about banana and guava.
misconceptions.C: This adds all four fruits. Only banana and guava are needed.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 6 children and 5 children make 11 children.

G4A_DATA_007.questionText: Six children got these marks in a spelling test: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many children got more than 15 marks?
hints: Here you count how many numbers in a list are bigger than a given number.
Go through the marks one at a time and tick each one that is bigger than 15. Start with 14: is it bigger than 15?
Example: Marks 6, 11, 8, 13, 5. The marks more than 10 are 11 and 13, so 2 children got more than 10.

stepByStep.text: Check each mark against 15.
14, 9 and 12 are less than 15. The marks 18, 20 and 17 are more than 15.
That makes 3 children with more than 15 marks.

misconceptions.A: One of the marks above 15 has been missed. Check 18, 20 and 17 again.
misconceptions.B: Good checking! 18, 20 and 17 are the marks above 15, so the count is 3.
misconceptions.C: This also counts 14, but 14 is less than 15. Count only the marks bigger than 15.
misconceptions.D: This counts all six children. Count only the children whose marks are bigger than 15.

G4A_DATA_008.questionText: Each child in a class chose one favourite game: Cricket 13, Kho-kho 8, Football 7, Carrom 4. How many children are there in the class?
hints: Every child chose exactly one game, so the whole class is all the groups put together.
Add the four numbers. A good start is 13 + 7, which makes a round number.
Example: Tea 9, Milk 11, Juice 5. All together that is 9 + 11 + 5 = 25 people.

stepByStep.text: Add cricket and football first.
Add kho-kho and carrom.
Put the two sums together.
There are 32 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the 4 children who chose carrom. Add all four groups.
misconceptions.B: This counts the number of games. The question asks for the number of children, so add the four numbers.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 13 + 8 + 7 + 4 = 32.
misconceptions.D: The ones add up to more than 10 here, so a ten must be carried. Try adding 13 + 7 first, then 8 + 4.

G4A_DATA_009.questionText: In a tally chart, a bundle stands for 5 and a single stroke stands for 1. Which of these shows 23?
hints: Think about how many full fives fit into the number, and what is left over.
Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. How many fives is that, and how many more do you need to reach 23?
Example: To show 12, count in fives: 5, 10. That is 2 bundles, and 12 - 10 = 2 single strokes.

stepByStep.text: Four fives make 20.
Find what is left after 20.
So 23 is shown by 4 bundles and 3 strokes.

misconceptions.A: This copies the digits 2 and 3 of the number 23. But 2 bundles are only 10, so this shows 13.
misconceptions.B: Lovely! 4 bundles make 20 and 3 strokes make 23.
misconceptions.C: 5 bundles are already 25, which is more than 23. Use fewer bundles.
misconceptions.D: 3 bundles make 15, and 4 more strokes make 19. Count in fives until you are close to 23.

G4A_DATA_010.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture of a sun stands for 2 sunny days. January has 5 pictures, February has 8 pictures, March has 6 pictures and April has 9 pictures. Which month had 16 sunny days?
hints: Each picture stands for more than one day, so the number of pictures is not the number of days.
Work out how many pictures are needed to show 16 days when each picture stands for 2 days.
Example: Each picture stands for 5 pens. To show 20 pens you need 20 divided by 5 = 4 pictures, so look for the row with 4 pictures.

stepByStep.text: Each picture stands for 2 days, so 16 days need 8 pictures.
The month with 8 pictures is February.
February had 16 sunny days.

misconceptions.A: January has 5 pictures, which stand for 10 sunny days. Find the month with 8 pictures.
misconceptions.B: March has 6 pictures, which stand for 12 sunny days. Find the month with 8 pictures.
misconceptions.C: April has 9 pictures, which stand for 18 sunny days. That is a little too many.
misconceptions.D: Yes! February has 8 pictures and 8 x 2 = 16 sunny days.

G4A_DATA_011.questionText: The heights of five plants in centimetres are: Rose 34, Tulsi 28, Neem 41, Mint 19, Lily 37. Which plant is the second tallest?
hints: Put the numbers in order from biggest to smallest, then pick the one in second place.
Find the tallest plant first. Which height is the biggest of 34, 28, 41, 19 and 37?
Example: Asha 22, Bina 30, Charu 26. From biggest to smallest: 30, 26, 22. The second biggest is 26, so Charu is second tallest.

stepByStep.text: From biggest to smallest the heights are 41, 37, 34, 28, 19.
The tallest is 41 (Neem). The next is 37.
37 cm is the height of Lily, so the second tallest plant is Lily.

misconceptions.A: Super! Neem is tallest at 41 cm, and Lily comes next at 37 cm.
misconceptions.B: Neem is the tallest plant. The question asks for the second tallest, the one just below it.
misconceptions.C: Rose is 34 cm, which is third. One plant is taller than Rose but shorter than Neem.
misconceptions.D: Tulsi is second in the list, but the list is not in order of height. Arrange the heights from biggest to smallest first.

G4A_DATA_012.questionText: The side of a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. The top of Tuesday's bar is exactly halfway between the marks 20 and 30. What number does Tuesday's bar show?
hints: When a bar ends between two marks, its value is between those two numbers.
Find the number that is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30. How far apart are 20 and 30?
Example: A bar ends halfway between 40 and 60. The marks are 20 apart, half of 20 is 10, and 40 + 10 = 50.

stepByStep.text: The marks 20 and 30 are 10 apart.
Half of 10 is 5.
Go 5 above 20.
Tuesday's bar shows 25.

misconceptions.A: 20 is the mark below the top of the bar. The bar goes up beyond 20, halfway to 30.
misconceptions.B: 30 is the mark above the top of the bar. The bar stops halfway before it reaches 30.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 25 is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30.
misconceptions.D: This adds 20 and 30. The bar ends between the two marks, so find the number in the middle of them.

G4A_DATA_013.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 3 kites. Ravi's row has 5 pictures and Meena's row has 8 pictures. How many more kites does Meena have than Ravi?
hints: This is a pictograph comparison. Remember that each picture stands for more than one kite.
Find how many more pictures Meena has than Ravi: 8 - 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 balls. Amit has 6 pictures and Sunil has 4 pictures. Amit has 2 more pictures, and 2 x 4 = 8 more balls.

stepByStep.text: Meena has 3 more pictures than Ravi.
Each picture stands for 3 kites.
Meena has 9 more kites than Ravi.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 3 extra pictures, each worth 3 kites, make 9 kites.
misconceptions.B: This is how many more pictures Meena has. Each picture stands for 3 kites, so multiply by 3.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of kites Meena has. The question asks how many more she has than Ravi.
misconceptions.D: This adds Ravi's 15 kites and Meena's 24 kites. To find how many more, subtract.

G4A_DATA_014.questionText: In a pictograph of library books, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures and Wednesday has 3 pictures. How many books were borrowed on the three days altogether?
hints: Find the total number of pictures, then change pictures into books.
Add the pictures for the three days: 4 + 6 + 3.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 pens. Three rows have 3, 5 and 4 pictures. That is 12 pictures, and 12 x 2 = 24 pens.

stepByStep.text: Add the pictures for the three days.
Each picture stands for 5 books.
65 books were borrowed altogether.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of pictures. Each picture stands for 5 books, so multiply by 5.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 13 pictures stand for 13 x 5 = 65 books.
misconceptions.C: This adds 5 to the 13 pictures. Each of the 13 pictures stands for 5 books, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: One picture has been missed. There are 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 pictures in all, not 12.

G4A_DATA_015.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 6 eggs. A farmer's chart has 5 pictures for Monday and 3 pictures for Tuesday. He packs all these eggs in boxes of 12. How many boxes does he fill?
hints: There are two parts here: first find the number of eggs, then share them into boxes.
Find the total number of pictures for the two days, then multiply by 6 to get the eggs.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 buns. There are 6 pictures, so 24 buns. Packed in bags of 8, that is 24 divided by 8 = 3 bags.

stepByStep.text: Add the pictures.
Each picture stands for 6 eggs.
Put the eggs in boxes of 12.
He fills 4 boxes.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of pictures. Change the pictures into eggs, then into boxes of 12.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of eggs. The question asks how many boxes of 12 they fill.
misconceptions.C: Great work! 48 eggs fill 4 boxes of 12.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts the pictures. Both days' eggs are packed, so add the pictures first.

G4A_DATA_016.questionText: A sweet shop sold 60 laddoos in four days. The table shows: Mon 12, Tue 18, Thu 14, but the number for Wednesday is smudged. How many laddoos were sold on Wednesday?
hints: You know the whole and three of its four parts. Think about how to find the missing part.
Add the three numbers you can read: 12 + 18 + 14.
Example: Total 50, and three days show 10, 15 and 5. These add to 30, so the missing day is 50 - 30 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Add the three known days.
Take this away from the total.
16 laddoos were sold on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: This is the total for the three known days. Take it away from 60 to find Wednesday.
misconceptions.B: This shares 60 equally among four days. The days are not equal, so subtract the known days from the total.
misconceptions.C: This adds the three days to 60. The 60 already includes them, so subtract.

G4A_DATA_017.questionText: Tickets sold at a mela: on Saturday, 20 adult tickets and 35 child tickets; on Sunday, 28 adult tickets and 30 child tickets. How many more tickets were sold on Sunday than on Saturday?
hints: Each day has two kinds of ticket. Find each day's total before you compare.
Add the adult and child tickets for Saturday: 20 + 35.
Example: Day 1 has 10 and 12 tickets, total 22. Day 2 has 15 and 14 tickets, total 29. Day 2 sold 29 - 22 = 7 more.

stepByStep.text: Saturday's total.
Sunday's total.
Compare the totals.
3 more tickets were sold on Sunday.

misconceptions.A: That is right! Sunday's 58 tickets are 3 more than Saturday's 55.
misconceptions.B: This compares only the adult tickets. Child tickets count too, so find each day's total.
misconceptions.C: This compares only the child tickets. Add adult and child tickets for each day first.
misconceptions.D: This adds all the tickets of both days. To find how many more, subtract Saturday's total from Sunday's.

G4A_DATA_018.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 4 children and Monday's row has 6 pictures. The chart is drawn again with each picture standing for 8 children. How many pictures will Monday's row have now?
hints: The number of children stays the same. Only the value of each picture changes.
Find how many children Monday's row shows: 6 pictures of 4 children each.
Example: 10 pictures of 2 pens each show 20 pens. If each picture stands for 5 pens, you need 20 divided by 5 = 4 pictures.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of children.
Each new picture stands for 8 children.
Monday's row will have 3 pictures.

misconceptions.A: This doubles the pictures. When each picture stands for more children, fewer pictures are needed.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 24 children need only 3 pictures of 8.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of children. The question asks how many pictures of 8 children are needed.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 6 by 8. Find the number of children first, then divide by 8.

G4A_DATA_019.questionText: In a pictograph, a full picture stands for 10 coconuts and a half picture stands for 5 coconuts. Monday's row has 3 full pictures and 1 half picture. Tuesday's row has 2 full pictures. How many coconuts were sold on the two days together?
hints: Work out each day's coconuts, counting full pictures and half pictures separately.
For Monday, find 3 full pictures of 10 and then add 5 for the half picture.
Example: A full picture is 4 and a half picture is 2. A row with 2 full pictures and 1 half picture shows 8 + 2 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Monday: 3 full pictures and a half picture.
Tuesday: 2 full pictures.
Add the two days.
55 coconuts were sold on the two days.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the half picture. A half picture stands for 5 coconuts, so add 5.
misconceptions.B: This counts the half picture as a full one. A half picture stands for only 5 coconuts.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Monday's 35 and Tuesday's 20 make 55.
misconceptions.D: This is how many more were sold on Monday. The question asks for both days together.

G4A_DATA_020.questionText: A tally chart of birds uses bundles of 5 and single strokes. Crows: 2 bundles and 3 strokes. Sparrows: 3 bundles and 1 stroke. Pigeons: 1 bundle and 4 strokes. How many birds were counted in all?
hints: Change each tally row into a number, then add the rows.
Start with crows: 2 bundles are 10, and 3 strokes more.
Example: Row one has 1 bundle and 2 strokes, which is 7. Row two has 2 bundles and 1 stroke, which is 11. Together 7 + 11 = 18.

stepByStep.text: Crows.
Sparrows.
Pigeons.
Add the three rows.
38 birds were counted in all.

misconceptions.A: This counts every bundle as 1. Each bundle stands for 5 birds.
misconceptions.B: This counts the bundles but leaves out the single strokes. Add the 3, 1 and 4 strokes too.
misconceptions.C: This adds only the single strokes. The 6 bundles stand for 30 more birds.

G4A_DATA_021.questionText: A bar graph shows kites sold: Mon 14, Tue 9, Wed 17, Thu 11. Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's bar. How many kites were sold on the five days altogether?
hints: One value is not given directly. Find it from the clue, then add all five days.
Find Friday's number first. It is twice Tuesday's number, which is 9.
Example: Mon 5, Tue 8, and Wednesday is twice Monday. Wednesday is 10, and the total is 5 + 8 + 10 = 23.

stepByStep.text: Friday is twice Tuesday.
Add Monday to Thursday.
Add Friday.
69 kites were sold altogether.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Four days give 51, Friday gives 18, and 51 + 18 = 69.
misconceptions.B: This is the total for Monday to Thursday. Friday's kites must be added too.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 for Friday. Twice as tall means 2 times Tuesday's 9, which is 18.
misconceptions.D: This takes Friday the same as Tuesday. Friday's bar is twice as tall, so it shows 18.

G4A_DATA_022.questionText: 40 children each chose one favourite game. Cricket was chosen by 16, football by 10 and badminton by 8. All the others chose kabaddi. How many children chose kabaddi?
hints: The whole group is known. The children who are left over after three games chose the fourth game.
Add the children who chose cricket, football and badminton: 16 + 10 + 8.
Example: 30 children; 12 chose red and 9 chose blue, the rest chose green. 12 + 9 = 21, so green got 30 - 21 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Add the three known games.
Take this away from all the children.
6 children chose kabaddi.

misconceptions.A: This is the number who chose the other three games. Take it away from 40.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 40 - 34 = 6.
misconceptions.C: This takes away cricket and football only. Badminton's 8 children must be taken away too.
misconceptions.D: This takes away cricket and badminton only. Football's 10 children must be taken away too.

G4A_DATA_023.questionText: Meera read 12 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 9 pages on Wednesday and 15 pages on Thursday. What is the average number of pages she read per day over these four days?
hints: An average shares the total equally over all the days, even a day when nothing was read.
Add the pages for all four days: 12 + 0 + 9 + 15.
Example: Goals in three matches are 4, 0 and 2. The total is 6, and 6 divided by 3 matches = 2 goals per match.

stepByStep.text: Add the pages.
There are 4 days, and Tuesday counts as a day too.
Share the total equally.
The average is 9 pages per day.

misconceptions.A: This divides by 3 and leaves Tuesday out. Tuesday is still one of the four days, so divide by 4.
misconceptions.B: This is the total number of pages. For the average, share the total equally among the 4 days.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 36 pages shared over 4 days is 9 pages per day.
misconceptions.D: This is the biggest number in the list. The average is the total shared equally over the 4 days.

G4A_DATA_024.questionText: A bar graph shows cups of tea sold: Mon 22, Tue 17, Wed 25, Thu 19. Which list puts the days in order from the shortest bar to the tallest bar?
hints: The shortest bar shows the smallest number and the tallest bar shows the biggest number.
Find the smallest of 22, 17, 25 and 19. That day comes first.
Example: Sun 8, Mon 5, Tue 9. From smallest to biggest the numbers are 5, 8, 9, so the order is Mon, Sun, Tue.

stepByStep.text: From smallest to biggest the numbers are 17, 19, 22, 25.
17 is Tuesday, 19 is Thursday, 22 is Monday and 25 is Wednesday.
The order from shortest to tallest is Tue, Thu, Mon, Wed.

misconceptions.A: This list goes from the tallest bar to the shortest. The question asks for shortest first.
misconceptions.B: Tuesday and Wednesday are in the right places, but Thursday's 19 is smaller than Monday's 22.
misconceptions.C: This is the order of the days in the week. Put them in order of their numbers instead.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! 17, 19, 22, 25 gives Tue, Thu, Mon, Wed.

G4A_DATA_025.questionText: A school has three clubs. Art: 9 girls and 6 boys. Music: 7 girls and 11 boys. Chess: 5 girls and 12 boys. Which club has the most children?
hints: Each club has girls and boys. Find each club's total before comparing.
Add the girls and boys in the Art club: 9 + 6.
Example: Team P has 4 girls and 9 boys, 13 in all. Team Q has 8 girls and 6 boys, 14 in all. Team Q has more children.

stepByStep.text: Art club.
Music club.
Chess club.
18 is the biggest total, so the club with the most children is Music.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Music has 18 children, more than Art's 15 and Chess's 17.
misconceptions.B: Art has the most girls, but the question asks about all children. Add girls and boys for each club.
misconceptions.C: Chess has the most boys, but with its girls it has 17 children. One club has more.
misconceptions.D: The totals are 15, 18 and 17, so they are not equal. Find the biggest total.

G4A_DATA_026.questionText: Children chose their favourite fruit: Mango 18, Apple 9, Banana 12, Orange 6, Grapes 3. Which fruit was chosen by exactly twice as many children as orange?
hints: Twice as many means two times a number. Find that number, then look for it in the list.
Orange was chosen by 6 children. Work out 2 times 6.
Example: Tea 4, Milk 8, Juice 10. Twice as many as tea is 2 x 4 = 8, and that is milk.

stepByStep.text: Orange was chosen by 6 children.
Twice as many as 6.
12 children chose banana, so the answer is Banana.

misconceptions.A: Mango's 18 is three times orange's 6. Twice 6 is 12.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 2 x 6 = 12, and 12 children chose banana.
misconceptions.C: Apple's 9 is 3 more than orange's 6, not twice as many. Twice 6 is 12.
misconceptions.D: Grapes' 3 is half of orange's 6. Twice as many means 2 times 6.

G4A_DATA_027.questionText: Hardik played 5 cricket matches. His average score was 32 runs per match. How many runs did he score in the 5 matches altogether?
hints: An average tells you what each match would have if the total were shared equally. Here you go back from the average to the total.
Think of every one of the 5 matches as having 32 runs.
Example: The average of 4 matches is 20 runs. The total is 4 x 20 = 80 runs.

stepByStep.text: The average is the total shared equally among the matches.
So the total is the average multiplied by the number of matches.
He scored 160 runs altogether.

misconceptions.A: This adds 32 and 5. The total is 5 lots of 32, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts 5 from 32. The total is 5 lots of 32, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 5 matches of 32 runs make 160 runs.
misconceptions.D: This is 2 lots of 32. There are 5 matches, so find 5 lots of 32.

G4A_DATA_028.questionText: The rainfall in a town, in millimetres, was: Mon 6, Tue 10, Wed 4, Thu 12, Fri 8. On how many days was the rainfall more than the average for the five days?
hints: There are two jobs here: find the average first, then compare each day with it.
Add the five numbers and divide the total by 5 to get the average.
Example: Values 3, 9, 6. The average is 18 divided by 3 = 6. Only 9 is more than 6, so 1 value is above the average.

stepByStep.text: Add the rainfall.
Find the average.
Compare each day with 8: only 10 and 12 are more than 8. Friday's 8 is equal to the average, not more.
The rainfall was more than the average on 2 days.

misconceptions.A: This also counts Friday. Friday's rainfall is equal to the average, and the question asks for more than the average.
misconceptions.B: This is the average itself. Now count the days whose rainfall is more than 8.
misconceptions.C: This counts every day that is different from the average. Count only the days above 8.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The average is 8, and only Tuesday and Thursday are above it.

G4A_DATA_029.questionText: Ananya's average mark in 4 tests was 18. After the 5th test, her average for all 5 tests became 20. How many marks did she get in the 5th test?
hints: An average multiplied by the number of tests gives the total. Compare the total before and after.
Find Ananya's total marks in the first 4 tests: 4 times 18.
Example: The average of 2 tests is 10, so the total is 20. After a 3rd test the average is 12, so the total is 36. The 3rd test was 36 - 20 = 16 marks.

stepByStep.text: Total of the first 4 tests.
Total of all 5 tests.
The difference is the 5th test.
She got 28 marks in the 5th test.

misconceptions.A: That is right! The total rose from 72 to 100, so the 5th test was 28.
misconceptions.B: A 5th mark of 20 would not pull an average of 18 all the way up to 20. Compare the two totals.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 to 20. The 5th test has to lift the average of all five tests by 2, so compare the totals 72 and 100.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two averages. Change each average into a total first, then subtract.

G4A_DATA_030.questionText: A pictograph shows old newspapers collected by two classes. Class 4A has 7 pictures and Class 4B has 4 pictures. Each picture stands for the same number of newspapers. Class 4A collected 21 more newspapers than Class 4B. How many newspapers did Class 4A collect?
hints: The value of one picture is not given. Use the extra pictures and the extra newspapers to find it.
Class 4A has 7 - 4 = 3 more pictures. These 3 pictures stand for the 21 extra newspapers.
Example: Row one has 6 pictures, row two has 4, and row one shows 10 more. The 2 extra pictures stand for 10, so each picture is 5 and row one shows 6 x 5 = 30.

stepByStep.text: Class 4A has 3 more pictures.
These 3 pictures stand for 21 newspapers.
Class 4A has 7 pictures of 7 newspapers each.
Class 4A collected 49 newspapers.

misconceptions.A: This is what Class 4B collected: 4 pictures of 7. The question asks about Class 4A.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! Each picture stands for 7, so 7 pictures stand for 49.
misconceptions.C: This is how many more Class 4A collected. Use it to find the value of one picture, then find 7 pictures.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 21 by 7. The 21 newspapers are shared by the 3 extra pictures, so each picture is 7.

G4A_DATA_031.questionText: Class 4 has 42 children, and 23 of them are girls. 15 children come to school by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys do NOT come by bus?
hints: Sort the children two ways: girls or boys, and bus or no bus. Find the boys' numbers step by step.
Find how many boys are in the class: 42 - 23.
Example: 30 children, 18 girls, so 12 boys. 10 come by bus and 6 of them are girls, so 4 bus boys. Boys not by bus: 12 - 4 = 8.

stepByStep.text: Boys in the class.
Boys who come by bus.
Boys who do not come by bus.
13 boys do not come by bus.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of boys who do come by bus. Take them away from all the boys.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of girls who do not come by bus. The question asks about boys.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 19 boys in all, 6 by bus, so 13 not by bus.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of all the boys. Take away the 6 boys who come by bus.

G4A_DATA_032.questionText: Vikram found the average of five numbers to be 20. Then he saw that he had copied one number as 25 when it was really 15. What is the correct average?
hints: A slip in one number changes the total, and the change is shared among all five numbers.
Find the total Vikram used: 5 times 20.
Example: The average of 4 numbers is 10, so the total is 40. One number was written as 12 instead of 4, so the true total is 40 - 8 = 32 and the true average is 32 divided by 4 = 8.

stepByStep.text: The total Vikram used.
The number was 10 too big, so take 10 off.
Share the correct total among the five numbers.
The correct average is 18.

misconceptions.A: This makes the total bigger. The copied number was too big, so the correct total is smaller.
misconceptions.B: This takes the whole 10 away from the average. The 10 is shared among five numbers, so the average falls by only 2.
misconceptions.C: This is the number that was copied badly. The average comes from the corrected total, 90, divided by 5.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The total drops from 100 to 90, and 90 divided by 5 is 18.

G4A_DATA_033.questionText: A shop sold school bags: Mon 14, Tue 18, Wed 10. On Saturday it sold as many bags as on Monday and Tuesday together. On Sunday it sold half as many bags as on Saturday. How many bags did it sell on these five days altogether?
hints: Two of the five numbers are hidden in clues. Find them one at a time, then add everything.
Find Saturday's number first: add Monday's 14 and Tuesday's 18.
Example: Mon 4, Tue 6. Saturday equals both together, 10, and Sunday is half of that, 5. The total is 4 + 6 + 10 + 5 = 25.

stepByStep.text: Saturday.
Sunday is half of Saturday.
Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday together.
Add all five days.
The shop sold 90 bags altogether.

misconceptions.B: This leaves out Sunday's 16 bags. Sunday is half of Saturday.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out Saturday's 32 bags. Saturday equals Monday and Tuesday together.
misconceptions.D: This takes Sunday the same as Saturday. Sunday is half of Saturday, so it is 16.

G4A_DATA_034.questionText: Four friends have 8, 14, 11 and 7 marbles. They share the marbles so that all four have the same number. How many marbles must the friend who had 14 give away?
hints: Sharing equally gives everyone the average. Find what each friend ends up with.
Add all the marbles: 8 + 14 + 11 + 7.
Example: Three friends have 1, 9 and 2 sweets. The total is 12, so each gets 12 divided by 3. The friend with 9 keeps that equal share and gives away the other 5 sweets.

stepByStep.text: Add all the marbles.
Share equally among 4 friends.
The friend with 14 keeps 10.
That friend must give away 4 marbles.

misconceptions.A: This is how many marbles each friend ends up with. The question asks how many the friend with 14 gives away.
misconceptions.B: That is right! Each friend ends with 10, so the friend with 14 gives away 4.
misconceptions.C: This is the gap between 14 and 8. Find the equal share first, then see how far 14 is above it.
misconceptions.D: This is the gap between 14 and 7. Find the equal share first, then see how far 14 is above it.

G4A_DATA_035.questionText: Riya and Kabir each drew a pictograph of their stamps. In Riya's chart each picture stands for 5 stamps and there are 12 pictures. In Kabir's chart each picture stands for 8 stamps and there are 7 pictures. Who has more stamps, and by how many?
hints: The two charts use different values for a picture, so you cannot compare the pictures directly.
Change Riya's pictures into stamps: 12 pictures of 5 stamps each.
Example: Chart one has 6 pictures of 2, which is 12. Chart two has 3 pictures of 5, which is 15. Chart two shows 15 - 12 = 3 more.

stepByStep.text: Riya's stamps.
Kabir's stamps.
Compare.
Riya has more stamps, by 4.

misconceptions.A: The gap of 4 is right, but check who has more: Riya has 60 stamps and Kabir has 56.
misconceptions.B: This compares the numbers of pictures, 12 and 7. Change the pictures into stamps first.
misconceptions.C: Super! Riya's 60 stamps are 4 more than Kabir's 56.
misconceptions.D: This compares the values of one picture, 8 and 5. Find each child's total stamps first.

G4A_DATA_036.questionText: Class 4A has 20 children and their average mark in a test is 30. Class 4B has 30 children and their average mark in the same test is 40. What is the average mark of all 50 children together?
hints: An average depends on how many children are in each group. Find the total marks of each class before you find the average of everyone.
Class 4A scored 20 × 30 marks in all. Work out the total for Class 4B in the same way, then add the two totals.
A similar one: 10 children average 6 and 30 children average 10. The totals are 10 × 6 = 60 and 30 × 10 = 300, which make 360. Then 360 ÷ 40 = 9, not the halfway number 8.

stepByStep.text: Find the total marks of Class 4A.
Find the total marks of Class 4B.
Add to get the total marks of all 50 children.
Share the total among 50 children.
The average mark of all 50 children is 36.

misconceptions.A: 35 is halfway between 30 and 40. That would be right only if both classes had the same number of children. Class 4B is bigger, so use the totals.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The total is 1800 marks for 50 children, which is 36 each. The bigger class pulls the average towards 40.
misconceptions.C: 34 leans towards the smaller class. Class 4B has more children, so the average must be closer to 40 than to 30. Try the totals again.
misconceptions.D: 70 is 30 + 40, the two averages added. An average of everyone must lie between 30 and 40. Find the total marks first.

G4A_DATA_037.questionText: A bar graph shows the books sold at a fair. The bottom line of the graph stands for 20 books, not 0, and each square above the bottom line stands for 5 more books. Saturday's bar is 3 squares tall and Sunday's bar is 6 squares tall. How many books were sold on the two days altogether?
hints: Check where the graph starts. A bar's height in squares only tells you how far it is above the bottom line.
Saturday's bar is 3 squares above a line that already stands for 20 books. Find Saturday's number first, then do the same for Sunday.
A similar one: the bottom line stands for 10 and each square stands for 2. Bars of 4 squares and 5 squares show 10 + 8 = 18 and 10 + 10 = 20, so together 18 + 20 = 38.

stepByStep.text: Saturday's bar is 3 squares above 20.
Sunday's bar is 6 squares above 20.
Add the two days.
Altogether 85 books were sold.

misconceptions.A: 45 is 9 squares of 5 books. That counts only the books above the bottom line. Each bar also includes the 20 books the bottom line stands for.
misconceptions.B: 65 adds the starting 20 only once. Each day's bar starts from 20, so the 20 belongs to Saturday and to Sunday.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Saturday is 35 and Sunday is 50, because each bar starts from 20. Together that is 85.
misconceptions.D: 50 is Sunday's number alone. The question asks for both days together, so add Saturday's books too.

G4A_DATA_038.questionText: In a class of 40 children, 24 like cricket and 20 like football. 6 children like neither game. How many children like both games?
hints: Some children have been counted twice, once for each game. First find how many children like at least one game.
Take away the 6 children who like neither game from 40. Compare that number with 24 + 20.
A similar one: 30 children, 18 like mango, 15 like banana and 5 like neither. So 25 like at least one fruit. The lists have 18 + 15 = 33 names, and 33 − 25 = 8 children like both.

stepByStep.text: Find the children who like at least one game.
Add the two lists.
The lists have 44 names but only 34 children, so the extra names are children counted twice.
10 children like both games.

misconceptions.A: 4 is 44 − 40. That forgets the 6 children who like neither game. Only 34 children are on the two lists.
misconceptions.B: 6 is the number who like neither game. The question asks about the children who like both.
misconceptions.C: 16 is 40 − 24, the children who do not like cricket. Think about who has been counted twice instead.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The two lists have 44 names for only 34 children, so 10 children are on both lists.

G4A_DATA_039.questionText: The average of five whole numbers is 8. Which of these statements is certainly true?

options.text: At least one of the numbers is exactly 8
At least one of the numbers is 8 or more
Three of the numbers are more than 8
None of the numbers is more than 16

hints: A statement is certainly true only if it holds for every possible set of numbers. Try to find a set that breaks each statement.
The five numbers must add up to 5 × 8 = 40. Try some unusual sets with this total, such as 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40.

A similar one: three whole numbers have an average of 5, so they add up to 15. The set 1, 1, 13 has no 5 in it and only one number above 5. But all three cannot be below 5, because then the total would be less than 15.

stepByStep.text: The five numbers add up to 40.
The set 0, 0, 0, 0, 40 has an average of 8. It has no 8 in it, only one number above 8, and a number above 16. So three of the statements can be broken.
If every number were less than 8, the total would be less than 40. That cannot happen.
So the statement that is certainly true is: at least one of the numbers is 8 or more.

misconceptions.A: This is true for a set like 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, but not for every set. Try 7, 7, 7, 7 and 12: the average is 8 and no number is 8.
misconceptions.B: Yes! If all five numbers were below 8 the total would be below 40, so at least one must be 8 or more.
misconceptions.C: Try the set 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40. Its average is 8, yet only one number is more than 8. Look for a statement no set can break.
misconceptions.D: Try the set 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40. Its average is 8, and 40 is more than 16. Look for a statement no set can break.

G4A_DATA_040.questionText: Riya wants to draw a pictograph for the kites sold on four days: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 30 and Thursday 42. Every picture must stand for the same number of kites, and she will use only whole pictures. She wants to draw as few pictures as possible. How many pictures will she draw altogether?
hints: Fewer pictures means each picture must stand for more kites. But every day's number must be made of whole pictures.
Look for the largest number that divides 12, 18, 30 and 42 exactly. That is the most one picture can stand for.
A similar one: for 8, 12 and 20 the largest number that divides all three is 4. With 4 for each picture, the rows have 2, 3 and 5 pictures, so 10 pictures altogether.

stepByStep.text: Each picture must stand for a number that divides 12, 18, 30 and 42 exactly. The largest such number is 6.
Find the pictures for each day.
Add the pictures.
She will draw 17 pictures altogether.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 6 is the largest number that divides all four, so the rows need 2, 3, 5 and 7 pictures, which is 17.
misconceptions.B: 34 pictures is what you get if each picture stands for 3 kites. Check whether a bigger number also divides 12, 18, 30 and 42.
misconceptions.C: 51 pictures is what you get if each picture stands for 2 kites. A picture can stand for more than that and still divide every number.
misconceptions.D: 6 is how many kites each picture stands for. The question asks how many pictures she draws, so divide each day's number by 6 and add.

G4A_DATA_041.questionText: A shop's sales of school bags were: Monday 20, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 25 and Friday 40. Thursday's number is smudged. The owner remembers that Thursday's number was exactly equal to the average of all five days. How many bags were sold on Thursday?
hints: If one day's number is the same as the average, it does not pull the average up or down. Think about what that says about the other four days.
Add the four numbers you know: 20, 35, 25 and 40. Then think about the average of just these four days.

A similar one: the known days are 10, 14 and 18 and the missing day equals the average of all four. The three known days total 42, so their average is 14. The missing day is 14, and the check works: 56 ÷ 4 = 14.

stepByStep.text: Add the four known days.
A day that equals the average leaves the average unchanged, so Thursday equals the average of the other four days.
Check with all five days.
30 bags were sold on Thursday.

misconceptions.A: 24 is 120 ÷ 5. That shares four days' sales among five days, as if Thursday sold nothing. Thursday's own bags must be in the total too.
misconceptions.B: With 25 on Thursday the total is 145 and the average is 29, not 25. Try a number that equals the average of the other four days.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The other four days average 30, and with Thursday at 30 the five-day total is 150, which is 30 a day.
misconceptions.D: With 40 on Thursday the total is 160 and the average is 32, not 40. Thursday must match the average exactly.

G4A_DATA_042.questionText: Riya is reading a storybook. The table shows the total number of pages she had read by the end of each day: Monday 12, Tuesday 30, Wednesday 41, Thursday 65, Friday 80. On which day did she read the most pages?
hints: The table gives running totals, not the pages read on each day. Think about how to get one day's reading from two totals.
On Tuesday she went from 12 pages to 30 pages. Subtract to find Tuesday's pages, then do the same for every day.
A similar one: running totals of 5, 14 and 20 over three days mean 5 pages, then 14 − 5 = 9 pages, then 20 − 14 = 6 pages. The middle day has the most, even though the last total is the biggest.

stepByStep.text: On Monday she read 12 pages.
Find the pages for Tuesday and Wednesday.
Find the pages for Thursday and Friday.
The largest of 12, 18, 11, 24 and 15 is 24.
She read the most pages on Thursday.

misconceptions.A: Friday has the biggest total, 80, but that counts all five days. On Friday itself she read 80 − 65 = 15 pages. Compare the daily amounts.
misconceptions.B: On Tuesday she read 30 − 12 = 18 pages. That is a good day, but check Thursday's pages too.
misconceptions.C: On Monday she read 12 pages. Find each day's pages by subtracting the total of the day before, then compare.
misconceptions.D: Yes! On Thursday she went from 41 to 65, which is 24 pages, more than on any other day.

G4A_DATA_043.questionText: Kabir took five spelling tests. His average mark in the first three tests was 10. His average mark in the last three tests was 16. His average mark in all five tests was 12. How many marks did he get in the third test?
hints: The third test belongs to both groups: the first three tests and the last three tests. Use totals, not averages.
Find the total of the first three tests and the total of the last three tests. Then find the total of all five tests.

A similar one with three tests: the first two average 4 (total 8), the last two average 7 (total 14), and all three average 5 (total 15). The middle test is counted twice in 8 + 14 = 22, so it is 22 − 15 = 7.

stepByStep.text: Find the total of the first three tests.
Find the total of the last three tests.
Find the total of all five tests.
Adding the two groups counts the third test twice.
Take away the real total to leave the third test.
He got 18 marks in the third test.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The two groups total 78 but the five tests total 60, so the test counted twice is worth 18.
misconceptions.B: 13 is halfway between 10 and 16. The third test is not the average of the two averages. Work with the totals of each group.
misconceptions.C: 12 is his average for all five tests. The third test can be quite different from the average. Find the totals and see which test is counted twice.
misconceptions.D: 26 is 10 + 16, the two averages added. Change each average into a total first: 30 and 48.

G4A_DATA_044.questionText: Ravi took five tests, each out of 20 marks. In four of them he got 12, 15, 9 and 18. He has forgotten the fifth mark, but he remembers that his average for the five tests was exactly equal to his mark in one of the five tests. What is the forgotten mark?
hints: The average of five marks must come out as a whole number here, because it equals one of the marks. Test the possible totals one at a time.
The four known marks add up to 54. The total of all five must be a number that 5 divides exactly. Which totals are possible if the fifth mark is 20 or less?

A similar one: known marks 7, 10 and 4 (total 21), with one mark out of 10 missing, and the average of the four equals one of the marks. Totals that 4 divides are 24 and 28. A missing 3 gives an average of 6, which is not one of the marks. A missing 7 gives an average of 7, which is. So the missing mark is 7.

stepByStep.text: Add the four known marks.
The total of five marks must divide exactly by 5. With a fifth mark from 0 to 20, the total can be 55, 60, 65 or 70, so the fifth mark is 1, 6, 11 or 16.
The averages would be 11, 12, 13 or 14.
Only 12 is one of his marks, and it goes with a total of 60.
The forgotten mark is 6.

misconceptions.A: A fifth mark of 1 gives a total of 55 and an average of 11. But 11 is not one of his five marks. Keep testing the other totals.
misconceptions.B: Yes! With 6 the total is 60 and the average is 12, which is the mark he got in one test.
misconceptions.C: A fifth mark of 11 gives a total of 65 and an average of 13. But 13 is not one of his marks. Try another total.
misconceptions.D: A fifth mark of 16 gives a total of 70 and an average of 14. But 14 is not one of his marks. Try another total.

G4A_DATA_045.questionText: Each of the 30 children in a class voted for exactly two different fruits out of mango, apple, banana and guava. Mango got 20 votes, apple got 15 votes and banana got 14 votes. How many votes did guava get?
hints: Count votes, not children. Each child gave more than one vote.
Find the total number of votes: 30 children with 2 votes each. Then add the votes for mango, apple and banana.
A similar one: 20 children each vote for two games out of three. That makes 40 votes. If cricket gets 18 and football gets 13, then kho-kho gets 40 − 18 − 13 = 9 votes.

stepByStep.text: Each child gave 2 votes, so find the total votes.
Add the votes for the three known fruits.
The rest of the votes went to guava.
Guava got 11 votes.
