G4A_EQUATIONS_016.questionText: A parking lot has only auto-rickshaws with 3 wheels each and cars with 4 wheels each. There are 10 vehicles and 34 wheels in all. How many cars are there?
hints: Imagine every vehicle is an auto-rickshaw and count the wheels. Then see how many wheels are missing.
10 auto-rickshaws would have 10 × 3 = 30 wheels. Each car has one more wheel than an auto-rickshaw.
A similar one: 8 vehicles, bicycles with 2 wheels and auto-rickshaws with 3, and 19 wheels. All bicycles would give 16 wheels; the 3 extra wheels mean 3 auto-rickshaws.

stepByStep.text: Suppose all 10 vehicles are auto-rickshaws.
Extra wheels that are really there.
Each car adds 1 extra wheel, so the 4 extra wheels mean 4 cars.
There are 4 cars.

misconceptions.A: 6 is the number of auto-rickshaws. The question asks for the cars.
misconceptions.B: This divides 34 by 4 as if nearly all were cars. But 8 cars and 2 auto-rickshaws would have 38 wheels.
misconceptions.C: Yes! If all 10 were auto-rickshaws there would be 30 wheels. The 4 extra wheels mean 4 of them are cars. Check: 4 × 4 + 6 × 3 = 34.
misconceptions.D: 5 cars and 5 auto-rickshaws would have 20 + 15 = 35 wheels, one too many.

G4A_EQUATIONS_017.questionText: Three friends collect shells. Jaya has twice as many shells as Bala. Chitra has 5 more shells than Bala. Together they have 45 shells. How many shells does Bala have?
hints: Call Bala's shells one share. Write the other two friends' shells using that share.
Jaya has 2 shares and Chitra has 1 share and 5 more. So 4 shares and 5 make 45.
A similar one: Anu has twice as many as Binu, Charu has 3 more than Binu, and together they have 27. Then 4 shares and 3 make 27, 4 shares are 24, and Binu has 6.

stepByStep.text: Bala has 1 share, Jaya has 2 shares, Chitra has 1 share and 5 more. That is 4 shares and 5.
Take away the extra 5.
Share among 4. Bala has 10 shells.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Without Chitra's extra 5 there are 40 shells in 4 equal shares, so Bala has 10. Check: 10 + 20 + 15 = 45.
misconceptions.B: 20 is Jaya's number, which is twice Bala's.
misconceptions.C: 15 is Chitra's number, which is 5 more than Bala's.
misconceptions.D: This shares 40 among 5. Bala's one share, Jaya's two shares and Chitra's one share make 4 shares.

G4A_EQUATIONS_018.questionText: The length of a rectangular garden is 3 m more than twice its breadth. The perimeter of the garden is 48 m. What is the length of the garden?
hints: Half the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Write the length in terms of the breadth.
Half of 48 is 24. The length is 2 breadths and 3 m, so length plus breadth is 3 breadths and 3 m.
A similar one: the length is 1 m more than twice the breadth, and the perimeter is 32 m. Half is 16 m, so 3 breadths and 1 m make 16 m; the breadth is 5 m and the length is 2 × 5 + 1 = 11 m.

stepByStep.text: One length and one breadth make half the perimeter.
The length is 2 breadths and 3 m, so 3 breadths and 3 m make 24 m.
Find the breadth.
The length is 17 m.

misconceptions.A: 7 m is the breadth. The length is twice the breadth and 3 m more.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Length and breadth together are 24 m. Three breadths and 3 m make 24 m, so the breadth is 7 m and the length is 2 × 7 + 3 = 17 m.
misconceptions.C: This uses the whole perimeter of 48 m for one length and one breadth. One length and one breadth make half the perimeter, 24 m.
misconceptions.D: This is twice the breadth. The length is 3 m more than that.

G4A_EQUATIONS_019.questionText: Raju and Sonu start with the same amount of money. Raju buys 3 notebooks and has ₹14 left. Sonu buys 4 notebooks of the same kind and has ₹2 left. What is the price of one notebook?
hints: Both boys had the same money. Compare what each bought and what each has left.
Sonu bought just one notebook more than Raju. See how much less money he has left.
A similar one: with the same money, Mina buys 2 pens and has ₹20 left, and Tina buys 3 pens and has ₹5 left. The extra pen cost 20 − 5 = ₹15.

stepByStep.text: Both started with the same money, so 3 notebooks and ₹14 equal 4 notebooks and ₹2.
Sonu bought 1 more notebook than Raju.
That one notebook used up the difference in the money left. One notebook costs ₹12.

misconceptions.A: This adds ₹14 and ₹2. Sonu's one extra notebook made his left-over money go down from ₹14 to ₹2, so subtract.
misconceptions.B: This halves ₹14. Compare the two boys instead: one more notebook, and ₹12 less left over.
misconceptions.C: The difference of ₹12 pays for just 1 extra notebook, not 2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Sonu bought one more notebook and has 14 − 2 = ₹12 less left, so a notebook costs ₹12.

G4A_EQUATIONS_020.questionText: Neha spends half of her money on a book. Then she spends ₹30 on a pen. She has ₹45 left. How much money did Neha have at first?
hints: You know the end, so work backwards, undoing the last thing first.
The last thing Neha did was spend ₹30. Add it back to ₹45.
A similar one: Ali spends half his money, then ₹10, and has ₹25 left. 25 + 10 = 35 is half, so he had ₹70.

stepByStep.text: Add back the ₹30 spent on the pen.
₹75 is the half left after the book, so double it.
Neha had ₹150 at first.

misconceptions.A: This doubles ₹45 first and then adds ₹30. Work backwards in order: add back the ₹30 first, then double.
misconceptions.B: ₹75 is what Neha had after buying the book. That is half of her money, so double it.
misconceptions.C: This adds ₹30 twice. Add ₹30 once to get ₹75, which is half of her money.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 45 + 30 = ₹75 was left after the book, and that is half, so she had ₹150. Check: 150 − 75 − 30 = 45.

G4A_EQUATIONS_021.questionText: Asha and Bina both start with the same number. Asha adds 8 to it and then doubles the result. Bina doubles the number and then adds 8. How much greater is Asha's answer than Bina's answer?
hints: Try the two sets of steps with a small number of your own and compare the two answers.
Start with 1. Asha: 1 + 8 = 9, and doubled that is 18. Now work out Bina's answer for the same start.
Similar problem: Raj adds 5 then multiplies by 3, and Sam multiplies by 3 then adds 5. Starting with 2, Raj gets 21 and Sam gets 11, so Raj's answer is 10 greater.

stepByStep.text: Try the number 1. Asha: 1 + 8 = 9, and double 9 is 18. Bina: double 1 is 2, and 2 + 8 = 10.
Asha is ahead by 18 − 10.
It is the same for any start: Asha doubles the 8 as well, so her 8 becomes 16, while Bina adds only 8.
16 − 8 = 8, so Asha's answer is 8 greater.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Asha's 8 gets doubled to 16 while Bina adds only 8, so Asha finishes 8 ahead whatever the starting number is.
misconceptions.B: It is tempting to think the same two steps give the same answer. Try both orders with the number 1 and compare.
misconceptions.C: Asha's 8 does become 16 when it is doubled. But Bina adds 8 too, so compare 16 with 8.
misconceptions.D: This halves the 8. Asha doubles her 8, so work through both sets of steps with a small number.

G4A_EQUATIONS_022.questionText: The two digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. When the digits are swapped, the new number is 27 more than the first number. What is the first number?
hints: Use one clue to make a short list of possible numbers, then test each of them with the other clue.
List the two-digit numbers whose digits add up to 9: 18, 27, 36, 45 and so on. Swap the digits of each and compare.
Similar problem: the digits add up to 7 and swapping gives a number 9 more. From 16, 25, 34, 43 test each: 34 swapped is 43, and 43 − 34 = 9, so the number is 34.

stepByStep.text: Numbers whose digits add up to 9: 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81, 90.
The swapped number must be greater, so the tens digit must be the smaller digit: try 18, 27, 36 and 45.
Only 36 gives a difference of 27, so the first number is 36.

misconceptions.A: 63 and 36 are the right pair, but 63 is the bigger one. The first number must be the smaller, because swapping makes it grow by 27.
misconceptions.B: The digits add up to 9, but swapping gives 54, which is only 9 more. Test the other numbers whose digits add up to 9.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 3 + 6 = 9, and swapping gives 63, which is exactly 27 more than 36.
misconceptions.D: 27 is the difference given in the story. Its digits do add up to 9, but swapping gives 72, which is 45 more.

G4A_EQUATIONS_023.questionText: Ravi has 4 times as many marbles as Sonu. Then each boy wins 5 more marbles. Now Ravi has 3 times as many marbles as Sonu. How many marbles did Sonu have at first?
hints: Test a possible answer in the story: work out both boys' marbles before and after, and see whether both clues hold.
Suppose Sonu had 5 at first. Then Ravi had 20. After 5 more each they have 10 and 25. Is 25 three times 10? Then try another start.
Similar problem: Mira has 3 times as many stickers as Nita; after each gets 4 more, Mira has twice as many. Try Nita = 4: Mira = 12, and afterwards 8 and 16. 16 is twice 8, so Nita had 4.

stepByStep.text: Test Sonu = 10. Then Ravi has 4 × 10 = 40 marbles.
After winning 5 each, Sonu has 15 and Ravi has 45.
45 is 3 times 15, so both clues fit.
Testing 5 gives 10 and 25, and testing 15 gives 20 and 65. Neither pair is 'three times', so only 10 fits.
Sonu had 10 marbles at first.

misconceptions.A: Great job! Sonu had 10 and Ravi 40; after 5 more each they have 15 and 45, and 45 is 3 times 15.
misconceptions.B: 15 is what Sonu has after winning 5 more. The question asks how many he had at first.
misconceptions.C: 40 is the number of marbles Ravi had at first. The question asks about Sonu.
misconceptions.D: Test it: Sonu 5 and Ravi 20 become 10 and 25, and 25 is not 3 times 10. Try a bigger start.

G4A_EQUATIONS_024.questionText: A basket has some mangoes. Asha takes half of the mangoes and 1 more. Then Bala takes half of the mangoes that are left and 1 more. Now 3 mangoes are left in the basket. How many mangoes were in the basket at first?
hints: Start from the end of the story and undo each step, the last step first.
Before Bala took his share there were more than 3 mangoes. He took half and 1 more, so first put back the 1, then double.
Similar problem: Ria takes half of some sweets and 2 more, and 4 are left. Put back the 2 to get 6, which is the other half, so there were 12 sweets.

stepByStep.text: Work backwards. After Bala there are 3 mangoes. Put back his extra 1.
That 4 is half of what Bala found, so before Bala there were 8 mangoes.
Put back Asha's extra 1. That gives 9, which is half of the basket.
Double it. Check: Asha takes 9 + 1 = 10, leaving 8; Bala takes 4 + 1 = 5, leaving 3.
There were 18 mangoes in the basket at first.

misconceptions.A: This doubles first and then adds 1. Going backwards, the extra 1 mango was taken last, so put it back first and then double.
misconceptions.B: This doubles twice and then adds both extra mangoes at the end. Each extra mango must be put back before its own doubling.
misconceptions.C: This doubles twice but leaves out the 1 extra mango that each child took.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Going backwards: 3 + 1 = 4, doubled is 8; then 8 + 1 = 9, doubled is 18.

G4A_EQUATIONS_025.questionText: In a game, Kavya wins 5 points for every round she wins and loses 2 points for every round she loses. She plays 20 rounds and finishes with 65 points. How many rounds did she win?
hints: Every round is either won or lost, so the two counts add up to the number of rounds. Test a possible number of wins.
Imagine she won all 20 rounds: she would have 100 points. Think about what changes each time one win becomes a loss.

Similar problem: 3 points for a win, 1 point lost for a loss, 10 rounds and 18 points. All wins would give 30. Each loss lowers the score by 3 + 1 = 4, and 30 − 18 = 12, so there were 3 losses and 7 wins.

stepByStep.text: If Kavya won all 20 rounds she would have 100 points.
Each lost round takes away the 5 points she would have won and 2 more, so it lowers the score by 7.
She is 100 − 65 = 35 points below 100, so she lost 5 rounds.
Check: 15 wins give 75 points and 5 losses take away 10, leaving 65.
She won 20 − 5 = 15 rounds.

misconceptions.A: This is 65 ÷ 5. But 13 wins would mean 7 losses, which take 14 points away and leave only 51. She must have won more rounds.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 15 wins give 75 points and 5 losses take away 10, leaving 65.
misconceptions.C: This adds the 20 rounds to the 65 points and divides by 5. Test it: 17 wins and 3 losses give 85 − 6 = 79 points.
misconceptions.D: 5 is the number of rounds she lost. The question asks how many she won.

G4A_EQUATIONS_026.questionText: At a stationery shop, 2 pens and 3 pencils cost ₹36. At the same shop, 2 pens and 5 pencils cost ₹48. What is the price of one pen?
hints: Compare the two purchases. Look at what is the same in both and what is extra in the second one.
Both purchases have 2 pens. The second has 2 more pencils and costs more. Use that to find the price of one pencil first.
Similar problem: 1 bun and 2 biscuits cost ₹10, and 1 bun and 4 biscuits cost ₹14. The 2 extra biscuits cost ₹4, so one biscuit is ₹2 and the bun is 10 − 4 = ₹6.

stepByStep.text: The second purchase has 2 extra pencils and costs 12 rupees more.
So one pencil costs 6 rupees.
In the first purchase the 3 pencils cost 18 rupees, so the 2 pens cost 18 rupees.
One pen costs 18 ÷ 2 = 9 rupees, so the price of one pen is ₹9.

misconceptions.A: ₹6 is the price of one pencil, a very good first step. Now use it to find the price of a pen.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The 2 extra pencils cost ₹12, so a pencil is ₹6; then 2 pens cost 36 − 18 = ₹18, and one pen is ₹9.
misconceptions.C: ₹12 is how much more the second purchase costs. It is the price of the 2 extra pencils.
misconceptions.D: ₹18 is the price of the 2 pens together. Share it between the 2 pens.

G4A_EQUATIONS_027.questionText: A teacher has between 20 and 40 children in her class. When they stand in rows of 4, 3 children are left over. When they stand in rows of 5, 2 children are left over. How many children are in the class?
hints: List the numbers that fit one clue, then check each of them against the other clue.
Numbers between 20 and 40 that leave 3 over in rows of 4 are 23, 27, 31, 35 and 39. Now test each of them in rows of 5.
Similar problem: between 10 and 20, rows of 3 leave 1 over and rows of 4 leave 1 over. Rows of 3 give 10, 13, 16, 19. In rows of 4, only 13 leaves 1 over, so the answer is 13.

stepByStep.text: Rows of 4 with 3 left over: the number is 3 more than a multiple of 4. Between 20 and 40 that gives 23, 27, 31, 35, 39.
Rows of 5 with 2 left over: the number must end in 2 or 7.
In the list, only 27 ends in 2 or 7.
Check: 27 is 6 rows of 4 and 3 over, and 27 is 5 rows of 5 and 2 over.
There are 27 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: 23 fits the rows of 4, with 3 left over. But in rows of 5 it leaves 3, not 2. Keep testing the next numbers.
misconceptions.B: 32 fits the rows of 5, with 2 left over. But in rows of 4 nobody is left over. Both clues must fit.
misconceptions.C: 35 fits the rows of 4, with 3 left over. But in rows of 5 nobody is left over.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 27 is 6 rows of 4 with 3 left over, and also 5 rows of 5 with 2 left over.

G4A_EQUATIONS_028.questionText: On a balance, 1 melon weighs the same as 2 mangoes and 1 guava together. Also, 1 mango weighs the same as 3 guavas. How many guavas weigh the same as 2 melons?
hints: Change every fruit into guavas, one swap at a time, so that only one kind of fruit is left.
Start with one melon: it equals 2 mangoes and 1 guava. Swap each mango for the guavas it equals.
Similar problem: 1 box weighs the same as 2 tins and 3 nuts, and 1 tin weighs the same as 2 nuts. Then 1 box is 4 nuts + 3 nuts = 7 nuts, and 3 boxes are 21 nuts.

stepByStep.text: 1 mango equals 3 guavas, so 2 mangoes equal 6 guavas.
1 melon equals 2 mangoes and 1 guava, which is 7 guavas.
The question asks about 2 melons.
2 melons weigh the same as 14 guavas.

misconceptions.A: Great job! One melon is 6 + 1 = 7 guavas, so 2 melons are 14 guavas.
misconceptions.B: 7 guavas balance one melon. The question asks about 2 melons.
misconceptions.C: This swaps the mangoes for guavas but leaves out the 1 guava that sits with them on the pan.
misconceptions.D: This counts only 1 mango in each melon. One melon balances 2 mangoes and 1 guava.

G4A_EQUATIONS_029.questionText: A number is as much greater than 36 as it is less than 86. What is the number?
hints: Picture the three numbers on a number line. Where must the unknown number sit between the other two?
The number is the same distance from 36 and from 86. First find how far apart 36 and 86 are.
Similar problem: a number is as much greater than 10 as it is less than 30. The gap is 20 and half of it is 10, so the number is 10 + 10 = 20.

stepByStep.text: The number is the same distance above 36 as it is below 86, so it is exactly halfway between them.
The gap from 36 to 86 is 50.
Half of the gap is 25.
Add this to 36. Check: 61 − 36 = 25 and 86 − 61 = 25.
The number is 61.

misconceptions.A: 50 is the gap between 36 and 86. The number sits in the middle of that gap.
misconceptions.B: 25 is how far the number is from 36 and from 86. Add it to 36 to find the number itself.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 61 is 25 more than 36 and 25 less than 86, exactly halfway.
misconceptions.D: This adds 36 and 86. The number must lie between them, so halve that total.

G4A_EQUATIONS_030.questionText: Two whole numbers add up to 12. When they are multiplied, the answer is 35. What is the difference between the two numbers?
hints: Find the two numbers first by testing pairs, then read again what the question asks for.
List pairs that multiply to 35, or pairs that add up to 12, and look for a pair that does both.
Similar problem: two numbers add up to 10 and multiply to 21. 3 × 7 = 21 and 3 + 7 = 10, so the numbers are 3 and 7, and their difference is 4.

stepByStep.text: Pairs of whole numbers that multiply to 35 are 1 and 35, and 5 and 7.
1 + 35 = 36, but 5 + 7 = 12, so the two numbers are 5 and 7.
The question asks for their difference.
The difference between the two numbers is 2.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The numbers are 5 and 7, and 7 − 5 = 2.
misconceptions.B: 7 is the bigger of the two numbers. Read the question once more: it asks for the difference between them.
misconceptions.C: 5 is the smaller of the two numbers. The question asks for the difference between the two numbers.
misconceptions.D: This is 35 − 12. First find the two numbers themselves, then subtract one from the other.

G4A_EQUATIONS_031.questionText: A shop sells pencils only in packs of 4 and packs of 7. Meena buys exactly 30 pencils. How many packs does she buy altogether?
hints: Test the possible numbers of the bigger packs one at a time, and see whether the rest can be made from the smaller packs.
Try 1 pack of 7: that leaves 23 pencils. Can 23 be made from packs of 4? Then try 2 packs of 7.
Similar problem: packs of 3 and packs of 5, exactly 19 pencils. With 2 packs of 5 there are 9 left, which is 3 packs of 3. That is 5 packs altogether.

stepByStep.text: Try the packs of 7 one at a time. With no packs of 7, 30 is not a multiple of 4.
1 pack of 7 leaves 23, 3 packs leave 9 and 4 packs leave 2. None of these is a multiple of 4.
2 packs of 7 leave 16, which is exactly 4 packs of 4.
So she buys 2 packs of 7 and 4 packs of 4.
Meena buys 6 packs altogether.

misconceptions.A: 2 is the number of packs of 7. She also buys packs of 4, and the question asks for all the packs.
misconceptions.B: 4 is the number of packs of 4. Add the packs of 7 as well.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! 2 packs of 7 and 4 packs of 4 make 14 + 16 = 30 pencils, which is 6 packs.
misconceptions.D: 8 packs of 4 hold 32 pencils, which is too many. She buys exactly 30, so some packs must be packs of 7.

G4A_EQUATIONS_032.questionText: When a number is divided by 8, the quotient is 9 and the remainder is the greatest remainder possible. What is the remainder when the same number is divided by 5?
hints: First rebuild the number from the divisor, the quotient and the remainder. Think carefully about how big a remainder can be.
A remainder is always smaller than the divisor. When dividing by 8, what is the greatest remainder?
Similar problem: a number divided by 6 gives quotient 4 and the greatest possible remainder, which is 5. The number is 6 × 4 + 5 = 29. Divided by 4, 29 leaves remainder 1.

stepByStep.text: A remainder must be smaller than the divisor, so the greatest remainder when dividing by 8 is 7.
Build the number from the divisor, quotient and remainder.
Now divide 79 by 5: 5 × 15 = 75, and 79 is 4 more than 75.
The remainder is 4.

misconceptions.A: This uses 8 as the remainder, which makes the number 80. A remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The greatest remainder is 7, so the number is 79, and 79 is 4 more than 75.
misconceptions.C: This uses 8 × 9 = 72 and leaves out the remainder. Add the greatest possible remainder first.
misconceptions.D: 7 is the greatest remainder when dividing by 8. One more step: build the number and divide it by 5.

G4A_EQUATIONS_033.questionText: Sunita is 30 years old and her daughter Pari is 6 years old. In how many years will Sunita be exactly 3 times as old as Pari?
hints: Both of them grow older together, so the gap between their ages never changes. Use that gap.
Sunita is 24 years older than Pari, now and always. When one age is 3 times the other, the gap is 2 times the smaller age.
Similar problem: a father is 38 and his son is 8. The gap is always 30. When the father is 3 times as old, the gap is 2 times the son's age, so the son is 15. That happens in 15 − 8 = 7 years.

stepByStep.text: Sunita is 24 years older than Pari, and this gap stays the same every year.
When Sunita is 3 times as old as Pari, the gap is 2 times Pari's age.
So Pari's age then is 12, and Sunita's is 36.
Pari is 6 now, so that is 12 − 6 years from now.
Sunita will be 3 times as old as Pari in 6 years.

misconceptions.A: In 4 years Pari is 10, and 30 is 3 times 10. But by then Sunita is 34, not 30. Both of them grow older.
misconceptions.B: 10 is 30 ÷ 3. Test it: in 10 years they are 40 and 16, and 40 is not 3 times 16.
misconceptions.C: 12 is Pari's age when it happens. The question asks how many years from now that is.
misconceptions.D: Well done! In 6 years Sunita is 36 and Pari is 12, and 36 is 3 times 12.

G4A_EQUATIONS_034.questionText: A snail is at the bottom of a well that is 10 m deep. Each day it climbs up 3 m, and each night it slips back 2 m. On which day does the snail first reach the top of the well?
hints: Follow the snail day by day, and think carefully about the last day: once it reaches the top it does not slip back.
After each full day and night the snail is 1 m higher. Find the height from which one day's climb of 3 m reaches the top.

Similar problem: a well 7 m deep, climbing 3 m each day and slipping 1 m each night. The snail starts day 2 at 2 m and day 3 at 4 m. On day 3 it climbs from 4 m to 7 m, so it reaches the top on the 3rd day.

stepByStep.text: Each full day and night the snail gains 1 m.
On its last day the snail climbs 3 m and is out, so it only needs to start a day at 7 m.
Gaining 1 m each full day and night, it starts a day at 7 m after 7 days and nights.
On the next day it climbs from 7 m to 10 m.
The snail first reaches the top on the 8th day.

misconceptions.A: A gain of 1 m each full day and night does suggest 10 days. But on its last day the snail climbs 3 m and is out before it can slip.
misconceptions.B: On the 7th day the snail starts at 6 m and climbs to 9 m, just short of the top. Follow it one more day.
misconceptions.C: This shares 10 m into climbs of 3 m and leaves out the slipping back each night.
misconceptions.D: Excellent thinking! The snail starts the 8th day at 7 m and climbs 3 m to reach 10 m before night comes.

G4A_FACTORS_001.questionText: Which of these numbers is a factor of 36?
hints: A factor of a number divides it exactly, with no remainder.
Try dividing 36 by each number, or look for 36 in each number's times table.
A similar one: is 6 a factor of 42? 6 × 7 = 42, so yes, 6 is a factor of 42.

stepByStep.text: A factor divides the number exactly.
36 ÷ 8, 36 ÷ 10 and 36 ÷ 14 all leave remainders.
9 × 4 = 36, so 9 is a factor of 36.

misconceptions.A: 36 ÷ 8 leaves a remainder of 4, so 8 is not a factor. Try the 9 times table.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 9 × 4 = 36, so 9 divides 36 exactly.
misconceptions.C: Multiples of 10 end in 0, and 36 does not.
misconceptions.D: 14 × 2 = 28 and 14 × 3 = 42, so 36 is skipped.

G4A_FACTORS_002.questionText: Which of these numbers is NOT a multiple of 7?
hints: Multiples of 7 are the numbers in the 7 times table, and the table carries on past 70.
Divide each number by 7 and see which one leaves a remainder.
A similar one: is 75 a multiple of 6? 6 × 12 = 72 and 6 × 13 = 78, so 75 is not a multiple of 6.

stepByStep.text: 42 = 7 × 6 and 63 = 7 × 9, so both are multiples of 7.
91 is also a multiple of 7.
54 lies between 49 and 56, so 54 is not a multiple of 7.

misconceptions.A: 42 = 7 × 6, so it is a multiple of 7. Look for the number that is not in the 7 times table.
misconceptions.B: 63 = 7 × 9, so it is a multiple of 7.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 7 × 7 = 49 and 7 × 8 = 56, so 54 is skipped.
misconceptions.D: 91 = 7 × 13, so it is a multiple of 7, even though it is beyond the usual tables.

G4A_FACTORS_003.questionText: Which of these is a composite number?
hints: A composite number has more than two factors. A prime number has exactly two: 1 and itself.
Test each number with small divisors such as 2, 3 and 5. The digit-sum rule for 3 is useful here.
A similar one: is 51 composite? 5 + 1 = 6, which is a multiple of 3, and 51 = 3 × 17, so 51 is composite.

stepByStep.text: A composite number can be divided exactly by a number other than 1 and itself.
23, 29 and 37 cannot be divided exactly by 2, 3 or 5, so they are prime.
3 + 9 = 12 is a multiple of 3, so 3 divides 39. This makes 39 a composite number.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 39 = 3 × 13, so it has factors other than 1 and itself.
misconceptions.B: 23 can be divided exactly only by 1 and 23, so it is prime.
misconceptions.C: 29 has no factors other than 1 and 29, so it is prime.
misconceptions.D: 37 has no factors other than 1 and 37, so it is prime.

G4A_FACTORS_004.questionText: Which list shows all the factors of 18?
hints: Factors come in pairs that multiply to give the number. Do not forget 1 and the number itself.
Start with 1 × 18. Then try 2, then 3, and so on, writing down each pair that works.
A similar one: the factors of 20. The pairs are 1 × 20, 2 × 10 and 4 × 5, so the factors are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20.

stepByStep.text: Find pairs of numbers that multiply to give 18.
A second pair.
The last pair is 3 × 6. 4 and 5 do not divide 18 exactly.
All the factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The pairs are 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6, giving all six factors.
misconceptions.B: This list leaves out 18 itself. Every number is a factor of itself.
misconceptions.C: This list leaves out 1 and 18. 1 and the number itself are always factors.
misconceptions.D: 4 does not belong, because 18 ÷ 4 leaves a remainder of 2.

G4A_FACTORS_005.questionText: A sweet shop packs laddoos 8 in a box, with none left over. Which of these could be the number of laddoos packed?
hints: If boxes of 8 are filled with none left over, the total must be a multiple of 8.
Check each number against the 8 times table: 40, 48, and so on.
A similar one: pencils packed 6 in a box with none left over. 42 works because 6 × 7 = 42, but 44 would leave 2 over.

stepByStep.text: With none left over, the total is a multiple of 8.
44, 54 and 62 are not in the 8 times table.
56 is a multiple of 8, so 56 laddoos could be packed.

misconceptions.A: 44 ÷ 8 leaves 4 laddoos over, since 8 × 5 = 40.
misconceptions.B: 54 ÷ 8 leaves 6 laddoos over, since 8 × 6 = 48.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 8 × 7 = 56, so 56 laddoos fill 7 boxes exactly.
misconceptions.D: 62 ÷ 8 leaves 6 laddoos over, since 8 × 7 = 56.

G4A_FACTORS_006.questionText: Which of these numbers is a common factor of 12 and 20?
hints: A common factor divides both numbers exactly.
Test each number on 12 first, then test it on 20.
A similar one: is 3 a common factor of 9 and 15? 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so yes.

stepByStep.text: A common factor must divide both 12 and 20 exactly.
3 and 6 do not divide 20, and 5 does not divide 12.
4 divides both, so 4 is a common factor of 12 and 20.

misconceptions.A: 3 is a factor of 12 but not of 20.
misconceptions.B: 5 is a factor of 20 but not of 12.
misconceptions.C: 6 is a factor of 12, but 20 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 5 = 20, so 4 divides both.

G4A_FACTORS_007.questionText: Three decoration lights blink at different speeds: one every 4 seconds, one every 6 seconds and one every 9 seconds. They all blink together now. After how many seconds will they next blink together?
hints: Each light blinks at multiples of its own number. They blink together at a number that is a multiple of all three.
List the multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27 and so on. Check each one to see whether 4 and 6 both divide it.
A similar one: lights blinking every 2, 3 and 5 seconds. The first number all three divide is 30, so they next blink together after 30 seconds.

stepByStep.text: The lights blink together at common multiples of 4, 6 and 9.
Multiples of 9 are 9, 18, 27, 36. Of these, 4 does not divide 9, 18 or 27.
4 and 6 both divide 36.
The lights next blink together after 36 seconds.

misconceptions.A: 18 is a multiple of 6 and 9, but not of 4, so the first light does not blink then.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 36 is the smallest number that 4, 6 and 9 all divide: 4 × 9, 6 × 6 and 9 × 4.
misconceptions.C: All three do blink together at 72 seconds, but that is the second time. They first meet earlier.
misconceptions.D: Multiplying 4 × 6 × 9 gives a common multiple, but not the smallest one.

G4A_FACTORS_008.questionText: A wall panel is 48 cm long and 60 cm wide. It is to be covered exactly with equal square tiles, with no cutting. What is the side of the largest square tile that can be used?
hints: The tile's side must fit a whole number of times along the length and along the width. So it must divide both numbers.
List the factors of 48 and see which of them also divide 60. Then choose the greatest.
A similar one: a 30 cm by 45 cm board. The numbers dividing both are 1, 3, 5 and 15, so the largest square tile has a side of 15 cm.

stepByStep.text: The side of the tile must be a factor of both 48 and 60.
Common factors of 48 and 60 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
The greatest of these is 12.
The largest square tile has a side of 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm tiles would fit, but larger tiles also fit. Look for the greatest number that divides both 48 and 60.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 is the greatest number that divides both 48 and 60: 48 = 12 × 4 and 60 = 12 × 5.
misconceptions.C: 24 divides 48, but 60 ÷ 24 leaves a remainder, so the tiles would not fit the width.
misconceptions.D: 240 is the smallest number that both 48 and 60 divide into. The tile's side must divide 48 and 60, so it cannot be bigger than them.

G4A_FACTORS_009.questionText: Two prime numbers add up to 30. Which of these numbers cannot be one of the two primes?
hints: For each number, find its partner that makes 30. Both numbers in the pair must be prime.
Subtract each number from 30 and ask whether the result is a prime number.
A similar one: two primes add up to 20. Can 3 be one of them? 20 − 3 = 17 is prime, so yes. Can 11? 20 − 11 = 9 = 3 × 3 is not prime, so no.

stepByStep.text: Find the partner of each number: 30 − 7 = 23, 30 − 11 = 19 and 30 − 13 = 17. All three partners are prime.
The partner of 5 is 25.
25 = 5 × 5 is not prime, so 5 cannot be one of the two primes.

misconceptions.A: 7 can be used, because 30 − 7 = 23 and 23 is prime.
misconceptions.B: 11 can be used, because 30 − 11 = 19 and 19 is prime.
misconceptions.C: 13 can be used, because 30 − 13 = 17 and 17 is prime.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 30 − 5 = 25, and 25 = 5 × 5 is not prime, so 5 cannot be used.

G4A_FACTORS_010.questionText: A three-digit number has 7 in the hundreds place and 4 in the ones place. Its tens digit is missing. What is the smallest digit that can go in the tens place so that the number is divisible by 3?
hints: A number is divisible by 3 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
The two known digits add to 7 + 4 = 11. Find the next multiple of 3 after 11.
A similar one: 5 in the hundreds place and 2 in the ones place. 5 + 2 = 7, and the next multiple of 3 is 9, so the smallest tens digit is 2, giving 522.

stepByStep.text: A number is divisible by 3 when its digits add up to a multiple of 3.
Add the known digits.
The next multiple of 3 is 12, which needs 1 more.
The smallest digit is 1, giving the number 714.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 7 + 1 + 4 = 12 is a multiple of 3, so 714 is divisible by 3, and no smaller digit will do.
misconceptions.B: 744 is divisible by 3, but a smaller digit also makes the digit sum a multiple of 3.
misconceptions.C: With 2 the digits add to 7 + 2 + 4 = 13, which is not a multiple of 3.
misconceptions.D: With 0 the digits add to 7 + 0 + 4 = 11, which is not a multiple of 3.

G4A_FACTORS_011.questionText: Which of these numbers is divisible by 6?
hints: A number is divisible by 6 when it is divisible by both 2 and 3.
First leave out any odd number. Then add the digits of each even number to test for 3.
A similar one: is 1,734 divisible by 6? It is even, and 1 + 7 + 3 + 4 = 15 is a multiple of 3, so yes.

stepByStep.text: To be divisible by 6, a number must be even and its digits must add to a multiple of 3.
3,471 is odd, so it is out.
Digit sums: 2,134 gives 10, 5,224 gives 13, and 4,572 gives 18.
18 is a multiple of 3 and the number is even, so 4,572 is divisible by 6.

misconceptions.A: 2,134 is even, but its digits add to 10, which is not a multiple of 3.
misconceptions.B: The digits of 3,471 add to 15, so 3 divides it, but it is odd, so 2 does not.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 4,572 is even and its digits add to 18, a multiple of 3, so both 2 and 3 divide it.
misconceptions.D: 5,224 is even, but its digits add to 13, which is not a multiple of 3.

G4A_FACTORS_012.questionText: Which of these numbers has exactly 3 factors?
hints: Factors usually come in pairs, which gives an even count. Think about when a pair is made of the same number twice.
List the factors of each number and count them.
A similar one: the factors of 49 are 1, 7 and 49, because 7 × 7 = 49. So 49 has exactly 3 factors.

stepByStep.text: List the factors of each number. 15 has 1, 3, 5, 15 and 21 has 1, 3, 7, 21.
27 has 1, 3, 9, 27. Each of these three numbers has 4 factors.
25 has only 1, 5 and 25, because 5 × 5 = 25. So 25 has exactly 3 factors.

misconceptions.A: 15 has four factors: 1, 3, 5 and 15.
misconceptions.B: 21 has four factors: 1, 3, 7 and 21.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The factors of 25 are 1, 5 and 25. The pair 5 × 5 gives only one new factor.
misconceptions.D: 27 has four factors: 1, 3, 9 and 27.

G4A_FACTORS_013.questionText: How many of the factors of 48 are even numbers?
hints: List all the factors of 48 in pairs first. Then sort them into odd and even.
Start the pairs: 1 × 48, 2 × 24, 3 × 16, and keep going until the pairs repeat.
A similar one: the factors of 20 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 and 20. The even ones are 2, 4, 10 and 20, so 4 of them are even.

stepByStep.text: List the factor pairs of 48: 1 × 48, 2 × 24, 3 × 16, 4 × 12 and 6 × 8.
Only 1 and 3 are odd.
8 of the factors of 48 are even numbers.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24 and 48. Leaving out 1 and 3 gives 8 even factors.
misconceptions.B: 10 is the number of all the factors of 48. Two of them, 1 and 3, are odd.
misconceptions.C: This counts the factor pairs. Each pair has two factors, so list all ten and pick out the even ones.
misconceptions.D: 2 is the number of odd factors, 1 and 3. The question asks for the even ones.

G4A_FACTORS_014.questionText: A flower seller can string all her marigolds into garlands of 10 flowers or into garlands of 15 flowers, with no flower left over either way. What is the smallest number of marigolds she could have?
hints: The number of flowers must be a multiple of 10 and also a multiple of 15.
List the multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45 and so on. Find the first that is also a multiple of 10.
A similar one: bunches of 4 flowers or of 6 flowers with none left over. Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, and 12 is the first that 4 divides, so the smallest number is 12.

stepByStep.text: The number must be a common multiple of 10 and 15.
Multiples of 15 are 15, 30, 45. 15 is not a multiple of 10.
30 is a multiple of 10.
The smallest number of marigolds is 30.

misconceptions.A: 10 × 15 = 150 would work, but a smaller number also works.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 30 = 10 × 3 = 15 × 2, and no smaller number is a multiple of both.
misconceptions.C: 5 divides both 10 and 15, but she needs a number that 10 and 15 both divide into.
misconceptions.D: 60 flowers would work, but it is not the smallest number that does.

G4A_FACTORS_015.questionText: What is the greatest prime factor of 84?
hints: Break the number down into prime numbers multiplied together. Then pick the greatest prime you used.
Start by dividing 84 by 2: 84 = 2 × 42. Keep splitting until every part is prime.
A similar one: 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, so the greatest prime factor of 60 is 5.

stepByStep.text: Split 84 into smaller factors.
Keep splitting until all the parts are prime.
The prime factors are 2, 3 and 7. The greatest prime factor of 84 is 7.

misconceptions.A: 21 is a factor of 84, but it is not prime, because 21 = 3 × 7.
misconceptions.B: 3 is a prime factor of 84, but there is a greater one.
misconceptions.C: 42 is a factor of 84, but it is not prime, because 42 = 2 × 21.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, and 7 is the greatest of these primes.

G4A_FACTORS_016.questionText: What is the smallest number that must be subtracted from 4,729 to get a number that is divisible by 9?
hints: A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
Add the digits: 4 + 7 + 2 + 9. Compare the total with the nearest multiple of 9 below it.
A similar one: for 3,152 the digits add to 11, which is 2 more than 9. So subtract 2 to get 3,150, which is divisible by 9.

stepByStep.text: Add the digits of 4,729.
The multiple of 9 just below 22 is 18.
Taking away 4 gives 4,725, which is divisible by 9. The smallest number to subtract is 4.

misconceptions.A: Adding 5 would also give a multiple of 9, but the question asks what to subtract. The digit sum 22 is 4 more than 18.
misconceptions.B: Taking away 2 leaves 4,727, whose digits add to 20. That is not a multiple of 9.
misconceptions.C: Taking away 9 does not help: the new number would still be 4 more than a multiple of 9.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The digits add to 22, which is 4 more than 18, so taking away 4 gives 4,725, whose digits add to 18.

G4A_FACTORS_017.questionText: A staircase has 50 steps, numbered 1 to 50. Anu steps only on every 3rd step (3, 6, 9 and so on). Biju steps only on every 4th step (4, 8, 12 and so on). How many steps are touched by neither of them?
hints: Count the steps each child touches, but be careful: some steps are touched by both.
Anu touches the multiples of 3 up to 50 and Biju the multiples of 4. Steps touched by both are multiples of 12.
A similar one with 20 steps and every 2nd and every 5th step: 10 steps and 4 steps, with 2 steps (10 and 20) counted twice. So 10 + 4 − 2 = 12 are touched and 20 − 12 = 8 are not.

stepByStep.text: Anu touches the multiples of 3 up to 50: there are 16.
Biju touches the multiples of 4 up to 50: there are 12. Steps touched by both are the multiples of 12: there are 4.
Steps touched by at least one child.
Steps touched by neither. The answer is 26.

misconceptions.A: This takes away 16 and 12 from 50. But the 4 steps that both touch (12, 24, 36 and 48) were counted twice, so add them back.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Anu touches 16 steps and Biju 12, with 4 counted twice, so 24 steps are touched and 50 − 24 = 26 are not.
misconceptions.C: 24 is the number of steps touched by at least one of them. The question asks for the steps left untouched.
misconceptions.D: This takes away only the 4 steps both of them touch. Take away every step that either of them touches.

G4A_FACTORS_018.questionText: From a bus stand, buses to Pune leave every 15 minutes and buses to Nashik leave every 20 minutes. One bus of each kind leaves at 6:00 in the morning. From 6:00 to 10:00 in the morning, counting both of these times, how many times do a Pune bus and a Nashik bus leave together?
hints: First find after how many minutes the two kinds of bus leave together again. Then count the times carefully, including the start.
Find the smallest number that is a multiple of both 15 and 20.
A similar one: bells ringing every 10 and 15 minutes, both at 2:00. They ring together every 30 minutes, so from 2:00 to 3:00 that is at 2:00, 2:30 and 3:00, which is 3 times.

stepByStep.text: Find the smallest common multiple of 15 and 20. Multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60, and 15 divides 60.
So the buses leave together every 60 minutes, that is, every hour.
They leave together 5 times.

misconceptions.A: The buses leave together every 60 minutes, which happens 4 times after 6:00. But 6:00 itself also counts.
misconceptions.B: This takes the buses to leave together every 30 minutes. 30 is a multiple of 15 but not of 20; the first common multiple is 60.
misconceptions.C: Yes! They leave together every 60 minutes: at 6:00, 7:00, 8:00, 9:00 and 10:00. That is 5 times.
misconceptions.D: This counts the Nashik buses after 6:00. Only some of them leave at the same time as a Pune bus.

G4A_FACTORS_019.questionText: Rohan has some marbles. When he puts them in groups of 4, or groups of 5, or groups of 6, there are always 3 marbles left over. What is the smallest number of marbles he could have, if he has more than 3?
hints: If the 3 extra marbles were put aside, the rest could be grouped exactly in 4s, 5s and 6s.
Find the smallest number that is a multiple of 4, 5 and 6. Multiples of 6 that end in 0 are worth checking.
A similar one: groups of 2, 3 or 4 always leave 1 over. The smallest number that 2, 3 and 4 all divide is 12, so the answer is 12 + 1 = 13.

stepByStep.text: Without the 3 extra marbles, the number is a multiple of 4, 5 and 6.
Multiples of 6 that are also multiples of 5 are 30, 60 and so on. 4 does not divide 30, but 4 divides 60.
Add the 3 marbles left over.
The smallest number of marbles is 63.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 60 is the smallest number that 4, 5 and 6 all divide, and 3 more gives 63, which leaves 3 over each time.
misconceptions.B: 60 makes exact groups of 4, 5 and 6 with nothing left. Rohan always has 3 left over, so add 3.
misconceptions.C: 123 does leave 3 over each time, but a smaller number does too. It comes from using 120 instead of the smallest common multiple, 60.
misconceptions.D: The 3 left-over marbles are extra, so add them to 60. 57 ÷ 4 leaves only 1 over.

G4A_FACTORS_020.questionText: I am a two-digit number. I am a multiple of 7. I am odd. My two digits add up to 10. Which number am I?
hints: Use one clue to make a short list, then test the other clues on that list.
Write the two-digit numbers whose digits add up to 10: 19, 28, 37 and so on. Then strike out the even ones.
A similar one: a two-digit multiple of 9 that is even and has 5 as its tens digit. The only multiple of 9 in the fifties is 54, and it is even, so the number is 54.

stepByStep.text: Two-digit numbers with digits adding to 10 are 19, 28, 37, 46, 55, 64, 73, 82 and 91.
The odd ones are 19, 37, 55, 73 and 91.
Of these only 91 is a multiple of 7.
The number is 91.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 91 = 7 × 13, it is odd, and 9 + 1 = 10.
misconceptions.B: 28 is a multiple of 7 and its digits add to 10, but it is even.
misconceptions.C: 73 is odd and its digits add to 10, but it is not a multiple of 7, since 7 × 10 = 70 and 7 × 11 = 77.
misconceptions.D: 49 is an odd multiple of 7, but its digits add to 13.

G4A_FACTORS_021.questionText: What is the smallest number that has exactly 6 factors?
hints: There is no quick rule here. Test numbers in order, list the factors of each one in pairs, and stop at the first number that has the right count.
Start with small numbers. The factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6, which is only four. Keep going with 8, 9, 10 and so on.
A similar problem: the smallest number with exactly 4 factors. 1 has one factor, 2, 3 and 5 have two each, 4 has three (1, 2, 4), and 6 has four (1, 2, 3, 6). So the smallest is 6.

stepByStep.text: Numbers up to 11 have at most four factors. For example, 6 has 1, 2, 3, 6 and 10 has 1, 2, 5, 10.
List the factors of 12 in pairs.
That gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, which is six factors.
No smaller number has six factors, so the smallest such number is 12.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, and no smaller number has six.
misconceptions.B: 18 does have six factors: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. But a smaller number has six factors too. Test the numbers before 18.
misconceptions.C: The number 6 has only four factors: 1, 2, 3 and 6. The question asks for a number with six factors.
misconceptions.D: 16 has five factors: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Count again and try another number.

G4A_FACTORS_022.questionText: How many numbers from 1 to 50 have exactly 3 factors?
hints: Factors usually come in pairs, so most numbers have an even number of factors. Think about which kind of number has a factor that pairs with itself.
Only square numbers have an odd number of factors. List the square numbers up to 50 and count the factors of each one.
A similar problem: which numbers from 1 to 10 have exactly 3 factors? The squares are 1, 4 and 9. 1 has one factor, 4 has 1, 2, 4 and 9 has 1, 3, 9. So there are 2 such numbers.

stepByStep.text: Only square numbers have an odd number of factors. The squares up to 50 are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 and 49.
Count the factors: 1 has one, 4 has three (1, 2, 4), 9 has three (1, 3, 9), 16 has five.
25 has three (1, 5, 25), 36 has nine, and 49 has three (1, 7, 49).
The numbers are 4, 9, 25 and 49. So 4 numbers have exactly 3 factors.

misconceptions.A: This counts every square number up to 50. Check 1, 16 and 36: they have one, five and nine factors.
misconceptions.B: One number is missing. Check the squares of 2, 3, 5 and 7, which are all 50 or less.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! Only 4, 9, 25 and 49 have exactly three factors.
misconceptions.D: This counts the prime numbers. A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, not three.

G4A_FACTORS_024.questionText: Buses to Pune leave a bus stand every 12 minutes, starting at 7:00 in the morning. Buses to Nashik leave every 18 minutes, starting at 7:06 in the morning. At what time do a Pune bus and a Nashik bus first leave at the same moment?
hints: The two kinds of bus do not start together, so a common multiple alone will not settle it. Write out the leaving times of each kind and look for the first time on both lists.
List the Pune times: 7:00, 7:12 and so on. Then list the Nashik times starting from 7:06, adding 18 minutes each time.
A similar problem: bell P rings every 10 minutes from 9:00 and bell Q rings every 15 minutes from 9:05. P rings at 9:00, 9:10, 9:20, 9:30. Q rings at 9:05, 9:20. The first time on both lists is 9:20.

stepByStep.text: Pune buses leave at 7:00, 7:12, 7:24, 7:36, ...
Nashik buses leave at 7:06, 7:24, 7:42, ...
Look for the first time that is on both lists.
A Pune bus and a Nashik bus first leave together at 7:24.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 7:24 is on both lists: 7:00, 7:12, 7:24 and 7:06, 7:24.
misconceptions.B: This adds 36 minutes, the LCM of 12 and 18, to 7:00. That would fit if both started at 7:00, but the Nashik buses start at 7:06. List the times instead.
misconceptions.C: This adds 36 minutes to 7:06. No Pune bus leaves at 7:42. List both sets of times and compare.
misconceptions.D: A Pune bus leaves at 8:12, but no Nashik bus does, and there is an earlier time on both lists.

G4A_FACTORS_025.questionText: Rina has fewer than 50 sweets. When she packs them in fives, 3 sweets are left over. When she packs them in sevens, 2 sweets are left over. How many sweets does Rina have?
hints: List the numbers that fit one of the two conditions. Then test each number on your list against the other condition.
Numbers that leave 2 when packed in sevens are 2, 9, 16 and so on. Write these out up to 50, then divide each one by 5.

A similar problem: fewer than 30 marbles, 1 left over in threes and 2 left over in fives. Numbers leaving 2 in fives: 2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27. Of these, 7 leaves 1 in threes, and so does 22. If there are fewer than 20, the count is 7.

stepByStep.text: List the numbers below 50 that leave 2 when divided by 7: 2, 9, 16, 23, 30, 37, 44.
Divide each by 5 and look for a remainder of 3.
Only one of them leaves 3.
Rina has 23 sweets.

misconceptions.A: Great thinking! 23 = 4 × 5 + 3 and 23 = 3 × 7 + 2, so both conditions fit.
misconceptions.B: 37 leaves 2 when packed in sevens, but in fives it also leaves 2, not 3.
misconceptions.C: 33 leaves 3 when packed in fives, but in sevens it leaves 5, not 2.
misconceptions.D: 38 leaves 3 when packed in fives, but in sevens it also leaves 3, not 2.

G4A_FACTORS_026.questionText: The children of a class stand in rows for a drill. In rows of 6, the last row has only 5 children. In rows of 8, the last row has only 7 children. There are more than 40 and fewer than 60 children. How many children are there?
hints: Look at how many children are missing from the last row each time. Think about what would happen if one more child joined the class.
With one more child, the rows of 6 would be complete and the rows of 8 would be complete too. Find a number between 40 and 60 that both 6 and 8 divide exactly.

A similar problem: in rows of 4 the last row has 3, and in rows of 5 the last row has 4, with between 30 and 50 children. One more child would fill every row, so that number is a common multiple of 4 and 5, which is 40. The class has 40 − 1 = 39 children.

stepByStep.text: Each time, the last row is 1 child short. With 1 more child, both kinds of row would be full.
So the number of children plus 1 is a common multiple of 6 and 8. Between 40 and 60 the only one is 48.
Take away the extra child.
There are 47 children.

misconceptions.A: 48 children would fill every row of 6 and every row of 8 exactly. Here each last row is one child short.
misconceptions.B: 53 leaves 5 in rows of 6, but in rows of 8 it also leaves 5, not 7.
misconceptions.C: This adds 1 to the common multiple. The last rows are one short, so take 1 away instead.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 47 = 7 × 6 + 5 and 47 = 5 × 8 + 7, one short of 48 each time.

G4A_FACTORS_027.questionText: A prime number has two digits and is less than 50. Its digits add up to 10. When its two digits are swapped, the new number is also a prime number. Which number is it?
hints: Test each condition in turn. For a number that looks prime, try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7 before you decide.
First keep only the choices whose digits add up to 10. Then swap the digits of each one and test the new number by dividing by 3 and by 7.

A similar problem: a two-digit prime below 20 whose digits add up to 4 and whose swapped number is also prime. 13 is prime and 1 + 3 = 4. Swapped it becomes 31, which cannot be divided exactly by 2, 3 or 5, so 31 is prime too. The number is 13.

stepByStep.text: The digits must add up to 10. That leaves 19 and 37, because 1 + 3 = 4 and 1 + 7 = 8.
Swap the digits of 19 to get 91. This is not a prime number.
Swap the digits of 37 to get 73. It cannot be divided exactly by 2, 3, 5 or 7, so 73 is a prime number.
The number is 37.

misconceptions.A: 19 is a prime and its digits add up to 10. But swapped it becomes 91, and 91 = 7 × 13, so 91 is not a prime.
misconceptions.B: 13 and 31 are both primes, but 1 + 3 = 4. The digits must add up to 10.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 3 + 7 = 10, and both 37 and 73 are prime numbers.
misconceptions.D: 17 and 71 are both primes, but 1 + 7 = 8. The digits must add up to 10.

G4A_FACTORS_028.questionText: Two prime numbers add up to 25. What is the product of these two prime numbers?
hints: Think about odd and even numbers. What kind of number do you get when you add two odd numbers?
25 is odd, so the two primes cannot both be odd. One of them must be even. Which prime number is even?
A similar problem: two primes add up to 15. One of them must be the even prime 2, so the other is 15 − 2 = 13, which is prime. Their product is 2 × 13 = 26.

stepByStep.text: Odd + odd is even, but 25 is odd. So one of the two primes must be even.
The only even prime number is 2, so the other prime is 23.
23 is a prime number, so the pair is 2 and 23.
Their product is 46.

misconceptions.A: This is 11 × 14. They add up to 25, but 14 is not a prime number.
misconceptions.B: Well done! One prime must be 2, the other is 23, and 2 × 23 = 46.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 22. They add up to 25, but 22 is not a prime number.
misconceptions.D: This is 12 × 13. They add up to 25, but 12 is not a prime number.

G4A_FACTORS_029.questionText: What is the greatest 3-digit number that can be divided exactly by 6 but cannot be divided exactly by 4?
hints: Start from the greatest 3-digit multiple of 6 and move down one multiple at a time. Test each one against the second condition.
A number divides by 6 when it is even and its digits add up to a multiple of 3. Find the greatest such 3-digit number, then check its last two digits to see whether 4 divides it.
A similar problem: the greatest 2-digit number that 6 divides but 4 does not. The multiples of 6 going down are 96, 90. 96 ÷ 4 = 24, so 96 is out. 90 ÷ 4 leaves a remainder, so the number is 90.

stepByStep.text: The greatest 3-digit multiple of 6 is 996.
Its last two digits are 96, and 4 divides 96, so 4 divides 996. It does not fit.
The next multiple of 6 going down is 990. Its last two digits are 90, and 4 does not divide 90.
The greatest such number is 990.

misconceptions.A: 996 is the greatest 3-digit multiple of 6, but 4 divides it too, because 4 divides 96. Step down to the next multiple of 6.
misconceptions.B: 994 cannot be divided by 4, but it cannot be divided by 6 either: its digits add up to 22, which is not a multiple of 3.
misconceptions.C: 978 fits both conditions, but it is not the greatest. Look at the multiples of 6 just below 996.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 990 = 6 × 165, and 4 does not divide 90, so 990 is the greatest number that fits.

G4A_FACTORS_030.questionText: How many numbers from 1 to 100 are multiples of 4 but not multiples of 6?
hints: Count the multiples of 4 first. Then think carefully about which of those are also multiples of 6, because only those need to be removed.
There are 100 ÷ 4 multiples of 4. A number that is a multiple of both 4 and 6 is a multiple of their LCM. Find the LCM of 4 and 6.

A similar problem: how many numbers from 1 to 60 are multiples of 2 but not of 3? There are 60 ÷ 2 = 30 multiples of 2. Those that are also multiples of 3 are the multiples of 6, and 60 ÷ 6 = 10. So 30 − 10 = 20 numbers fit.

stepByStep.text: Count the multiples of 4 from 1 to 100.
A multiple of both 4 and 6 is a multiple of 12. Count these: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96.
Remove them from the multiples of 4.
So 17 numbers are multiples of 4 but not multiples of 6.

misconceptions.A: This takes away all 16 multiples of 6. Many of those, like 6 and 18, were never multiples of 4. Remove only the multiples of 12.
misconceptions.B: This is the count of all the multiples of 4. Some of them, like 12 and 24, are multiples of 6 too and must be removed.
misconceptions.C: This removes only the multiples of 24. The first number that is a multiple of both 4 and 6 is 12.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! There are 25 multiples of 4, and 8 of them are multiples of 12, leaving 17.

G4A_FACTORS_031.questionText: A number is a factor of 60. It is a multiple of 4. It is not a multiple of 3. It is greater than 4. Which number is it?
hints: There are four conditions. A number must pass every one of them, so test each choice against all four.
First check which of the choices are factors of 60 by dividing 60 by each one. Then test what is left against the other conditions.

A similar problem: a factor of 30 that is a multiple of 5, not a multiple of 2, and greater than 5. The factors of 30 that are multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15 and 30. Of these, 10 and 30 are multiples of 2, and 5 is not greater than 5. So the number is 15.

stepByStep.text: Of these, the multiples of 4 are 4, 12, 20 and 60.
12 and 60 are multiples of 3, so they are out. 4 is not greater than 4, so it is out.
The number is 20.

misconceptions.A: 12 is a factor of 60 and a multiple of 4, but 12 = 3 × 4, so it is a multiple of 3. The number must not be.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 20 divides 60, it is 4 × 5, and 3 does not divide it.
misconceptions.C: 40 is a multiple of 4 and not a multiple of 3, but 60 ÷ 40 leaves a remainder, so 40 is not a factor of 60.
misconceptions.D: 60 is a factor of itself and a multiple of 4, but 60 = 3 × 20, so it is a multiple of 3. The number must not be.

G4A_FACTORS_032.questionText: What is the greatest number that divides both 50 and 74 and leaves a remainder of 2 each time?
hints: If a division leaves a remainder, take the remainder away and the division becomes exact. Then use what you know about common factors.
Take 2 away from each number: 50 − 2 and 74 − 2. The number you want must divide both of these exactly.

A similar problem: the greatest number that divides 23 and 38 leaving a remainder of 3 each time. Take 3 away: 20 and 35. Their HCF is 5, and 23 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 3, 38 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder 3. So the number is 5.

stepByStep.text: Take the remainder away from each number.
The number wanted must divide 48 and 72 exactly, and be as large as possible. That is their HCF.
The common factors of 48 and 72 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24.
Check: 50 = 24 × 2 + 2 and 74 = 24 × 3 + 2. The greatest such number is 24.

misconceptions.A: 2 is the HCF of 50 and 74, but it divides them exactly and leaves no remainder. Take the remainder 2 away from each number first.
misconceptions.B: 12 does leave a remainder of 2 each time, but a greater number does so too. Look for the HCF of 48 and 72.
misconceptions.C: 4 does leave a remainder of 2 each time, but much greater numbers do so too. Look for the HCF of 48 and 72.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! 48 and 72 have HCF 24, and both 50 and 74 leave 2 when divided by 24.

G4A_FRACTIONS_001.questionText: A jug holds 7/8 litre of lassi. Meena pours out 5/12 litre for her brother. How much lassi is left in the jug?
hints: This is a taking-away problem with fractions whose bottom numbers are different. The pieces must be the same size before you can subtract.
Find a number that both 8 and 12 divide into exactly, and change both fractions so that they have that bottom number.
A similar one: 3/4 − 1/6. Both 4 and 6 divide into 12, so 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/6 = 2/12. Then 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12.

stepByStep.text: The smallest number that both 8 and 12 divide into is 24.
Change both fractions to twenty-fourths.
Subtract the top numbers and keep the bottom number.
11/24 litre of lassi is left in the jug.

misconceptions.A: Yes! In twenty-fourths, 21/24 − 10/24 leaves 11/24 litre.
misconceptions.B: This comes from subtracting the tops and the bottoms separately (7 − 5 and 12 − 8). Make the bottom numbers the same first, then subtract only the tops.
misconceptions.C: This is what you get by adding the two amounts. Lassi was poured out, so take 10/24 away from 21/24.
misconceptions.D: Here the bottom number became 24 but the tops stayed 7 and 5. When 8 becomes 24 the 7 must become 21, and the 5 becomes 10.

G4A_FRACTIONS_002.questionText: A ribbon is 5 1/4 m long. Kavya cuts off 2 2/3 m to wrap a gift. How long is the ribbon now?
hints: This is subtraction of mixed numbers. Make the fraction parts the same kind, then check whether the first fraction part is big enough to subtract from.
Write 1/4 and 2/3 in twelfths. Is 3/12 big enough to take 8/12 away from? If not, break one whole from the 5 into 12/12.
A similar one: 4 1/6 − 1 1/2. In sixths, 1/2 = 3/6. 1/6 is too small, so 4 1/6 becomes 3 7/6. Then 3 7/6 − 1 3/6 = 2 4/6 = 2 2/3.

stepByStep.text: Write the fraction parts in twelfths.
3/12 is smaller than 8/12, so take one whole from the 5 and turn it into 12/12.
Subtract the wholes and the fraction parts.
The ribbon is now 2 7/12 m long.

misconceptions.A: This takes 5 − 2 = 3 and then the smaller fraction from the bigger one (2/3 − 1/4). The 2/3 has to be taken from the 5 1/4, so one whole must be broken up first.
misconceptions.B: The fraction part 7/12 is right, but one whole was broken into twelfths to get it. That leaves 4 wholes, and 4 − 2 = 2.
misconceptions.C: The whole number 2 is right. For the fraction part, 15/12 − 8/12 is 7/12, not 8/12 − 3/12.
misconceptions.D: Well done! After breaking one whole into twelfths, 4 15/12 − 2 8/12 = 2 7/12 m.

G4A_FRACTIONS_003.questionText: A baker cuts every cake into 6 equal slices. By evening she has sold 47 slices. How many cakes is that, written as a mixed number?
hints: Each cake is 6 sixths. You are turning a number of sixths into whole cakes and left-over slices.
Work out how many full groups of 6 slices fit into 47 slices, and how many slices are left over.
A similar one: 29 slices when each cake has 4 slices. 29 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 1, so that is 7 whole cakes and 1/4 of a cake: 7 1/4.

stepByStep.text: 47 slices, each one-sixth of a cake, is the fraction 47/6.
Divide 47 by 6.
7 whole cakes and 5 slices out of 6 make 7 5/6 cakes.

misconceptions.A: Right! 7 full cakes use 42 slices, and the 5 slices left are 5/6 of a cake: 7 5/6.
misconceptions.B: The 7 and the 5 are right, but the left-over slices are sixths of a cake. The bottom number stays 6, not 47.
misconceptions.C: This rounds up to 48 slices. 47 slices is a little less than 8 cakes: 7 full cakes and 5 slices more.
misconceptions.D: The 7 and the 5 have changed places. The number of full cakes (7) is the whole number and the left-over slices (5) go on top of the 6.

G4A_FRACTIONS_004.questionText: Which of these numbers is the greatest? 3 2/5, 17/4, 4 1/8, 25/6
hints: Some of these are mixed numbers and some are improper fractions. Put them all in the same form before you compare.
Change 17/4 and 25/6 into mixed numbers. Then compare the whole-number parts first.
A similar one: which is greater, 13/5 or 2 1/2? 13/5 = 2 3/5. Both have 2 wholes, and 3/5 is more than 1/2, so 13/5 is greater.

stepByStep.text: Change the improper fractions to mixed numbers.
3 2/5 has only 3 wholes, so it is the smallest. The other three all have 4 wholes.
Compare the fraction parts 1/4, 1/8 and 1/6. With the same top number, the smaller bottom number gives the bigger piece, so 1/4 is the biggest.
The greatest number is 17/4.

misconceptions.A: 3 2/5 has only 3 wholes, while the others have 4 wholes each. Look at the whole-number part first.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 17/4 is 4 1/4, and a quarter is bigger than a sixth or an eighth.
misconceptions.C: 4 1/8 can look big because of the 8, but an eighth is a small piece. Compare 1/8 with 1/4 and 1/6.
misconceptions.D: 25/6 has the biggest top number, but it is only 4 1/6. Change each one to a mixed number before comparing.

hints: To put several fractions in order, give them all the same bottom number. Then the top numbers tell you the order.
4, 8, 12 and 3 all divide into 24. Change each fraction into twenty-fourths.
A similar one: order 1/2, 7/10 and 3/5. In tenths they are 5/10, 7/10 and 6/10, so from smallest to greatest: 1/2, 3/5, 7/10.

stepByStep.text: Change every fraction to twenty-fourths.
Do the same for the other two.
Order the top numbers: 14, 15, 16, 18.
From smallest to greatest: 7/12, 5/8, 2/3, 3/4.

misconceptions.A: These are in order, but from greatest to smallest. The question asks for smallest first.
misconceptions.B: This puts the top numbers 2, 3, 5, 7 in order. A bigger top number does not always mean a bigger fraction; change them all to twenty-fourths first.
misconceptions.C: Nearly there. Check the first two: 5/8 is 15/24 and 7/12 is 14/24, so 7/12 is the smaller one.
misconceptions.D: Yes! In twenty-fourths they are 14, 15, 16 and 18, which gives 7/12, 5/8, 2/3, 3/4.

G4A_FRACTIONS_006.questionText: Four friends ran before school. Asha ran 3/5 km, Bala ran 3/4 km, Chitra ran 3/10 km and Dev ran 3/7 km. Who ran the second longest distance?
hints: All four fractions have the same top number. Think about what the bottom number tells you about the size of each piece.
When the top numbers are the same, the fraction with the smallest bottom number is the biggest. Put 4, 5, 7 and 10 in order.
A similar one: 2/9, 2/3 and 2/5. Thirds are the biggest pieces, then fifths, then ninths. So the longest is 2/3 and the second longest is 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Every distance is 3 pieces of a kilometre, so only the size of the pieces matters.
Quarters are bigger than fifths, fifths are bigger than sevenths, and sevenths are bigger than tenths.
From longest to shortest: 3/4 (Bala), 3/5 (Asha), 3/7 (Dev), 3/10 (Chitra).
The second longest distance was run by Asha.

misconceptions.A: Right! Bala's 3/4 km is the longest and Asha's 3/5 km comes next.
misconceptions.B: Bala's 3/4 km is the longest of all. The question asks who came second.
misconceptions.C: Chitra's fraction has the biggest bottom number, but tenths are the smallest pieces, so 3/10 km is the shortest run.
misconceptions.D: Dev's 3/7 km is the third longest. Fifths are bigger pieces than sevenths, so 3/5 is more than 3/7.

G4A_FRACTIONS_007.questionText: Ravi has Rs. 240. He spends 3/8 of it on a cricket ball and 1/3 of it on a book. How much money does he have left?
hints: This is a fraction-of-an-amount story with two parts. Find each amount spent, then see what is left.
To find 3/8 of Rs. 240, first find 1/8 of 240 by dividing by 8.
A similar one: Rs. 120, with 1/4 and 1/3 of it spent. 1/4 of 120 is 30 and 1/3 of 120 is 40. 120 − 30 − 40 = Rs. 50 left.

stepByStep.text: Find 3/8 of 240. One eighth is 30, so three eighths is 90.
Find 1/3 of 240.
Add the money spent.
Subtract from Rs. 240. Ravi has Rs. 70 left.

misconceptions.A: Rs. 170 is the money Ravi spent. The question asks how much is left, so take it away from Rs. 240.
misconceptions.B: This takes away only the cricket ball (Rs. 90). The book costs 1/3 of Rs. 240 as well.
misconceptions.C: Well done! He spends Rs. 90 and Rs. 80, and 240 − 170 leaves Rs. 70.
misconceptions.D: This takes 1/3 of the money left after the ball. The story says 1/3 of it, meaning 1/3 of the whole Rs. 240.

G4A_FRACTIONS_008.questionText: In a class, 3/5 of the children are girls. There are 18 girls. How many children are there in the class?
hints: Here you know a part and must find the whole. Think of the class as 5 equal groups, with 3 of the groups being girls.
3 equal groups make 18 girls. Find how many children are in one group.
A similar one: 2/7 of a class is 8 children. One seventh is 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the whole class is 4 × 7 = 28 children.

stepByStep.text: 3/5 of the class is 18 children, so 3 equal parts make 18.
Find one part (one fifth).
The whole class is 5 parts.
There are 30 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 18 by 3. But 18 is already three of the five parts; divide by 3 to find one part.
misconceptions.B: Yes! One fifth of the class is 6 children, so five fifths is 30 children.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 18 by 5, as if 18 were one fifth. 18 is three fifths, so one fifth is 6.
misconceptions.D: 12 is the number of boys. The question asks for all the children, girls and boys together.

G4A_FRACTIONS_009.questionText: Kiran has read 2/7 of his storybook. He still has 150 pages to read. How many pages does the book have?
hints: The 150 pages are the part not yet read. First work out what fraction of the book that part is.
If 2/7 has been read, then 5/7 is left. So 5 equal parts of the book make 150 pages.
A similar one: after reading 1/4 of a book, 90 pages are left. 90 pages is 3/4, so 1/4 is 30 pages and the book has 4 × 30 = 120 pages.

stepByStep.text: Find the fraction still to be read.
5/7 of the book is 150 pages, so one seventh is 30 pages.
The whole book is seven sevenths.
The book has 210 pages.

misconceptions.A: Right! 150 pages is 5/7 of the book, so 1/7 is 30 pages and the book has 210 pages.
misconceptions.B: This treats the 150 pages as 2/7 of the book. They are the pages left, which is 5/7 of the book.
misconceptions.C: 60 is the number of pages Kiran has read. The question asks for all the pages in the book.
misconceptions.D: This adds one seventh (30 pages) to 150. Kiran has read two sevenths, so add 60 pages.

G4A_FRACTIONS_010.questionText: What must be subtracted from 3 1/2 to get 1 5/6?
hints: The number you take away is the gap between the two numbers. So this is a subtraction of mixed numbers.
Work out 3 1/2 − 1 5/6. Start by writing 1/2 in sixths.
A similar one: what must be subtracted from 2 1/4 to get 1 1/2? 2 1/4 − 1 1/2 = 9/4 − 6/4 = 3/4.

stepByStep.text: The number to subtract is 3 1/2 − 1 5/6.
Write both as improper fractions in sixths.
Subtract.
10/6 = 5/3 = 1 2/3, so 1 2/3 must be subtracted.

misconceptions.A: This takes 3 − 1 = 2 and then 5/6 − 1/2. The 5/6 has to be taken from the 1/2, so a whole must be broken into sixths first.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 21/6 − 11/6 = 10/6, which is 1 2/3.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two numbers. The number to subtract is the gap between them: 3 1/2 − 1 5/6.
misconceptions.D: The whole number 1 is right. The fraction part is 4/6, and dividing top and bottom by 2 gives 2/3.

G4A_FRACTIONS_011.questionText: Twelve beads are threaded on a string in this order: R R B G R B B R G R B R, where R is a red bead, B is a blue bead and G is a green bead. What fraction of the beads are blue, in lowest terms?
hints: A fraction of a group is the number you are counting over the number in the whole group. Then make the fraction as simple as you can.
Count the blue beads carefully along the row. That count goes on top, and 12 goes on the bottom.
A similar one: in a row of 10 beads, 4 are yellow. The fraction is 4/10, and dividing the top and bottom by 2 gives 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Count the blue beads in the row: there are 4.
There are 12 beads in all, so the fraction that is blue is 4/12.
Divide the top and bottom by 4.
1/3 of the beads are blue.

misconceptions.A: 1/2 is the fraction of red beads (6 out of 12). The question asks about the blue beads.
misconceptions.B: 1/6 is the fraction of green beads (2 out of 12). Count the blue beads instead.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 4 of the 12 beads are blue, and 4/12 in lowest terms is 1/3.
misconceptions.D: There are 4 blue beads, but the fraction is 4 out of 12, not 1 out of 4. Put the count over 12 and then simplify.

G4A_FRACTIONS_012.questionText: A fraction is equal to 3/5. Its numerator and denominator add up to 40. What is its denominator?
hints: Fractions equal to 3/5 are made by multiplying its top and bottom by the same number. Look for the one whose two numbers have the right total.
In 3/5 itself the top and bottom add up to 8. How many times does 8 go into 40?
A similar one: a fraction equal to 2/3 whose top and bottom add up to 20. 2 + 3 = 5 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so multiply both by 4 to get 8/12. Its denominator is 12.

stepByStep.text: Fractions equal to 3/5 come from multiplying the top and bottom by the same number: 6/10, 9/15, 12/20 and so on.
In 3/5 the top and bottom add up to 8. We need a total of 40, which is 5 times as much.
Multiply the top and bottom by 5.
15 + 25 = 40, so the denominator is 25.

misconceptions.A: 15 is the numerator of the fraction 15/25. The question asks for the denominator, the bottom number.
misconceptions.B: 24 is 3/5 of 40. But 40 is the total of the top and bottom together, so share it into 3 parts and 5 parts.
misconceptions.C: 8 is 3 + 5, a useful first step. Next see how many times 8 goes into 40 and multiply the top and bottom by that number.
misconceptions.D: Right! 15/25 equals 3/5 and 15 + 25 = 40, so the denominator is 25.

G4A_FRACTIONS_013.questionText: Anu drank 1/2 litre of water in the morning, 3/4 litre in the afternoon and 5/8 litre in the evening. How much water did she drink in all?
hints: You are adding three fractions with different bottom numbers. Change them into the same kind of piece first.
2 and 4 both divide into 8, so write 1/2 and 3/4 as eighths.
A similar one: 1/2 + 1/4 + 3/8. In eighths that is 4/8 + 2/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, which is 1 1/8.

stepByStep.text: Change the first two fractions to eighths.
Add the three fractions.
15/8 is 8/8 and 7/8 more, so Anu drank 1 7/8 litres.

misconceptions.A: This adds the tops (1 + 3 + 5) and the bottoms (2 + 4 + 8). Only the tops are added, and only after the bottoms are made the same.
misconceptions.B: Here 1/2 was written as 2/8. Half of 8 eighths is 4 eighths, so 1/2 = 4/8.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 4/8 + 6/8 + 5/8 = 15/8, which is 1 7/8 litres.
misconceptions.D: The top 15 is right, but the bottom numbers were added as well. When eighths are added, the answer is still in eighths: 15/8.

G4A_FRACTIONS_014.questionText: Rahul's school day is 6 hours long. He spends 1 hour 30 minutes of it in maths lessons. What fraction of the school day is spent on maths?
hints: To write one time as a fraction of another, both must be in the same unit.
Change 6 hours into minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes into minutes. Then put the maths time over the whole school day.
A similar one: what fraction of 3 hours is 36 minutes? 3 hours = 180 minutes, so the fraction is 36/180, and that simplifies to 1/5.

stepByStep.text: Change both times into minutes.
Write the maths time over the school day.
Divide the top and bottom by 90.
1/4 of the school day is spent on maths.

misconceptions.A: This uses only the 1 hour and leaves out the 30 minutes. The maths time is 90 minutes in all.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 90 minutes out of 360 minutes is 1/4 of the school day.
misconceptions.C: This reads 1 hour 30 minutes as 1.30 hours. Thirty minutes is half an hour, so work in minutes: 90 out of 360.
misconceptions.D: 1/3 of 6 hours would be 2 hours. Maths takes 1 hour 30 minutes, which is 90 minutes out of 360.

G4A_FRACTIONS_015.questionText: Which of these fractions lies between 1/3 and 1/2?
hints: To see whether a fraction lies between two others, write them all with the same bottom number.
In twelfths, 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/2 = 6/12. Look for a fraction that is more than 4/12 but less than 6/12.
A similar one: which lies between 1/4 and 1/2, 3/8 or 5/8? In eighths, 1/4 = 2/8 and 1/2 = 4/8. 3/8 sits between 2/8 and 4/8, so there it is 3/8.

stepByStep.text: Write 1/3 and 1/2 in twelfths.
5/12 is more than 4/12 and less than 6/12.
The fraction that lies between 1/3 and 1/2 is 5/12.

misconceptions.A: Right! 1/3 is 4/12 and 1/2 is 6/12, and 5/12 sits exactly between them.
misconceptions.B: 1/4 is 3/12, which is less than 1/3 (4/12). A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.
misconceptions.C: 7/12 is more than 6/12, so it is bigger than 1/2. Look for a fraction just under one half.
misconceptions.D: 3/10 is very close, but 3/10 = 9/30 and 1/3 = 10/30, so 3/10 is just below 1/3.

G4A_FRACTIONS_016.questionText: A tailor uses 2 3/4 m of cloth for a kurta and 1 5/6 m of cloth for a shirt. How much cloth does he use altogether?
hints: This is addition of mixed numbers. Add the whole numbers, add the fraction parts, and watch for fraction parts that make more than one whole.
Write 3/4 and 5/6 in twelfths and add them. Is the total more than 12/12?
A similar one: 1 2/3 + 2 1/2. In sixths, 4/6 + 3/6 = 7/6 = 1 1/6. The wholes are 1 + 2 = 3. So the total is 3 + 1 1/6 = 4 1/6.

stepByStep.text: Add the whole numbers.
Add the fraction parts in twelfths.
19/12 is one whole and 7/12.
3 + 1 7/12 = 4 7/12, so he uses 4 7/12 m of cloth.

misconceptions.A: The fraction parts add up to 19/12, which is 1 7/12. That extra whole must be added to the 3 wholes.
misconceptions.B: This adds the tops (3 + 5) and the bottoms (4 + 6). Change 3/4 and 5/6 to twelfths before adding.
misconceptions.C: Here 3/4 was written as 3/12. When 4 becomes 12 the top must be multiplied by 3 too, so 3/4 = 9/12.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The fraction parts make 19/12 = 1 7/12, and with the 3 wholes that is 4 7/12 m.

G4A_FRACTIONS_017.questionText: 3 pizzas are shared equally among 4 children. Each child eats only half of his or her share. What fraction of a pizza does each child eat?
hints: There are two steps: first find each child's share, then find half of that share.
3 pizzas shared equally among 4 children gives each child 3/4 of a pizza. Now think about half of 3/4.
A similar one: 2 cakes shared equally among 5 children gives each child 2/5 of a cake. Half of 2 fifths is 1 fifth, so each child would eat 1/5.

stepByStep.text: 3 pizzas shared among 4 children gives each child 3/4 of a pizza.
Cut each quarter into two eighths, so 3/4 is the same as 6/8.
Half of 6 eighths is 3 eighths, so each child eats 3/8 of a pizza.

misconceptions.A: 3/4 is each child's full share. Each child eats only half of that share.
misconceptions.B: This takes 1/2 away from 3/4. Half of a share means splitting the share into two equal parts, not subtracting one half.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Each share is 3/4, and half of 3/4 is 3/8 of a pizza.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the share. Eating half of the share gives a smaller amount than 3/4, not a bigger one.

G4A_FRACTIONS_018.questionText: Which of these fractions is closest to 1/2? 3/8, 5/9, 2/3, 4/11
hints: Closest to 1/2 means the smallest gap from 1/2. Half of the bottom number tells you what the top would be for exactly one half.
For 3/8, exactly half would be 4/8, so 3/8 is 1/8 away. Find the gap for each of the other three in the same way.
A similar one: is 4/7 or 3/5 closer to 1/2? 4/7 − 1/2 = 1/14 and 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10. 1/14 is the smaller gap, so 4/7 is closer.

stepByStep.text: Find how far 3/8 is from 1/2.
Find how far 5/9 is from 1/2.
In the same way, 2/3 is 1/6 away and 4/11 is 3/22 away.
Compare the gaps 1/8, 1/18, 1/6 and 3/22. The smallest is 1/18, because 3/22 is even more than 3/24, which is 1/8.
The fraction closest to 1/2 is 5/9.

misconceptions.A: 3/8 is 1/8 away from 1/2. That is close, but 5/9 is only 1/18 away.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 5/9 is just 1/18 more than 1/2, the smallest gap of the four.
misconceptions.C: 2/3 is 1/6 away from 1/2, the biggest gap of the four. Work out each gap by subtracting.
misconceptions.D: 4/11 is 3/22 below 1/2, which is a little more than 1/8. Look for a fraction with a smaller gap.

G4A_FRACTIONS_019.questionText: A cricket match has 50 overs. 35 overs have been bowled. What fraction of the overs is still to be bowled, in lowest terms?
hints: Read carefully which part the question asks about: the overs already bowled, or the overs still to come.
First subtract to find how many overs are still to be bowled. Put that number over 50.
A similar one: 40 overs with 24 bowled. 16 are left, so the fraction is 16/40. Dividing the top and bottom by 8 gives 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Find the overs still to be bowled.
Write this as a fraction of all 50 overs.
Divide the top and bottom by 5.
3/10 of the overs is still to be bowled.
