A similar one: 25 children in a square stand 5 to a side. Four sides of 5 make 20, but the 4 corner children were counted twice, so 20 − 4 = 16 children are on the edge.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of children on each side.
Four sides of 12 would count each corner child twice.
Take away the 4 corners that were counted twice.
44 children hold a flag.

misconceptions.A: 48 is 4 × 12. Each corner child stands on two sides and has been counted twice. Take away the 4 extra counts.
misconceptions.B: 40 is 4 × 10. That leaves out all four corner children. Count 12 on the top and bottom rows and 10 more on each side.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Four sides of 12 make 48, less the 4 corners counted twice, which leaves 44.
misconceptions.D: 12 is the number of children on one side. The flags are held all the way round the square.

G4A_SQUARES_040.questionText: A square floor is covered with 225 tiles, in equal rows and columns. The tiles along both diagonals (from each corner to the opposite corner) are red, and all the other tiles are white. How many red tiles are there?
hints: Find how many tiles are in each row. Then think about whether the two diagonals share a tile.
225 is 15 × 15. Each diagonal has 15 tiles. With an odd number like 15, the two diagonals cross on one tile in the middle.
A similar one: a floor of 7 rows of 7 tiles. Each diagonal has 7 tiles and they share the middle tile, so there are 7 + 7 − 1 = 13 red tiles.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of tiles in each row.
Each diagonal has 15 tiles.
Because 15 is odd, the diagonals cross on the middle tile, which was counted twice.
There are 29 red tiles.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Each diagonal has 15 tiles, and they share the one in the middle, so 15 + 15 − 1 = 29.
misconceptions.B: 30 is 15 + 15. The two diagonals cross on the middle tile, so that tile has been counted twice.
misconceptions.C: 15 is the number of tiles on one diagonal. There are two diagonals to count.
misconceptions.D: 60 is 4 × 15, which is like counting around the sides. The diagonals run from corner to corner through the middle, 15 tiles each.

G4A_SQUARES_041.questionText: Some numbers can be made by adding two perfect squares. For example, 13 = 4 + 9. Which of these numbers can NOT be made by adding two perfect squares?
hints: For each number, try taking away each perfect square that is smaller than it. See whether what is left is also a perfect square.
The perfect squares to use are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. For 20, try 20 − 16 = 4. Is 4 a perfect square? Test the other numbers in the same way.
A similar one: can 11 be made? 11 − 1 = 10, 11 − 4 = 7 and 11 − 9 = 2, and none of 10, 7 and 2 is a perfect square. So 11 cannot be made, but 10 can, because 1 + 9 = 10.

stepByStep.text: The perfect squares to use are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25.
Three of the numbers can be made.
For 21, take away each square: 20, 17, 12 and 5 are left. None of these is a perfect square.
The number that cannot be made is 21.

misconceptions.A: 20 can be made: 4 + 16 = 20. Test each of the other numbers by taking away 1, 4, 9, 16 or 25.
misconceptions.B: 34 can be made: 9 + 25 = 34. Test each of the other numbers by taking away 1, 4, 9, 16 or 25.
misconceptions.C: 29 can be made: 4 + 25 = 29. Test each of the other numbers by taking away 1, 4, 9, 16 or 25.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Taking 1, 4, 9 or 16 away from 21 leaves 20, 17, 12 or 5, and none of these is a perfect square.

G4A_SQUARES_042.questionText: Soldiers stand in a square formation, with the same number in every row and every column. Then 3 full rows and 3 full columns of soldiers march away, and the soldiers who remain still form a square. In all, 69 soldiers marched away. How many soldiers were there at first?
hints: The soldiers who leave are the difference between a big square and a smaller square. Test square numbers.
If each side had 10 soldiers, the square left would have sides of 7, and 100 − 49 = 51 would leave. That is too few, so try bigger squares.
A similar one: 2 rows and 2 columns leave, 36 soldiers in all. Try sides of 10 and 8: 100 − 64 = 36. So there were 100 soldiers at first.

stepByStep.text: The square at first has some number on each side, and the square left has 3 fewer on each side.
Test sides of 12 and 9.
Test sides of 13 and 10.
This matches the 69 soldiers who marched away.
There were 169 soldiers at first.

misconceptions.A: 529 is 23 × 23, from 69 ÷ 3 = 23. But the rows and columns that leave share some soldiers, so 69 is not simply 3 rows. Test it: 529 − 400 = 129, not 69.
misconceptions.B: With 144 soldiers the sides are 12, and the square left has sides of 9. Then 144 − 81 = 63 soldiers leave, not 69. Try the next square.
misconceptions.C: Yes! A square of 13 by 13 has 169 soldiers, the square left is 10 by 10, and 169 − 100 = 69.
misconceptions.D: With 196 soldiers the sides are 14, and the square left has sides of 11. Then 196 − 121 = 75 soldiers leave, not 69. Try a smaller square.

G4A_SQUARES_043.questionText: In each of these, the two numbers add up to 60. Which product is the greatest?
hints: Compare each product with the one where the two numbers are equal. Try the same idea with small numbers first.
Try numbers that add up to 10: 5 × 5 = 25, 4 × 6 = 24, 3 × 7 = 21. What happens to the product as the two numbers move further apart?
A similar one with numbers that add up to 20: 10 × 10 = 100, 9 × 11 = 99, 8 × 12 = 96 and 7 × 13 = 91. The equal pair gives the greatest product, and each step apart makes it smaller.

stepByStep.text: All four pairs add up to 60, so compare how far apart the two numbers are.
With small numbers that add up to 10, the products get smaller as the numbers move apart.
The same happens here.
The greatest product is 30 × 30.

misconceptions.A: 29 × 31 = 899, which is 1 less than the greatest. When two numbers have the same sum, the product is greatest when they are equal.
misconceptions.B: Yes! When the sum stays at 60, the equal pair gives the greatest product: 30 × 30 = 900.
misconceptions.C: 28 × 32 = 896. Moving the two numbers further apart makes the product smaller. Look for the pair that is closest together.
misconceptions.D: 33 is the biggest number here, but its partner 27 is the smallest. 27 × 33 = 891, the least of the four. Look for the pair that is closest together.

G4A_SQUARES_044.questionText: Look at the pattern: 11 × 11 = 121, 111 × 111 = 12321, 1111 × 1111 = 1234321. What is the sum of the digits of 11111 × 11111?
hints: Look at how the digits in each answer climb up and come back down. Predict the next answer before adding its digits.
The answers climb to 2, then 3, then 4, and come back down to 1. Write the answer that climbs to 5, then add all its digits.
A similar one: 1111 × 1111 = 1234321. Its digits add up to 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 16, which is 4 × 4.

stepByStep.text: The answers climb by one digit each time and come back down: 121, 12321, 1234321.
So the next answer climbs to 5 and comes back down.
Add the digits going up, then the digits going down.
Add the two parts.
The sum of the digits is 25.

misconceptions.A: 15 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5, the digits on the way up. The number also comes back down through 4, 3, 2 and 1, so add those too.
misconceptions.B: 9 is how many digits the answer has. The question asks for the sum of those digits.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The answer is 123454321 and its digits add up to 25, which is 5 × 5.
misconceptions.D: 45 is the sum of all the digits from 1 to 9. This number climbs only as far as 5 before coming back down.

G4A_SQUARES_045.questionText: Kabir's age this year is a perfect square. Nine years from now, his age will be a perfect square again. How old is Kabir this year?
hints: Write out the perfect squares in order and look at the gaps between neighbours.
The squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49. Test each one as Kabir's age: add 9 and see whether you land on another square.
A similar one with a gap of 5: 1 + 5 = 6 is not a square, but 4 + 5 = 9 is. So the age would be 4.

stepByStep.text: List the perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49.
Add 9 to each and look for another square: 10, 13, 18, 25, 34, 45, 58.
Only 25 is a perfect square, and it comes from 16.
After 16 the gaps between squares are more than 9, so there is no other answer.
Kabir is 16 years old this year.

misconceptions.A: 9 is a perfect square, but 9 + 9 = 18 is not. Test the other squares in the same way.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 16 is 4 × 4, and nine years later Kabir is 25, which is 5 × 5.
misconceptions.C: 25 is a perfect square, but 25 + 9 = 34 is not. It is the age Kabir will reach, not his age this year.
misconceptions.D: 36 is a perfect square, but 36 + 9 = 45 is not. Test the smaller squares.

G4A_SQUARES_046.questionText: By which smallest number must 12 be multiplied so that the answer is a perfect square greater than 100?
hints: First find the smallest multiplier that gives any perfect square. Then check the extra condition, and look for the next multiplier if you need to.
12 is 2 × 2 × 3. Multiplying by 3 gives 36, a perfect square, but 36 is not greater than 100. To keep a perfect square, multiply 36 by another perfect square.

A similar one: the smallest multiplier of 8 that gives a square greater than 50. Multiplying 8 by 2 gives the square of 4, which is too small. Multiply that by 4 and you have 8 × 8 = 64, which is greater than 50. So the multiplier is 8.

stepByStep.text: 12 is 2 × 2 × 3, so it needs one more 3 to become a perfect square.
36 is not greater than 100. To stay a perfect square, multiply 36 by the next perfect square, 4.
Find the multiplier of 12 that gives 144.
The smallest number to multiply by is 12.

misconceptions.A: 12 × 3 = 36 is a perfect square, but it is not greater than 100. Look for the next multiplier that gives a perfect square.
misconceptions.B: 12 × 9 = 108 is greater than 100, but 108 is not a perfect square. It lies between 100 and 121.
misconceptions.C: 12 × 27 = 324 is a perfect square greater than 100, but a smaller multiplier also works. Try the ones between 3 and 27.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 12 × 12 = 144, which is a perfect square greater than 100, and no smaller multiplier does this.

G4A_SQUARES_047.questionText: Anu picks any odd number greater than 1, squares it and then subtracts 1. What is the greatest number that will always divide her answer exactly, whatever odd number she picks?
hints: Try several odd numbers, not just one. Look for what all the answers have in common.
With 3 the answer is 9 − 1 = 8. With 5 it is 25 − 1 = 24. Try 7 and 9 too, then look for the greatest number that divides every answer.
A similar one: pick any even number, square it, and ask what always divides the answer. From 2, 4 and 6 you get 4, 16 and 36. The greatest number dividing all of these is 4.

stepByStep.text: Try the first few odd numbers.
Look for numbers that divide 8, 24, 48 and 80 exactly. The divisor cannot be more than 8, because the first answer is 8.
8 divides all four.
The greatest number that always divides her answer is 8.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The answers 8, 24, 48 and 80 are all multiples of 8, and since 8 itself is one of the answers, nothing bigger can divide them all.
misconceptions.B: 4 does divide every answer, but a greater number does too. Look at 8, 24, 48 and 80 again.
misconceptions.C: 24 divides the answer for 5, which is 24, but not the answer for 3, which is 8. The number must work for every odd number.
misconceptions.D: 16 divides the answer for 7, which is 48, but not the answer for 3, which is 8. The number must work for every odd number.

G4A_SQUARES_048.questionText: The year 2025 is a perfect square, because 45 × 45 = 2025. How many years after 2025 is the next year that is a perfect square?
hints: The next perfect square comes from the next whole number. You do not need to multiply it out if you know how far apart neighbouring squares are.
The next square is 46 × 46. The gap between the squares of two neighbouring numbers is the sum of those two numbers. Which two numbers do you add here?
A similar one: 20 × 20 = 400. The next square is 21 × 21, and the gap is 20 + 21 = 41, so the next square is 441.

stepByStep.text: The next perfect square after 45 × 45 is 46 × 46.
Neighbouring squares differ by the sum of the two numbers.
Check by multiplying.
The next perfect-square year is 91 years after 2025.

misconceptions.A: 90 is 2 × 45. The gap between 45 × 45 and 46 × 46 is 45 + 46, which is one more than that.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The next square is 46 × 46 = 2116, and 2116 − 2025 = 91.
misconceptions.C: 46 is the number you square next. The question asks how many years lie between 2025 and 46 × 46.
misconceptions.D: 100 years later is 2125, which is not a perfect square: 46 × 46 = 2116. Find the gap from 2025 to 2116.

G4A_TIME_001.questionText: A train leaves Pune station at 17:20 on the 24-hour clock. What is this time on the 12-hour clock?
hints: On the 24-hour clock, hours bigger than 12 are afternoon or evening times.
Take 12 away from the hours: 17 - 12. The minutes stay the same.
Example: 14:35 on the 24-hour clock. 14 - 12 = 2, so it is 2:35 pm.

stepByStep.text: 17 is more than 12, so the time is after noon and is a pm time.
Take 12 away from the hours.
The minutes stay as 20, so the time is 5:20 pm.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 17 - 12 = 5, so 17:20 is 5:20 pm.
misconceptions.B: This takes 10 away from 17. Noon is 12 o'clock, so take away 12.
misconceptions.C: The hour 5 is right, but 17:20 comes after noon, so it is pm.
misconceptions.D: This takes 13 away from 17. Noon is 12 o'clock, so take away 12.

G4A_TIME_002.questionText: How many days are there altogether in the months of June and July?
hints: You need to remember how many days each month has. The knuckle trick or the rhyme 'Thirty days has September' can help.
June has 30 days. How many days does July have?
Example: December has 31 days and January has 31 days. Together they have 31 + 31 = 62 days.

stepByStep.text: June has 30 days.
July has 31 days.
Add them.
June and July have 61 days altogether.

misconceptions.A: This takes both months as 30 days. July has 31 days.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 30 + 31 = 61.
misconceptions.C: This takes both months as 31 days. June has only 30 days.
misconceptions.D: This is too few. June has 30 days and July has 31 days.

G4A_TIME_003.questionText: How many days are there in February 2028?
hints: February is the only month whose length changes. It depends on whether the year is a leap year.
A year like this is a leap year if 4 divides it exactly. Try dividing 2028 by 4.
Example: For February 2023, divide 2023 by 4. It leaves a remainder of 3, so 2023 is not a leap year and its February has 28 days.

stepByStep.text: Check whether 4 divides 2028 exactly.
There is no remainder, so 2028 is a leap year.
In a leap year February has one extra day, so February 2028 has 29 days.

misconceptions.A: February has 28 days in an ordinary year. Check whether 2028 is a leap year by dividing it by 4.
misconceptions.B: February never has 30 days. It has 28 days, or one more in a leap year.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 2028 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
misconceptions.D: February never has 31 days. It has 28 days, or one more in a leap year.

G4A_TIME_004.questionText: A film is 135 minutes long. How long is that in hours and minutes?
hints: One hour is 60 minutes. See how many full hours fit into the minutes, and what is left.
Two hours are 120 minutes. Is 135 more than 120? How much more?
Example: 80 minutes. One hour is 60 minutes, and 80 - 60 = 20, so 80 minutes is 1 hour 20 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Two full hours fit into 135 minutes.
Find the minutes left over.
135 minutes is 2 hours 15 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This reads 135 as 1 hour and 35 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
misconceptions.B: The 2 hours are right, but 2 hours use up 120 minutes, leaving 15 minutes.
misconceptions.C: 3 hours would be 180 minutes, which is more than 135. Only 2 full hours fit.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 120 minutes make 2 hours, and 15 minutes are left.

G4A_TIME_005.questionText: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 10 days from today?
hints: The days of the week repeat every 7 days. Take out the full weeks first.
7 days from Wednesday is Wednesday again. How many days are left out of 10 after taking away 7?
Example: Today is Monday. 9 days later: 7 days bring Monday again, and 2 more days give Wednesday.

stepByStep.text: After 7 days it is Wednesday again.
Days still to count.
Three days after Wednesday: Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
It will be Saturday.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 7 days bring Wednesday again, and 3 more days bring Saturday.
misconceptions.B: This counts Wednesday itself as the first day. Start counting from tomorrow, Thursday.
misconceptions.C: This counts one day too many. After the full week, only 3 more days are needed.
misconceptions.D: Wednesday comes again after 7 days. There are 3 more days to count after that.

G4A_TIME_006.questionText: Arjun's school starts at 8:00 am and ends at 1:30 pm. How long is his school day?
hints: The time passes 12 noon, so count in two parts: up to noon, and after noon.
Find how long it is from 8:00 am to 12 noon.
Example: From 9:00 am to 2:15 pm. From 9:00 am to noon is 3 hours, and from noon to 2:15 pm is 2 hours 15 minutes, so 5 hours 15 minutes in all.

stepByStep.text: From 8:00 am to 12 noon.
From 12 noon to 1:30 pm is 1 hour 30 minutes.
4 hours and 1 hour 30 minutes make 5 hours 30 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 1 from 8. The clock passes 12 noon, so count up to noon and then on to 1:30 pm.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 4 hours before noon and 1 hour 30 minutes after noon make 5 hours 30 minutes.
misconceptions.C: This counts one hour too many. From 8:00 am to noon is 4 hours, then add 1 hour 30 minutes.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out an hour. From 8:00 am to noon is 4 hours, then add 1 hour 30 minutes.

G4A_TIME_007.questionText: Dadi's favourite TV serial starts at a quarter to 7 in the evening. What is this time on the 24-hour clock?
hints: First write the time with hours and minutes, then change it to the 24-hour clock.
A quarter to 7 means 15 minutes before 7 o'clock. Which hour is it still in, and how many minutes past?
Example: A quarter to 4 in the afternoon is 3:45 pm. Adding 12 to the hours gives 15:45.

stepByStep.text: A quarter to 7 is 15 minutes before 7 o'clock, which is 6:45.
It is evening, so the time is 6:45 pm.
For a pm time, add 12 to the hours.
On the 24-hour clock the time is 18:45.

misconceptions.A: This is a quarter past 7 in the evening. A quarter to 7 is 15 minutes before 7 o'clock.
misconceptions.B: 6:45 is right, but this is the morning time. For the evening, add 12 to the hours.
misconceptions.C: Well done! A quarter to 7 in the evening is 6:45 pm, which is 18:45.
misconceptions.D: This puts 45 minutes after 7 o'clock. A quarter to 7 is before 7, in the hour of 6.

G4A_TIME_008.questionText: A train journey from Kanyakumari to Jammu takes exactly 3 days. How many hours is that?
hints: Think about how many hours make one full day, counting day and night together.
One day has 24 hours. Find 3 lots of 24.
Example: 2 days are 2 x 24 = 48 hours.

stepByStep.text: One full day has 24 hours.
Multiply by 3 days.
The journey takes 72 hours.

misconceptions.A: This uses 12 hours for a day. A full day, with its night, has 24 hours.
misconceptions.B: This multiplies by 60. There are 60 minutes in an hour, but 24 hours in a day.
misconceptions.C: This adds 3 and 24. Three days are 3 lots of 24 hours, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: That is right! 3 x 24 = 72 hours.

G4A_TIME_009.questionText: A night bus leaves Bengaluru at 9:30 pm. The journey to Chennai takes 6 hours 45 minutes. At what time does the bus reach Chennai?
hints: The journey crosses midnight, so the answer will be an am time on the next day. Add the hours and the minutes in parts.
Add the 6 hours first. Going 6 hours on from 9:30 pm passes midnight: where do you land?
Example: Leave at 10:40 pm and travel 3 hours 30 minutes. Three hours later it is 1:40 am, and 30 more minutes make 2:10 am.

stepByStep.text: Add 6 hours to 9:30 pm: it becomes 3:30 am the next day.
Now add 45 minutes. 30 minutes take the time to 4:00 am.
The remaining minutes.
The bus reaches Chennai at 4:15 am.

misconceptions.A: The 75 minutes from 30 + 45 make 1 hour and 15 minutes. Carry that extra hour to the hours.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 6 hours later is 3:30 am, and 45 minutes more is 4:15 am.
misconceptions.C: The numbers are right, but the bus travels through the night, so it arrives in the early morning, am.
misconceptions.D: This goes back 6 hours 45 minutes. The journey time must be added to the starting time.

G4A_TIME_010.questionText: A train leaves Mumbai at 22:40 and reaches Goa at 05:10 the next morning. How long is the journey?
hints: The journey crosses midnight. Split it into the part before midnight and the part after midnight.
Find how long it is from 22:40 to midnight, which is 24:00.
Example: From 23:15 to 02:30 the next day. Up to midnight is 45 minutes, and after midnight is 2 hours 30 minutes, so 3 hours 15 minutes in all.

stepByStep.text: From 22:40 to midnight is 1 hour 20 minutes.
From midnight to 05:10 is 5 hours 10 minutes.
Add: 1 hour 20 minutes and 5 hours 10 minutes make 6 hours 30 minutes.
The journey takes 6 hours 30 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 05:10 from 22:40. The train arrives the next day, so count on through midnight.
misconceptions.B: This is one hour too long. From 22:40 to midnight is only 1 hour 20 minutes.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 1 hour 20 minutes before midnight and 5 hours 10 minutes after make 6 hours 30 minutes.
misconceptions.D: This adds 40 minutes and 10 minutes. Before midnight there are only 20 minutes left in the hour after 22:40.

G4A_TIME_011.questionText: In a certain month, the 5th is a Tuesday. What day of the week is the 23rd of the same month?
hints: The same day of the week comes again every 7 days. Jump forward in sevens from the date you know.
Add 7 to the 5th again and again to find other Tuesdays: 5, 12, and so on.
Example: The 3rd is a Monday. The 10th and 17th are also Mondays, so the 20th, three days later, is a Thursday.

stepByStep.text: The Tuesdays are 7 days apart.
So the 19th is a Tuesday.
Days from the 19th to the 23rd.
Four days after Tuesday: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
The 23rd is a Saturday.

misconceptions.A: This stops one day early. From Tuesday the 19th, count 4 days on to reach the 23rd.
misconceptions.B: This goes one day too far. From Tuesday the 19th, count 4 days on to reach the 23rd.
misconceptions.C: This counts only 2 days on from the 19th. The 23rd is 4 days after the 19th.
misconceptions.D: That is right! The 19th is a Tuesday, and 4 days later is Saturday.

G4A_TIME_012.questionText: How many days after 20 February 2024 is 5 March 2024?
hints: Count the days left in February, then the days in March. Check how long February is in that year.
2024 can be divided exactly by 4, so it is a leap year. How many days does its February have?
Example: From 25 February 2023 to 4 March 2023. February 2023 has 28 days, so 3 days are left in February, and 4 more in March make 7 days.

stepByStep.text: 2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
Days left in February after the 20th.
Add the 5 days of March.
5 March 2024 is 14 days after 20 February 2024.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 9 days are left in February 2024, and 5 days of March make 14.
misconceptions.B: This takes February as 28 days. 2024 is a leap year, so its February has 29 days.
misconceptions.C: This takes February as 30 days. In the leap year 2024, February has 29 days.
misconceptions.D: This takes February as 31 days. In the leap year 2024, February has 29 days.

G4A_TIME_013.questionText: Anil practises the tabla for 40 minutes every day. For how long does he practise in one week?
hints: Find the total minutes for the week, then change the minutes into hours and minutes.
A week has 7 days. Find 7 lots of 40 minutes.
Example: 50 minutes a day for 3 days is 150 minutes. Two hours are 120 minutes, so that is 2 hours 30 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Minutes in one week.
Four hours are 240 minutes.
Minutes left over.
He practises for 4 hours 40 minutes in one week.

misconceptions.A: This counts only 5 days. Anil practises every day, and a week has 7 days.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 280 minutes is 4 hours 40 minutes.
misconceptions.C: This reads 280 as 2 hours and 80 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes, so 280 minutes hold 4 full hours.
misconceptions.D: The 4 hours are right. Check the minutes left: 280 - 240.

G4A_TIME_014.questionText: A month has 30 days, and its 1st day is a Saturday. How many Sundays are there in this month?
hints: Find the date of the first Sunday, then keep jumping forward 7 days until the month ends.
If the 1st is a Saturday, the first Sunday is the very next day, the 2nd.
Example: A month of 30 days begins on a Monday. Its first Sunday is the 7th, and the others are the 14th, 21st and 28th, so that month has 4 Sundays.

stepByStep.text: The 1st is a Saturday, so the 2nd is the first Sunday.
Add 7 each time: the Sundays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th.
The 30th is still inside the month.
There are 5 Sundays in this month.

misconceptions.A: 30 days hold 4 full weeks and 2 extra days. The extra days here are a Saturday and a Sunday, so there is one more Sunday.
misconceptions.B: A sixth Sunday would be on the 37th, and the month has only 30 days.
misconceptions.C: Great counting! The Sundays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th.
misconceptions.D: Keep adding 7 until the month ends: 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 are all Sundays.

G4A_TIME_015.questionText: Kavya's train leaves at 14:10. She wants to reach the station 25 minutes before the train leaves, and it takes her 35 minutes to travel from home to the station. What is the latest time she can leave home?
hints: Work backwards from the train time. Both the early arrival and the travel time come before the train leaves.
Add the two amounts of time she needs before 14:10: 25 minutes and 35 minutes.
Example: A bus leaves at 16:30. Rahul wants to be 10 minutes early and needs 20 minutes to get there. He needs 30 minutes in all, so he leaves at 16:00, which is 4:00 pm.

stepByStep.text: Total time needed before the train leaves.
60 minutes is 1 hour.
One hour before 14:10 is 13:10.
Change to the 12-hour clock.
The latest she can leave home is 1:10 pm.

misconceptions.A: This is the time she wants to reach the station. She must leave home 35 minutes before that.
misconceptions.B: This takes away only the 35 minutes of travel. She also wants to be 25 minutes early.
misconceptions.C: This goes forward from the train time. She has to leave home before the train, so count backwards.
misconceptions.D: Well done! She needs 60 minutes in all, and one hour before 14:10 is 1:10 pm.

G4A_TRIANGLES_001.questionText: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. What kind of triangle is it?

options.text: These sides cannot make a triangle

hints: Triangles are named by how many of their sides are equal. Compare the three lengths.
Two of the lengths are 5 cm and the third is 8 cm. How many sides are equal?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 7 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm has three different lengths, so it is a scalene triangle.

stepByStep.text: The two shorter sides together are 10 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so the sides do make a triangle.
Exactly two sides are equal: 5 cm and 5 cm.
A triangle with exactly two equal sides is an isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Here the third side is 8 cm, not 5 cm.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Two sides are 5 cm and the third is different, so it is isosceles.
misconceptions.C: A scalene triangle has three different sides. Here two of the sides are the same.
misconceptions.D: The two shorter sides add up to 10 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so they do close up into a triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_002.questionText: The angles of a triangle are 35°, 55° and 90°. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: Triangles can be named by their biggest angle. Is it less than 90°, exactly 90°, or more than 90°?
The biggest of the three angles is 90°. What is an angle of 90° called?
A similar one: a triangle with angles 30°, 40° and 110° has one angle bigger than 90°, so it is an obtuse-angled triangle.

stepByStep.text: The biggest angle is 90°.
An angle of 90° is a right angle.
A triangle with one right angle is a right-angled triangle.

misconceptions.A: In an acute-angled triangle all three angles are less than 90°. Here one angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.B: An obtuse-angled triangle has one angle more than 90°. Here the biggest angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! One angle is 90°, a right angle.
misconceptions.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60° each. These three angles are all different.

G4A_TRIANGLES_003.questionText: All three sides of a triangle have different lengths. By its sides, what is the triangle called?
hints: There are three names for triangles by their sides: one for three equal sides, one for two equal sides, and one for no equal sides.
This triangle has no two sides the same. Which of the three names is for that?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm has all sides equal, so it is called an equilateral triangle.

stepByStep.text: Three equal sides make an equilateral triangle, and two equal sides make an isosceles triangle.
This triangle has no equal sides at all.
A triangle with three different sides is a scalene triangle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Scalene means no two sides are equal.
misconceptions.B: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. Here all three are different.
misconceptions.C: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides. Here all three are different.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled is a name that comes from the angles. The question asks for the name that comes from the sides.

G4A_TRIANGLES_004.questionText: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of 9 cm each. Its third side is 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
hints: The perimeter is the distance all the way around, so add all three sides.
The three sides are 9 cm, 9 cm and 6 cm. Add them.
A similar one: equal sides of 5 cm each and a third side of 4 cm give a perimeter of 5 + 5 + 4 = 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: The three sides are 9 cm, 9 cm and 6 cm.
Add them.
The perimeter is 24 cm.

misconceptions.A: 15 cm adds 9 and 6 only. There are two sides of 9 cm.
misconceptions.B: 21 cm uses one side of 9 cm and two of 6 cm. It is the 9 cm side that comes twice.
misconceptions.C: 54 comes from multiplying 9 by 6. For perimeter, add the three sides.

G4A_TRIANGLES_005.questionText: A triangle has angles 100°, 40° and 40°. Which name describes it best?
hints: The name has two parts. One part comes from the biggest angle. The other part comes from how many angles, and so how many sides, are equal.
The biggest angle is 100°. Is that less than, equal to, or more than 90°? Then look at the two angles of 40°.
A similar one: a triangle with angles 90°, 45° and 45° has a right angle and two equal angles, so it is a right-angled isosceles triangle.

stepByStep.text: The biggest angle is 100°, which is more than 90°, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
Two angles are equal, both 40°. The sides opposite equal angles are equal, so two sides are equal.
It is an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: Acute-angled means every angle is less than 90°. Here one angle is 100°.
misconceptions.B: Scalene means no sides are equal. Two equal angles give two equal sides.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 100° makes it obtuse-angled, and the two angles of 40° make it isosceles.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled needs an angle of exactly 90°. The biggest angle here is 100°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_006.questionText: Which of these sets of lengths cannot be the sides of a triangle?
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one.
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the total with the longest length. Watch for a total that is only equal, not greater.
A similar one: 2 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm cannot make a triangle, because 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 7 and the short sides cannot meet.

stepByStep.text: 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 5, and 6 + 6 = 12 is more than 11. These two sets make triangles.
7 + 8 = 15 is more than 14, so this set makes a triangle too.
4 + 5 = 9 is only equal to the longest side, 9. The two short sides would lie flat along the long side.
The set that cannot make a triangle is 4 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 5, so these lengths do make a triangle.
misconceptions.B: 6 + 6 = 12 is more than 11, so these lengths do make a triangle, a rather flat one.
misconceptions.C: 7 + 8 = 15 is more than 14, so these lengths do make a triangle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 4 + 5 is exactly 9, so the two short sides cannot rise above the long side to form a triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_007.questionText: In a right-angled triangle, one of the two acute angles is twice the other. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. In a right-angled triangle one angle is 90°, so think about what is left for the other two.
The two acute angles together make 90°. One is twice the other, so think of them as 1 part and 2 parts.
A similar one: in a right-angled triangle one acute angle is 4 times the other. Five equal parts make 90°, so one part is 18°. The angles are 18° and 72°, and the smallest is 18°.

stepByStep.text: The two acute angles together.
One angle is 1 part and the other is 2 parts, so 3 parts make 90°.
The acute angles are 30° and 60°.
The smallest angle is 30°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°, and 60° is twice 30°.
misconceptions.B: 60° is the bigger of the two acute angles. The question asks for the smallest angle.
misconceptions.C: 45° would make the two acute angles equal. One of them must be twice the other.
misconceptions.D: 15° comes from sharing 90° into too many parts. One part and two parts make 3 parts in all.

G4A_TRIANGLES_008.questionText: The perimeter of an isosceles triangle is 40 cm. The side that is different from the other two is 12 cm. How long is each of the equal sides?
hints: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides. Take away the side you know, and what is left belongs to the two equal sides.
Take 12 cm away from 40 cm. The rest is shared equally between the two equal sides.
A similar one: perimeter 26 cm and a different side of 6 cm. The two equal sides share 26 − 6 = 20 cm, so each is 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: Take the different side away from the perimeter.
The two equal sides share this equally.
Each equal side is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: 28 cm is the two equal sides together. Share it between the two sides.
misconceptions.C: 20 cm is half the perimeter. Take away the 12 cm side before halving.
misconceptions.D: 16 cm comes from taking 12 away twice. The 12 cm side appears only once.

G4A_TRIANGLES_009.questionText: All three angles of a triangle are equal. What is the sum of any two of its angles?
hints: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°. If they are all equal, you can find one of them.
Share 180° equally among three angles to find each one. Then add two of them.
A similar one: a right-angled triangle has two equal angles. They share 180 − 90 = 90°, so each is 45°, and those two together make 90°.

stepByStep.text: The three equal angles add up to 180°, so find one angle.
Add two of the angles.
The sum of any two angles is 120°.

misconceptions.A: 60° is one angle. The question asks for two of them added together.
misconceptions.B: 180° is the sum of all three angles. Add only two of them.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Each angle is 60°, and 60° + 60° = 120°.
misconceptions.D: 90° would be right for the two equal angles of a right-angled triangle. Here each angle is 60°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_010.questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 7 cm and 10 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length the third side can have?
hints: In a triangle, any two sides together must be longer than the third side. Use this to find how long the third side is allowed to be.
Add the two sides you know. The third side must be shorter than this total, not equal to it.
A similar one: with sides 4 cm and 6 cm, the third side must be shorter than 4 + 6 = 10 cm. The greatest whole number is 9 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the two known sides.
The third side must be shorter than 17 cm. At exactly 17 cm the two sides would lie flat along it.
The greatest whole number less than 17 is 16.
The greatest length of the third side is 16 cm.

misconceptions.A: At 17 cm the other two sides would lie flat along the third side and no triangle would form. It must be a little shorter.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 7 + 10 = 17 is more than 16, so the triangle closes, and 16 is the greatest whole number that fits.
misconceptions.C: 18 cm is longer than the other two sides put together, so they could not reach each other.
misconceptions.D: 3 cm is the difference of the two sides. That is about the shortest end, and the question asks for the greatest length.

G4A_TRIANGLES_011.questionText: Jay has four sticks of lengths 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm. He picks three sticks at a time to make a triangle. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way of choosing three sticks from the four. Then test each choice: the two shorter sticks together must be longer than the longest one.
There are four ways to choose three sticks: leave out one stick each time. Begin with 3, 5 and 7, and compare 3 + 5 with 7.
A similar one: sticks of 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. Of the four choices, only 2, 3 and 4 works, because 2 + 3 = 5 is more than 4. So 1 triangle can be made.

stepByStep.text: Sticks 3, 5, 7: 3 + 5 = 8 is more than 7, so this makes a triangle.
Sticks 3, 5, 10: 3 + 5 = 8 is less than 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 3, 7, 10: 3 + 7 = 10 is only equal to 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 5, 7, 10: 5 + 7 = 12 is more than 10, so this makes a triangle.
He can make 2 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: 4 is the number of ways to choose three sticks, but not every choice closes into a triangle. Test each one.
misconceptions.B: 3 counts the sticks 3, 7 and 10 as a triangle. But 3 + 7 is exactly 10, so those sticks would lie flat.
misconceptions.C: There is more than one. Both 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10 pass the test.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Only 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10 make triangles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_012.questionText: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the two equal sides is 3 times each of the other two angles. How big is that angle?
hints: In an isosceles triangle the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Think of the angles as equal parts that add up to 180°.
Call each of the two equal angles 1 part. The angle between the equal sides is then 3 parts. How many parts are there altogether?
A similar one: if the top angle is twice each base angle, the angles are 2 parts, 1 part and 1 part. Four parts make 180°, so one part is 45° and the top angle is 90°.

stepByStep.text: The two equal angles are 1 part each, and the angle between the equal sides is 3 parts.
Five parts make 180°, so find one part.
The angle between the equal sides is 3 parts.
That angle is 108°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The angles are 108°, 36° and 36°, which add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: 36° is each of the two equal angles. The angle asked for is 3 times as big.
misconceptions.C: 135° comes from sharing 180° into 4 parts. There are 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 parts.
misconceptions.D: 60° is the angle when all three angles are equal. Here one angle is 3 times each of the others.

G4A_TRIANGLES_013.questionText: In a triangle, the second angle is 20° more than the first angle, and the third angle is 20° more than the second. What is the largest angle?
hints: The three angles add up to 180°. Describe the second and third angles by how much more they are than the first.
The second angle is the first plus 20°, and the third is the first plus 40°. So three times the first angle, plus 60°, makes 180°.
A similar one: the second angle is 10° more than the first and the third is 10° more than the second. Three times the first plus 30° is 180°, so the first is 50° and the largest is 70°.

stepByStep.text: The third angle is 20° + 20° = 40° more than the first.
Take the extra 20° and 40° away from 180°. What is left is three times the first angle.
Find the first angle.
The largest angle is the third one.
The largest angle is 80°.

misconceptions.A: 40° is the first, smallest angle. The largest is 40° more than that.
misconceptions.B: 60° is the second, middle angle. The third angle is 20° more.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The angles are 40°, 60° and 80°, which add up to 180°.
misconceptions.D: 100° would make the angles 60°, 80° and 100°, which add up to 240°. The three angles must total 180°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_014.questionText: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 50 cm. One of its sides is 12 cm long. Which of these can be the lengths of its other two sides?
hints: There are two things to check: two of the three sides must be equal, and the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
The 12 cm side could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the side that is different. Work out the sides in each case and test whether they can close into a triangle.
A similar one: an isosceles triangle with perimeter 20 cm and one side 4 cm. Sides 4, 4 and 12 cannot close, because 4 + 4 is less than 12. Sides 4, 8 and 8 can, so the other sides are 8 cm and 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: If 12 cm is one of the equal sides, the sides are 12, 12 and 26.
But 12 + 12 = 24 is less than 26, so those sides cannot close into a triangle.
If 12 cm is the different side, the equal sides share the rest.
Check: 12 + 19 is more than 19, so the triangle closes. The other two sides are 19 cm and 19 cm.

misconceptions.A: These add up to 50 cm with two equal sides, but 12 + 12 = 24 is less than 26, so the sides cannot meet.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 + 19 + 19 = 50, two sides are equal, and the triangle closes.
misconceptions.C: These add up to 50 cm, but 12, 14 and 24 are all different, so the triangle would not be isosceles.
misconceptions.D: These add up to 50 cm, but 12, 18 and 20 are all different, so the triangle would not be isosceles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_015.questionText: Which of these statements about triangles is true?

options.text: A triangle can have two obtuse angles
An equilateral triangle can be right-angled
A scalene triangle can have two equal angles
A right-angled triangle can be isosceles

hints: Test each statement with two facts: the three angles of a triangle add up to 180°, and equal sides sit opposite equal angles.
For each statement, try to write down three angles that would fit it and still add up to 180°. If you cannot, the statement is not true.
A similar test: can a triangle have two right angles? 90° + 90° is already 180°, which leaves nothing for the third angle. So it cannot.

stepByStep.text: Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180°, so a triangle cannot have them.
An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°, so it never has a right angle.
Two equal angles give two equal sides, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides.
Angles of 90°, 45° and 45° add up to 180° and two of them are equal. So the true statement is: A right-angled triangle can be isosceles.

misconceptions.A: Each obtuse angle is more than 90°, so two of them are already more than 180°. A triangle has room for only one.
misconceptions.B: Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so none of them can be 90°.
misconceptions.C: Equal angles always sit opposite equal sides. A scalene triangle has no equal sides, so it has no equal angles.
misconceptions.D: Yes! A triangle with angles 90°, 45° and 45° is both right-angled and isosceles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_016.questionText: Meera has a thin straw 12 cm long. She cuts it into three pieces, each a whole number of centimetres long, and joins the pieces end to end to make a triangle. How many different triangles can she make? (Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one.)
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one. List the ways to split the straw in an orderly way and test each.
The longest piece must be shorter than half of 12 cm, so it can be at most 5 cm. Start with a longest piece of 5 cm and find the other two.

Similar problem: a 10 cm straw. The longest piece must be less than 5 cm, so try 4 cm: the other two add up to 6 cm, giving 2, 4, 4 and 3, 3, 4. A longest piece of 3 cm would need the others to add up to 7 cm, which is too much. So a 10 cm straw gives 2 triangles.

stepByStep.text: The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, so the longest side is less than 6 cm.
Longest side 5 cm: the other two add up to 7 cm. They can be 2 cm and 5 cm, or 3 cm and 4 cm.
Longest side 4 cm: the other two add up to 8 cm, so they must be 4 cm and 4 cm.
A longest side of 3 cm or less cannot reach a total of 12 cm.
So Meera can make 3 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Only 2, 5, 5 and 3, 4, 5 and 4, 4, 4 close up into a triangle, which makes 3.
misconceptions.B: This counts every way to split 12 into three pieces. Many of them, like 1, 1, 10, cannot close up into a triangle. Test each split.
misconceptions.C: This also counts 1, 5, 6 and 2, 4, 6 and 3, 3, 6. In those, the two short pieces only just reach along the long one and lie flat. They need to be longer.
misconceptions.D: Good try! Check your list once more: one of your four may have two short pieces that add up to exactly the long piece.

G4A_TRIANGLES_017.questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 11 cm long. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths can the third side have?
hints: The third side cannot be too short or too long. Find the shortest and the longest whole number it can be, then count carefully.
The third side must be longer than 11 - 6 and shorter than 11 + 6. Decide whether those two end numbers themselves are allowed.
Similar problem: sides of 4 cm and 9 cm. The third side must be more than 5 cm and less than 13 cm, so it can be 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12 cm. That is 7 different lengths.

stepByStep.text: The third side must be longer than the difference of the other two.
The third side must be shorter than the sum of the other two.
A side of exactly 5 cm or exactly 17 cm would make the three sides lie flat, so the third side can be 6 cm up to 16 cm.
Count the whole numbers from 6 to 16.
So the third side can have 11 different lengths.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 cm and 17 cm too. With those lengths the sides lie flat in a line and no triangle is made.
misconceptions.B: This is 17 - 5. Subtracting does not count the whole numbers strictly between 5 and 17. Try listing them.
misconceptions.C: Almost! Count again from 6 up to 16, pointing at each number once.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The third side can be any whole number from 6 cm to 16 cm, and that is 11 lengths.

G4A_TRIANGLES_018.questionText: In an isosceles triangle, one angle is 4 times another angle. The triangle has no obtuse angle. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The equal angles could be the two small ones or the two big ones. Try both and see which fits everything the question says.
Call the small angle one part. Then the angles are either 1, 1 and 4 parts, or 1, 4 and 4 parts. All the parts together make 180°.

Similar problem: in an isosceles triangle one angle is 2 times another and no angle is a right angle. Parts 1, 1, 2 give 45°, 45°, 90°, which has a right angle. Parts 1, 2, 2 give 5 parts = 180°, so one part is 36°. The smallest angle is 36°.

stepByStep.text: First case: the two equal angles are the small ones. The parts are 1, 1 and 4.
That gives 30°, 30° and 120°. But 120° is obtuse, so this case is not allowed.
Second case: the two equal angles are the big ones. The parts are 1, 4 and 4.
That gives 20°, 80° and 80°. No angle is obtuse, so this is the triangle.
So the smallest angle is 20°.

misconceptions.A: This comes from angles of 30°, 30° and 120°. Look at the 120°: the question says there is no obtuse angle. Try the other case.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! The angles are 20°, 80° and 80°: one is 4 times another and none is obtuse.
misconceptions.C: This divides 180° by 5, as if there were only two angles. A triangle has three angles, and two of them are equal.
misconceptions.D: With 45° the equal angles would be 45° and 45°, leaving 90°. Is any angle then 4 times another? Try using parts.

G4A_TRIANGLES_019.questionText: Two triangles are both isosceles, and each of them has an angle of 40°. The two triangles do not have the same set of angles. What is the difference between the largest angle of one triangle and the largest angle of the other?
hints: In an isosceles triangle, a given angle can be one of the two equal angles, or it can be the angle that is different. That gives two different triangles.
First let 40° be one of the two equal angles and find the third angle. Then let 40° be the different angle and find the two equal ones.

Similar problem with 20°: if 20° is one of the equal angles, the angles are 20°, 20°, 140°. If 20° is the different angle, the others are 80° each. The largest angles are 140° and 80°, and their difference is 60°.

stepByStep.text: If 40° is one of the two equal angles, the third angle is what is left from 180°.
If 40° is the different angle, the two equal angles share what is left.
So the triangles have angles 40°, 40°, 100° and 40°, 70°, 70°.
Subtract the two largest angles.
So the difference between the two largest angles is 30°.

misconceptions.A: This is 100° - 40°, the difference inside one triangle. The question asks about the largest angle of each of the two triangles.
misconceptions.B: 100° is the largest angle of one triangle. Now find the largest angle of the other triangle and subtract.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The largest angles are 100° and 70°, and 100 - 70 = 30.
misconceptions.D: 70° is the largest angle of one triangle. Find the largest angle of the other one and take the difference.

G4A_TRIANGLES_020.questionText: An isosceles triangle has one side of 5 cm and another side of 11 cm. What is its perimeter?
hints: The third side must be equal to one of the two sides you know. Try each choice, and check that the three sides can really make a triangle.
If the third side is 5 cm, the sides are 5, 5 and 11. Add the two short sides and compare with the long side.
Similar problem: an isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm and 9 cm. Sides 4, 4, 9 cannot meet because 4 + 4 is less than 9. Sides 4, 9, 9 can. The perimeter is 4 + 9 + 9 = 22 cm.

stepByStep.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, so the third side is either 5 cm or 11 cm.
Try 5 cm: the two short sides together must be longer than the longest side.
10 cm is shorter than 11 cm, so sides of 5, 5 and 11 cannot make a triangle.
So the third side is 11 cm. Add the three sides.
So the perimeter is 27 cm.

misconceptions.A: Exactly right! The sides must be 5 cm, 11 cm and 11 cm, which add up to 27 cm.
misconceptions.B: This uses sides 5, 5 and 11. Try to picture it: the two 5 cm sides together are only 10 cm, so they cannot reach across the 11 cm side.
misconceptions.C: This adds only the two sides given. A triangle has three sides, so find the third one first.
misconceptions.D: This adds 5 + 5 + 11 + 11, which is four sides. A triangle has only three. Decide which length is repeated.

G4A_TRIANGLES_021.questionText: Aman has a big box of sticks. Every stick is 3 cm, 4 cm or 8 cm long, and there are plenty of each length. He makes a triangle using three sticks as its three sides. The sticks may have the same length. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way to choose three lengths: all the same, two the same, and all different. Then test each choice to see whether it can really make a triangle.
Start with the three choices where all sticks are equal. Then take two equal sticks with one different stick, and check that the two shorter sticks together are longer than the longest.
Similar problem: sticks of 2 cm and 5 cm only. The choices are 2, 2, 2 and 5, 5, 5 and 2, 2, 5 and 2, 5, 5. In 2, 2, 5 the short sticks add up to only 4 cm, so it is out. That leaves 3 triangles.

stepByStep.text: All three sticks equal: 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 4 and 8, 8, 8. All three make triangles.
Two equal and one different: 3, 3, 4 and 3, 4, 4 and 3, 8, 8 and 4, 8, 8 make triangles.
But 3, 3, 8 and 4, 4, 8 do not, because the two short sticks are not longer than the long one.
All different: 3, 4, 8 does not make a triangle either.
Count the choices that are left.
So Aman can make 7 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: Lovely work! Three equal-sided triangles and four with two equal sides make 7.
misconceptions.B: This counts every choice of three sticks. Test 3, 3, 8 and 3, 4, 8 and 4, 4, 8: can the short sticks reach across the 8 cm stick?
misconceptions.C: Nearly there! Look again at 4, 4, 8. The two 4 cm sticks add up to exactly 8 cm, so they lie flat along the long stick.
misconceptions.D: These are only the triangles with three equal sticks. Aman may also mix lengths, such as 3, 3, 4.

G4A_TRIANGLES_022.questionText: The three angles of a triangle are whole numbers of degrees, and all three are different. What is the largest size the smallest angle can have?
hints: To make the smallest angle as big as possible, the three angles should be as close to each other as they can be while staying different.
If all three were equal they would be 60° each. They must be different, so think about three whole numbers very close to 60 that add up to 180.
Similar problem: three different whole numbers add up to 30. Equal shares would be 10 each. The closest different numbers are 9, 10 and 11, so the smallest can be at most 9.

stepByStep.text: If the three angles were equal, each would be 60°.
The angles must be different, so the smallest must be less than 60°.
Try 59° for the smallest. The other two must add up to 121°, and 60° and 61° do that.
So the largest size the smallest angle can have is 59°.

misconceptions.A: A smallest angle of 60° would force all three angles to be 60°. The question says all three are different.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Angles of 59°, 60° and 61° are all different and add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: Angles like 58°, 60° and 62° do fit, but the smallest can be a little bigger than this. Try 59°.
misconceptions.D: If the smallest angle were 89°, the other two would each be at least 90°, and the total would pass 180°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_023.questionText: Which of these statements is true for every triangle?

options.text: Its largest angle is more than 60°
It has at least two acute angles
Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90°
Exactly one of its angles is 60° or more

hints: A statement is true for every triangle only if no triangle at all breaks it. For each statement, try to think of a triangle that breaks it.
Test each statement on some special triangles: the equilateral triangle, a right-angled triangle, and an isosceles triangle with angles 40°, 70°, 70°.

Similar problem: is 'every triangle has an angle of less than 60°' always true? Test the equilateral triangle: its angles are 60°, 60°, 60°, and none is less than 60°. One triangle that breaks the statement is enough, so it is not always true.

stepByStep.text: The equilateral triangle has angles 60°, 60°, 60°. Its largest angle is not more than 60°, and its two smallest angles add up to 120°.
A triangle with angles 40°, 70°, 70° has two angles of 60° or more, not exactly one.
Could a triangle have two angles that are not acute? Two angles of 90° or more already use up the whole 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle.
So at most one angle can be right or obtuse, and the other two must be acute.
The statement true for every triangle is: it has at least two acute angles.

misconceptions.A: This is true for almost every triangle. Check the equilateral triangle: its largest angle is exactly 60°, not more.
misconceptions.B: Well reasoned! Two angles of 90° or more would leave nothing for the third angle, so two angles are always acute.
misconceptions.C: This holds for obtuse-angled triangles only. Try 60°, 60°, 60°: the two smallest angles add up to 120°.
misconceptions.D: Try a triangle with angles 40°, 70° and 70°. How many of its angles are 60° or more?

G4A_TRIANGLES_024.questionText: Five equilateral triangles, each with sides of 4 cm, are placed in a row. The first points up, the second points down, the third points up, and so on. Each triangle shares one whole side with the next triangle, so together they make one flat shape with no gaps. What is the perimeter of this shape?
hints: The perimeter is only the outside edge. Every side that two triangles share is inside the shape, and it is hidden for both of those triangles.
Count how many sides are shared between neighbours in a row of five triangles. Each shared side removes one side from each of two triangles.

Similar problem: three equilateral triangles of side 5 cm in a row. All sides together make 9 sides. There are 2 shared sides, and each hides 2 sides, so 9 - 4 = 5 sides stay outside. The perimeter is 5 x 5 = 25 cm.

stepByStep.text: Five separate triangles have 15 sides in all.
In a row of five triangles there are 4 places where two neighbours share a side.
Each shared side hides one side of each neighbour, so 8 sides are hidden.
Count the sides left on the outside and multiply by 4 cm.
So the perimeter of the shape is 28 cm.

misconceptions.A: This is the total of all five separate perimeters. Once the triangles are joined, the shared sides are inside the shape.
misconceptions.B: Good try! This takes away each shared side once. A shared side belongs to two triangles, so it must come off twice.
misconceptions.C: This takes away one side too few. Count again: 15 sides in all, and 8 of them are hidden inside.
misconceptions.D: Wonderful! Seven sides of 4 cm stay on the outside, and 7 x 4 = 28.

G4A_TRIANGLES_025.questionText: The sides of a triangle are three consecutive whole numbers of centimetres, such as 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. What is the smallest perimeter such a triangle can have?
hints: Start from the smallest consecutive numbers, but check each time that the three lengths can really close up into a triangle.
Try 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm first. Add the two shorter sides and compare the total with the longest side.

Similar problem: the sides are three consecutive even numbers. Try 2, 4, 6: 2 + 4 is only equal to 6, so they lie flat. Try 4, 6, 8: 4 + 6 = 10 is more than 8, so it is a triangle. The smallest perimeter is 4 + 6 + 8 = 18 cm.

stepByStep.text: Try the smallest set, 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm. The two shorter sides only equal the longest side, so they lie flat.
Try the next set, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. The two shorter sides are longer than the longest side.
So 2, 3, 4 is the smallest such triangle. Add its sides.
So the smallest perimeter is 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: This is 1 + 2 + 3. Check those sides: 1 cm and 2 cm together only just reach along the 3 cm side, so no triangle is made.
misconceptions.B: Sides of 3, 4 and 5 cm do make a triangle, but there is a smaller set that works too. Try 2, 3, 4.
misconceptions.C: A perimeter of 3 cm would need sides of 1, 1 and 1 cm, and those are not consecutive numbers.
misconceptions.D: Spot on! 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm is the smallest set that closes up, and 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.

G4A_TRIANGLES_026.questionText: The perimeter of a triangle is 30 cm, and each side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length its longest side can have?
hints: The longest side cannot take too much of the perimeter. The other two sides together must still be longer than it.
Suppose the longest side is 15 cm. Work out what is left for the other two sides together, and compare.

Similar problem: perimeter 20 cm. If the longest side were 10 cm, the other two would add up to 10 cm and lie flat. With 9 cm, the other two add up to 11 cm, which is more. So the greatest longest side is 9 cm.

stepByStep.text: The other two sides together must be longer than the longest side.
Try 15 cm. The other two sides add up to 15 cm, which is only equal, so they lie flat.
Try 14 cm. The other two sides add up to 16 cm, which is more than 14 cm.
Sides such as 14 cm, 14 cm and 2 cm make a real triangle.
So the greatest length of the longest side is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: This leaves only 1 cm and 1 cm for the other sides. Two tiny sides cannot reach across a 28 cm side.
misconceptions.B: Yes! With 14 cm, the other two sides share 16 cm, which is just enough to close the triangle.
misconceptions.C: So close! With 15 cm, the other two sides add up to exactly 15 cm. They need to be longer than the longest side.
misconceptions.D: 10 cm is the side of the equilateral triangle. The longest side can be made bigger than that. How big, before the others cannot reach?

G4A_TRIANGLES_027.questionText: A triangle is right-angled. One of its angles is 4 times another of its angles, and all three angles are whole numbers of degrees. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: One angle is 90°. Decide which two angles are in the '4 times' relation: could the right angle be one of them? Use the clue about whole numbers.
If 90° were 4 times another angle, that angle would be 90 ÷ 4. Check whether that is a whole number. If not, the relation is between the two acute angles.

Similar problem: in a right-angled triangle, one acute angle is 5 times the other acute angle. The two acute angles add up to 90°, and they make 6 equal parts. One part is 90 ÷ 6 = 15°, so the angles are 15°, 75° and 90°.

stepByStep.text: If the right angle were 4 times another angle, that angle would not be a whole number.
So the relation is between the two acute angles. Together they make 90°.
One acute angle is 1 part and the other is 4 parts, 5 parts in all.
The angles are 18°, 72° and 90°.
So the smallest angle is 18°.

misconceptions.A: Excellent! The acute angles are 18° and 72°, and 72 is 4 times 18.
misconceptions.B: This is 90° divided by 4. The question says every angle is a whole number of degrees, so the right angle is not the one that is 4 times another.
misconceptions.C: This divides the full 180° into 5 parts. One angle is already 90°, so only the other 90° is shared between the two acute angles.
misconceptions.D: 72° is one of the angles, but it is the bigger acute angle. The question asks for the smallest angle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_028.questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 9 cm and 4 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres, and the perimeter of the triangle is a multiple of 7. How long is the third side?
hints: Two things must both be true: the three sides must be able to make a triangle, and the perimeter must be in the 7 times table. Find the possible third sides first.
The third side must be more than 9 - 4 and less than 9 + 4. For each allowed length, the perimeter is 13 plus that length.

Similar problem: sides 5 cm and 8 cm, perimeter a multiple of 10. The third side is between 3 cm and 13 cm, so the perimeter is between 16 cm and 26 cm. The only multiple of 10 there is 20, so the third side is 20 - 13 = 7 cm.

stepByStep.text: The third side must be more than 5 cm and less than 13 cm.
So the third side is from 6 cm to 12 cm, and the perimeter is from 19 cm to 25 cm.
The only multiple of 7 from 19 to 25 is 21.
Take away the two known sides.
So the third side is 8 cm.

misconceptions.A: A 1 cm side gives a perimeter of 14 cm, which is a multiple of 7. But can 1 cm and 4 cm together reach across the 9 cm side?
misconceptions.B: A 15 cm side gives a perimeter of 28 cm. But 9 cm and 4 cm together are only 13 cm, too short to meet across 15 cm.
misconceptions.C: Super! Sides of 9, 4 and 8 cm make a triangle, and the perimeter is 21 cm, which is 7 x 3.
misconceptions.D: The perimeter must be a multiple of 7, not the side itself. With a 7 cm side the perimeter would be 20 cm.

G4A_TRIANGLES_029.questionText: Triangle ABC is isosceles. Angle A is 50°. Angle B is bigger than angle A and also bigger than angle C. What is angle C?
hints: In an isosceles triangle two angles are equal. There are three ways to choose the equal pair. Test each one against what the question says about angle B.
Angle B is bigger than both other angles, so angle B cannot be one of the equal pair. Which two angles must be equal, then?

Similar problem: triangle PQR is isosceles, angle P is 40°, and angle Q is bigger than both other angles. Angle Q cannot be in the equal pair, so angle R equals angle P, which is 40°. Then angle Q is 180 - 40 - 40 = 100°.

stepByStep.text: Angle B is bigger than each of the other two, so angle B is not equal to either of them.
The equal pair must be angle A and angle C.
So angle C is 50°, and angle B is what is left.
Check: 80° is bigger than 50°, as the question says.
So angle C is 50°.

misconceptions.A: This shares the remaining 130° equally between angle B and angle C. Then angle B would be equal to angle C, not bigger than it.
misconceptions.B: 80° is the size of angle B in this triangle. The question asks for angle C.
misconceptions.C: 130° is what is left for angle B and angle C together. Angle C is only part of that.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Angle B is the odd one out, so angle C matches angle A at 50°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_030.questionText: Two angles of a triangle add up to 110°. The bigger of these two angles is 30° more than the smaller one. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: To name a triangle you need all three angles. Find the two angles described, then do not forget the third one.
Take the extra 30° away from 110°. What is left is twice the smaller angle.

Similar problem: two angles add up to 100° and differ by 20°. Taking 20 from 100 leaves 80, so the smaller is 40° and the bigger is 60°. The third angle is 180 - 100 = 80°. All three are different, so that triangle is scalene.

stepByStep.text: Take away the extra 30°. What is left is two equal shares.
So the two angles are 40° and 70°.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 40°, 70° and 70°. Two of them are equal.
So it is an isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: The two angles described, 70° and 40°, are different. Now find the third angle and compare it with them.
misconceptions.B: A right-angled triangle needs an angle of 90°. Work out all three angles and check.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The angles are 40°, 70° and 70°, and two equal angles make the triangle isosceles.
misconceptions.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°. Here the two angles described differ by 30°.

G4A_UNITS_001.questionText: A cycle track is 4 km 75 m long. What is its length in kilometres?
hints: Kilometres are bigger than metres, so the metres become a decimal part of a kilometre. Remember how many metres make 1 km.
1 km = 1000 m, so divide the 75 m by 1000 to turn it into kilometres. Then join it to the 4 km.
A similar one: 2 km 40 m. 40 ÷ 1000 = 0.04, so 2 km 40 m = 2.04 km.

stepByStep.text: 1 km = 1000 m, so to change metres into kilometres we divide by 1000.
Change the 75 m into kilometres.
Add the 4 whole kilometres. The track is 4.075 km long.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 75 m is 75 thousandths of a kilometre, which is 0.075 km, so the track is 4.075 km long.
misconceptions.B: This treats 75 m as 0.75 km, but 0.75 km is 750 m. Since 1 km has 1000 m, 75 m needs three decimal places: 0.075.
misconceptions.C: This puts one zero too many after the point. 75 m out of 1000 m is 0.075 km, not 0.0075 km.
misconceptions.D: The whole kilometres must stay as 4. Only the 75 m changes into a decimal part of a kilometre: 75 ÷ 1000.

G4A_UNITS_002.questionText: Meera's water bottle holds 1.2 litres. She drinks 350 ml. How many millilitres of water are left in the bottle?
hints: The two amounts are in different units. Make the units the same before you subtract.
Change 1.2 litres into millilitres: multiply by 1000. Then take away what Meera drank.
A similar one: a jug holds 1.5 litres and 400 ml is poured out. 1.5 litres = 1500 ml, and 1500 − 400 = 1100 ml are left.

stepByStep.text: Change litres into millilitres: 1 litre = 1000 ml.
Take away the 350 ml that Meera drank.
850 ml of water are left in the bottle.

misconceptions.A: This adds the 350 ml. Meera drank that water, so take it away from 1200 ml.
misconceptions.B: This reads 1.2 litres as 1020 ml. But 0.2 litre is 200 ml, so 1.2 litres is 1200 ml.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 1.2 litres is 1200 ml, and 1200 − 350 = 850 ml.
misconceptions.D: Changing 1.2 litres to 1200 ml is the right start. Check the subtraction once more: 1200 − 350 leaves 850.

G4A_UNITS_003.questionText: A new pencil is 14 cm 6 mm long. After a month of sharpening it is 12 cm 9 mm long. How many millimetres shorter has it become?
hints: Both lengths mix centimetres and millimetres. It is easiest to write each one in millimetres only.
1 cm = 10 mm, so 14 cm 6 mm = 140 mm + 6 mm. Do the same for the other length, then subtract.
A similar one: 9 cm 2 mm − 7 cm 8 mm. That is 92 mm − 78 mm = 14 mm.

stepByStep.text: Change the first length into millimetres.
Change the second length into millimetres.
Subtract. The pencil has become 17 mm shorter.

misconceptions.A: This takes 12 cm from 14 cm and 6 mm from 9 mm. The 9 mm belongs to the shorter pencil, so change both lengths fully into millimetres first: 146 and 129.
misconceptions.B: Close! When 9 mm cannot be taken from 6 mm, one centimetre is borrowed, so only 1 cm is left over, not 2 cm. 146 − 129 = 17.
misconceptions.C: This looks only at the millimetre parts. The centimetres matter too: 14 cm 6 mm is 146 mm and 12 cm 9 mm is 129 mm.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! 146 mm − 129 mm = 17 mm.

G4A_UNITS_004.questionText: Amma buys 1 kg 750 g of potatoes and 2 kg 400 g of onions. What is the total weight of the vegetables in kilograms?
hints: Add kilograms to kilograms and grams to grams. Watch out if the grams come to more than 1000.
750 g + 400 g = 1150 g. Think about how many kilograms and grams that is.
A similar one: 2 kg 600 g + 1 kg 900 g. The grams make 1500 g = 1 kg 500 g, so the total is 4 kg 500 g = 4.5 kg.

stepByStep.text: Add the grams.
1150 g is 1 kg 150 g. Add the kilograms, with the 1 kg carried over.
The total is 4 kg 150 g. Since 150 g = 0.15 kg, the vegetables weigh 4.15 kg.

misconceptions.A: The grams add up to 1150 g, which is more than 1 kg. That extra kilogram must be carried over to the kilograms.
misconceptions.C: The total is 4 kg 150 g. 150 g is 0.150 kg, so it is written 4.15 kg, not 4.015 kg.
misconceptions.D: This writes 3 kg and 1150 g side by side. 1150 g is 1 kg 150 g, so the total is 4 kg 150 g.

G4A_UNITS_005.questionText: A fruit seller has 7 dozen bananas. He sells 3 score bananas. How many bananas are left?
hints: Dozen and score are names for fixed numbers. Change both into plain numbers of bananas first.
1 dozen = 12, so find 7 × 12. 1 score = 20, so find 3 × 20.
A similar one: 5 dozen eggs, and 2 score are sold. 5 × 12 = 60 and 2 × 20 = 40, so 60 − 40 = 20 eggs are left.

stepByStep.text: 1 dozen = 12.
1 score = 20.
Subtract the bananas sold. 24 bananas are left.

misconceptions.A: This counts a score as 12. A dozen is 12, but a score is 20, so 3 score is 60 bananas.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 7 dozen is 84 and 3 score is 60, and 84 − 60 = 24.
misconceptions.C: This counts a score as 10. A score is 20, so 3 score is 60 bananas.
misconceptions.D: This adds the bananas sold. They have gone, so take 60 away from 84.

G4A_UNITS_006.questionText: A box holds 1 gross of pencils. A teacher takes pencils from it and gives 2 pencils to each of 54 children. How many pencils remain in the box?
hints: A gross is a fixed number, like a dozen. Find how many pencils are in the box and how many are given out.
1 gross = 12 dozen = 144. Now work out 54 × 2.
A similar one: from 1 gross of erasers, 3 are given to each of 40 children. 40 × 3 = 120, and 144 − 120 = 24 remain.

stepByStep.text: 1 gross = 12 dozen.
Pencils given to the children.
Subtract. 36 pencils remain in the box.

misconceptions.A: This gives only 1 pencil to each child. Each child gets 2, so 54 × 2 = 108 pencils are given away.
misconceptions.B: This counts a gross as 120. A gross is 12 dozen, which is 144.
misconceptions.C: The plan is right: 144 − 108. Check the subtraction once more and you will get 36.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 1 gross is 144, the children get 108, and 144 − 108 = 36.

G4A_UNITS_007.questionText: A milkman pours 750 ml of milk into each of 6 packets. How many litres of milk does he use?
hints: First find the total in millilitres, then change it into litres.
Work out 6 × 750. Then remember that 1000 ml make 1 litre.
A similar one: 8 cups of 250 ml each. 8 × 250 = 2000 ml, and 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 litres.

stepByStep.text: Find the total milk in millilitres.
Change into litres: 1000 ml = 1 litre.
The milkman uses 4.5 litres of milk.

misconceptions.A: Great! 6 × 750 ml = 4500 ml, and 4500 ÷ 1000 = 4.5 litres.
misconceptions.B: 6 × 750 = 4500 ml. To change millilitres into litres divide by 1000, not by 100.
misconceptions.C: 6 × 750 = 4500 ml. Dividing by 1000 gives 4.5, so check where the decimal point goes.
misconceptions.D: 4500 is the number of millilitres. The question asks for litres, so divide by 1000.

G4A_UNITS_008.questionText: Ravi's school is 850 m from his home. He walks to school and back on each of the 5 school days. How many kilometres does he walk in the week?
hints: Find how far Ravi walks in one day, then in five days. Change to kilometres at the end.
To school and back is 850 m two times. Work out 850 × 2 first.
A similar one: a park is 600 m away and Tara goes there and back on 4 days. 600 × 2 = 1200 m a day, and 1200 × 4 = 4800 m = 4.8 km.

stepByStep.text: Distance in one day, there and back.
Distance in 5 days.
Change metres into kilometres. Ravi walks 8.5 km in the week.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the walk to school. Ravi also walks back, so each day he walks 850 m twice.
misconceptions.B: The total is 8500 m. Dividing by 1000 gives 8.5 km, so check the decimal point.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 850 × 2 = 1700 m a day, 1700 × 5 = 8500 m in the week, and that is 8.5 km.
misconceptions.D: This is the distance for one day. There are 5 school days, so multiply by 5.

G4A_UNITS_009.questionText: A carpenter cuts a plank 3 m long into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece in centimetres?
hints: The answer is wanted in centimetres, so change the plank's length into centimetres before sharing it.
3 m = 300 cm. Now divide 300 by 8.
A similar one: a 2 m ribbon cut into 8 equal pieces. 2 m = 200 cm, and 200 ÷ 8 = 25 cm each.

stepByStep.text: Change metres into centimetres: 1 m = 100 cm.
Share equally among 8 pieces.
Each piece is 37.5 cm long.

misconceptions.B: One piece cannot be longer than the whole plank of 300 cm. 300 ÷ 8 = 37.5.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 3 m = 300 cm, and 300 ÷ 8 = 37.5 cm.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 3 by 8. The plank is being cut into pieces, so change 3 m into 300 cm and divide by 8.

G4A_UNITS_010.questionText: A stack of 40 equal coins is 6 cm tall. How thick is one coin, in millimetres?
hints: All 40 coins together make the height of the stack. Change the height into millimetres, then share it.
6 cm = 60 mm. Now divide 60 by 40.
A similar one: 20 coins make a stack 5 cm tall. 5 cm = 50 mm, and 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 mm for each coin.

stepByStep.text: Change centimetres into millimetres: 1 cm = 10 mm.
Share the height among 40 coins.
One coin is 1.5 mm thick.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 6 cm = 60 mm, and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 mm for each coin.
misconceptions.B: Forty coins that are each 15 mm thick would make a stack 600 mm tall. 6 cm is only 60 mm, and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5.
misconceptions.C: This divides 6 by 40 without changing centimetres into millimetres. 6 cm = 60 mm, and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5.
misconceptions.D: This comes from multiplying 6 and 40. The stack's height is shared among the coins, so divide 60 mm by 40.

G4A_UNITS_011.questionText: Which of these lengths is the greatest?
hints: Lengths can be compared only when they are in the same unit. Metres is a good choice here.
Change each length into metres. For example, 1.08 km = 1.08 × 1000 m.
A similar one: which is greater, 2.5 km or 2 km 60 m? 2.5 km = 2500 m and 2 km 60 m = 2060 m, so 2.5 km is greater.

stepByStep.text: Change each length into metres: 1.08 km = 1080 m and 1 km 800 m = 1800 m.
1008 m is already in metres, and 10800 cm = 108 m.
Compare 1080, 1800, 1008 and 108. The greatest is 1800 m, which is 1 km 800 m.

misconceptions.A: 1.08 km is 1080 m. That is less than 1 km 800 m, which is 1800 m.
misconceptions.B: Yes! In metres the four lengths are 1800 m, 1080 m, 1008 m and 108 m, so 1 km 800 m is the greatest.
misconceptions.C: 1008 m is only a little more than 1 km. 1 km 800 m is 1800 m, which is greater.
misconceptions.D: The number looks big, but centimetres are small. 10800 cm is only 108 m.

G4A_UNITS_012.questionText: One tablet contains 250 mg of medicine. How many grams of medicine are there in a strip of 10 tablets?
hints: Find the total in milligrams first, then change it into grams.
10 × 250 = 2500 mg. Remember that 1000 mg make 1 g.
A similar one: 4 tablets of 500 mg each. 4 × 500 = 2000 mg, and 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 g.

stepByStep.text: Medicine in 10 tablets, in milligrams.
Change milligrams into grams: 1000 mg = 1 g.
The strip contains 2.5 g of medicine.

misconceptions.A: 10 × 250 = 2500 mg. To change milligrams into grams divide by 1000, not by 100.
misconceptions.B: This is the medicine in one tablet: 250 mg = 0.25 g. The strip has 10 tablets.
misconceptions.C: 2500 is the number of milligrams. Divide by 1000 to change it into grams.

G4A_UNITS_013.questionText: A tailor has 5 m of cloth. He uses 2 m 35 cm to stitch a kurta. How much cloth is left?
hints: This is a subtraction of lengths. It helps to write both lengths in centimetres.
5 m = 500 cm and 2 m 35 cm = 235 cm. Now subtract.
A similar one: 4 m − 1 m 20 cm. That is 400 cm − 120 cm = 280 cm, which is 2 m 80 cm.

stepByStep.text: Write both lengths in centimetres: 5 m = 500 cm and 2 m 35 cm = 235 cm.
Subtract.
265 cm is 2 m 65 cm. So 2 m 65 cm of cloth is left.

misconceptions.A: This takes away only the 2 m and keeps the 35 cm. The 35 cm must be taken away as well.
misconceptions.B: 100 − 35 = 65 is right, but one of the 5 metres was changed into 100 cm, so only 4 − 2 = 2 whole metres are left.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two lengths. The cloth was used up, so subtract.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 500 cm − 235 cm = 265 cm, which is 2 m 65 cm.

G4A_UNITS_014.questionText: A running track is 4 hectometres long. Sunil runs 5 rounds of the track. How many kilometres does he run?
hints: Change hectometres into metres first. 'Hecto' means one hundred.
1 hectometre = 100 m, so one round is 4 × 100 m. Then find 5 rounds.
A similar one: a path is 3 hectometres long and Riya walks it 10 times. 3 × 100 = 300 m, and 300 × 10 = 3000 m = 3 km.

stepByStep.text: 1 hectometre = 100 m. Find the length of one round in metres.
Distance for 5 rounds.
Change metres into kilometres. Sunil runs 2 km.

misconceptions.A: This takes a hectometre as 1000 m. A hectometre is 100 m, so one round is 400 m.
misconceptions.B: Great! One round is 400 m, 5 rounds are 2000 m, and 2000 m is 2 km.
misconceptions.C: This takes a hectometre as 10 m. A hectometre is 100 m, so one round is 400 m.
